      "body": "# LP Optimum ↔ Game-Theoretic Optimal Strategy\n\n**Theorem.** Let $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ be a finite matrix\ngame with value $\\operatorname{val}(A) \\in \\mathbb{R}$\n([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.value]]).\n\n1. The pair $(x^*, v^*)$ is optimal for player 1's LP\n   ([[math.linear_programming.minimax_bridge.player_1_lp]]) **if and only if** $x^*$ is a maxmin\n   (optimal) mixed strategy for player 1 and $v^* = \\operatorname{val}(A)$.\n\n2. The pair $(y^*, w^*)$ is optimal for player 2's LP\n   ([[math.linear_programming.minimax_bridge.player_2_lp]]) **if and only if** $y^*$ is a minmax\n   (optimal) mixed strategy for player 2 and $w^* = \\operatorname{val}(A)$.\n\n3. Any pair $(x^*, y^*)$ obtained from LP optima is a saddle point of\n   $A$ ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.saddle_point]]); conversely every saddle point\n   gives optimal LP solutions.\n\n## Proof\n\n**(⇒)** *LP optimum gives optimal strategy.* If $(x^*, v^*)$ is\noptimal for player 1's LP, then by the constraint\n$xA \\ge v^* \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_J$ at $(x^*, v^*)$, player 1's mixed\nstrategy $x^*$ guarantees at least $v^*$ against every pure column,\nhence against every mixed column. By LP-duality with\n[[math.linear_programming.minimax_bridge.player_2_lp]] and\n[[math.linear_programming.strong_duality]], $v^* = w^*$ equals the LP\ncommon value, which is also $\\operatorname{val}(A)$ by the standard\nmaxmin-minmax characterisation.\n\n**(⇐)** *Optimal strategy gives LP optimum.* If $x^*$ achieves\n$\\max_x \\min_j (xA)_j = \\operatorname{val}(A)$, then\n$(x^*, \\operatorname{val}(A))$ satisfies all LP constraints and\nattains the objective at $v = \\operatorname{val}(A)$. Symmetric for\nplayer 2.\n\nThe saddle-point statement (3) follows by combining (1) and (2):\noptimal $(x^*, y^*)$ jointly satisfy\n$x^* A \\ge \\operatorname{val}(A) \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_J$ and\n$A y^* \\le \\operatorname{val}(A) \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_I$, which is exactly\nthe saddle-point characterisation\n([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.optimal_pairs_are_saddle_points]]).\n\n## Significance\n\nThis theorem is the *clean conversion* between the LP and game-theoretic\nviewpoints:\n\n- **Algorithmically**, it lets us compute optimal mixed strategies with\n  any LP solver (simplex, interior-point, ...) — the entire\n  computational complexity of zero-sum games is exactly the LP\n  complexity.\n- **Mathematically**, it says LP-duality and the minimax theorem are\n  equivalent statements\n  ([[math.minimax.lp_duality_minimax_proof]]).\n- **Structurally**, support and strong-complementarity properties\n  ([[math.minimax.support_complementarity]],\n  [[math.minimax.strong_complementarity]]) transfer cleanly\n  between the two pictures.\n\n## References\n\n- [AGT Section 1.4.2, Thm. 1.11] Nisan, Roughgarden, Tardos, and Vazirani,\n  *Algorithmic Game Theory*.\n- [MFoGT Section 2.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Player-1 LP Formulation of a Matrix Game\n\nFor a matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ played row-by-column,\nthe **player-1 (maxmin) linear program** seeks a mixed strategy\n$x \\in \\Delta(I)$ ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.mixed_strategy_simplex]]) and a\nscalar $v$ such that every pure column response of player 2 yields at\nleast $v$:\n\n$$\n\\boxed{\\begin{aligned}\n\\text{maximise} \\quad & v \\\\\n\\text{subject to} \\quad & \\sum_{i \\in I} x_i \\, A_{ij} \\;\\ge\\; v &&\\text{for every } j \\in J, \\\\\n                & \\sum_{i \\in I} x_i = 1, \\\\\n                & x_i \\ge 0 &&\\text{for every } i \\in I.\n\\end{aligned}}\n$$\n\nThe decision variables are $(x, v) \\in \\mathbb{R}^{I} \\times \\mathbb{R}$;\nthe constraints encode \"$x A \\ge v \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_J$\" plus probability\nnormalisation.\n\n## Standard reformulations\n\n- Eliminate $v$ via $v = \\min_j (x A)_j$; the LP becomes\n  $\\max_{x \\in \\Delta(I)} \\min_{j \\in J} (x A)_j$, which is the\n  matrix-game **maxmin** definition.\n- Add slack variables $s_j \\ge 0$ with $\\sum_i x_i A_{ij} - s_j = v$ to\n  put the LP in standard form for the simplex algorithm.\n\n## Solution interpretation\n\nAt any feasible $(x, v)$, $v$ is a *guaranteed* lower bound on player\n1's expected payoff against any pure column. At an optimal $(x^*, v^*)$:\n\n- $v^* = \\operatorname{val}(A)$ ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.value]]).\n- $x^*$ is a maxmin (Nash) strategy for player 1\n  ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.optimal_strategy_sets]]).\n\nThe dual LP corresponds to player 2's minmax LP\n([[math.linear_programming.minimax_bridge.player_2_lp]]); strong duality\n([[math.linear_programming.strong_duality]]) gives the minimax theorem\n([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [AGT Section 1.4.2] Nisan, Roughgarden, Tardos, and Vazirani,\n  *Algorithmic Game Theory*. LP formulation of matrix games.\n- [MFoGT Section 2.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.\n- Owen, G. (1995). *Game Theory*. Ch. 3 on LP and matrix games."

      "body": "# Player-2 LP Formulation of a Matrix Game\n\nFor a matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ played row-by-column,\nthe **player-2 (minmax) linear program** seeks a mixed strategy\n$y \\in \\Delta(J)$ ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.mixed_strategy_simplex]]) and a\nscalar $w$ such that every pure row response of player 1 yields at most\n$w$:\n\n$$\n\\boxed{\\begin{aligned}\n\\text{minimise} \\quad & w \\\\\n\\text{subject to} \\quad & \\sum_{j \\in J} A_{ij}\\, y_j \\;\\le\\; w &&\\text{for every } i \\in I, \\\\\n                & \\sum_{j \\in J} y_j = 1, \\\\\n                & y_j \\ge 0 &&\\text{for every } j \\in J.\n\\end{aligned}}\n$$\n\nThe constraints encode \"$A y \\le w \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_I$\" plus\nprobability normalisation on $y$.\n\n## Duality with player 1's LP\n\nThe player-2 LP is **exactly the dual** of player 1's LP\n([[math.linear_programming.minimax_bridge.player_1_lp]]) in the standard LP duality sense\n(write player 1's LP in equality / slack form; take the LP dual; the\nresult is player 2's LP after relabelling).\n\nStrong LP duality\n([[math.linear_programming.strong_duality]]) then yields:\n\n- *Feasibility on both sides*: both LPs are feasible — player 1's LP\n  has $v = \\min_j A_{ij}$ for $x = e_i$; player 2's LP has analogous\n  feasibility.\n- *Optimal value equality*: $v^* = w^* = \\operatorname{val}(A)$\n  ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.value]]) — the minimax theorem\n  ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) re-derived from LP\n  duality.\n- *Complementary slackness*: optimal solutions $(x^*, y^*)$ satisfy\n  support / complementarity conditions\n  ([[math.minimax.support_complementarity]],\n  [[math.minimax.strong_complementarity]]).\n\n## See also\n\n- [[math.linear_programming.minimax_bridge.lp_optimal_iff_optimal_strategy]] formalises the\n  bijection between LP optima and game-theoretic optimal strategies.\n- [[math.minimax.lp_duality_minimax_proof]] is the explicit\n  proof-plan turning LP duality into the matrix-game minimax theorem.\n- [[math.linear_programming.minimax_bridge.zero_sum_lp_bridge]] discusses the AGT-style\n  presentation of the same equivalence.\n\n## References\n\n- [AGT Section 1.4.2] Nisan, Roughgarden, Tardos, and Vazirani,\n  *Algorithmic Game Theory*.\n- [MFoGT Section 2.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Zero-Sum Linear Programming Bridge\n\nThe row player's maximum safe-value linear program and the column player's\nminimum safe-value dual linear program should be connected to the matrix-game\nguarantee definitions.  Once optimal row and column safe strategies are\navailable, they form a mixed Nash equilibrium of the zero-sum game.\n\nThis bridge is the natural entry point for algorithmic game theory treatments\nof zero-sum computation.\n\n*Proof.* The row LP maximizes a scalar $v$ subject to the inequalities saying\nthat the chosen mixed row strategy guarantees at least $v$ against every pure\ncolumn. The dual column LP minimizes a scalar $w$ subject to the inequalities\nsaying that the chosen mixed column strategy holds every pure row payoff to at\nmost $w$. Strong duality gives optimal solutions with $v=w$. These two sets of\ninequalities are exactly the saddle-point inequalities for the matrix payoff, so\nthe resulting mixed strategies form a zero-sum Nash equilibrium and realize the\nmatrix-game value.\n\n## References\n\n- [AGT, Section 1.4.2, Thm. 1.11] Nisan, Roughgarden, Tardos, and Vazirani, *Algorithmic Game Theory*. Optimal zero-sum LP solutions form a Nash equilibrium."

      "body": "# Strong Complementarity For Linear Programming\n\n## Setup\n\nFor the standard-form primal/dual pair over a linearly ordered field\n$\\mathbb{K}$:\n\n- **Primal** $\\mathrm{P}$: $\\min \\langle c, x\\rangle$ subject to $Ax \\ge b$ and $x \\ge 0$.\n- **Dual** $\\mathrm{D}$: $\\max \\langle u, b\\rangle$ subject to $u^{\\mathsf T} A \\le c$ and $u \\ge 0$.\n\n## Statements\n\n### Weak complementary slackness\n\nFor **every** optimal primal–dual pair $(x, u)$ (i.e. $x$ primal-feasible,\n$u$ dual-feasible, $\\langle c, x\\rangle = \\langle u, b\\rangle$), the\ncomponentwise products vanish:\n\n- for every row $i$: $u_i \\cdot (A_i x - b_i) = 0$;\n- for every column $j$: $x_j \\cdot (c_j - u^{\\mathsf T} A_j) = 0$.\n\nEquivalently, strict primal slack at row $i$ forces $u_i = 0$, and strict\ndual slack at column $j$ forces $x_j = 0$.\n\n### Strong complementary slackness\n\nIf both $\\mathrm{P}$ and $\\mathrm{D}$ are feasible (so that strong duality\ngives a matching optimal pair), then there **exist** optimal $(x^*, u^*)$\nsatisfying the strict biconditional:\n\n- for every row $i$: $(A_i x^* - b_i) > 0 \\iff u^*_i = 0$;\n- for every column $j$: $(c_j - (u^*)^{\\mathsf T} A_j) > 0 \\iff x^*_j = 0$.\n\nEquivalently, **exactly one** of each complementary pair is strictly\npositive in the strong pair. Combined with weak CS, this is the same as\nthe \"strict sum\" form\n\n$$\n  (A_i x^* - b_i) + u^*_i > 0\n  \\quad \\text{and} \\quad\n  x^*_j + (c_j - (u^*)^{\\mathsf T} A_j) > 0\n  \\quad \\text{for every } i, j,\n$$\n\nwhich is the shape stated in the Lean theorem\n`EconCSLib.LinearProgramming.exists_strong_complementary_pair`. The Lean\ntheorem is parametrized by an explicit optimal pair $(x_0, u_0)$ with\nmatching value $v$ (rather than \"P and D feasible\") to keep the lemma\nreusable; the \"feasibility\" hypothesis form follows by composing with\n[[node:math.linear_programming.strong_duality]].\n\n## Proof\n\n### Weak CS\n\nTake any optimal pair $(x, u)$. Compute\n$$\n  \\sum_i u_i\\,(A_i x - b_i) + \\sum_j x_j\\,(c_j - u^{\\mathsf T} A_j)\n   = \\langle u, Ax\\rangle - \\langle u, b\\rangle\n     + \\langle c, x\\rangle - \\langle u^{\\mathsf T} A, x\\rangle\n   = \\langle c, x\\rangle - \\langle u, b\\rangle = 0,\n$$\nusing bilinearity (the cross terms cancel) and primal/dual optimality.\nEach summand on the left is $\\ge 0$ (a nonneg variable times a nonneg\nslack), so each is exactly $0$.\n\n### Strong CS\n\nThe proof has two parts: a **per-index dichotomy** (one optimal pair\nstrictly positive on the chosen complementary pair) and an **averaging\nstep** that combines $|I| + n$ per-index pairs.\n\n**Per-row dichotomy.** Fix $i_0 \\in I$. Consider the sub-LP\n\n$$\n  \\alpha_{i_0} \\;:=\\; \\sup\\{\\,(Ax - b)_{i_0} \\;:\\; Ax \\ge b,\\; x \\ge 0,\\; \\langle c, x\\rangle \\le v^*\\,\\}\n$$\n\nwhere $v^*$ is the common primal–dual optimum. Either:\n\n- **Case A**: $\\alpha_{i_0} > 0$. Then there is a primal-optimal $x^*$\n  with $(A x^* - b)_{i_0} > 0$. Pair $(x^*, u^0)$ with any dual-optimal\n  $u^0$.\n- **Case B**: $\\alpha_{i_0} = 0$. Then $(Ax-b)_{i_0} \\le 0$ on every\n  primal-optimal $x$. Apply\n  [[node:math.linear_algebra.farkas_lemma]] to the system $\\{Ax \\ge b,\n  x \\ge 0, -\\langle c, x\\rangle \\ge -v^*\\}$ with the implied bound\n  $(Ax - b)_{i_0} \\le 0$. The Farkas certificate produces multipliers\n  $(\\mu, \\nu, \\lambda) \\ge 0$ with\n  $$\n    (\\mu + e_{i_0})^{\\mathsf T} A \\le \\lambda \\cdot c, \\quad\n    \\langle \\mu, b\\rangle + b_{i_0} \\ge \\lambda \\cdot v^*.\n  $$\n  If $\\lambda > 0$, set $u'' := (\\mu + e_{i_0})/\\lambda$: dual-feasible\n  with $u''_{i_0} \\ge 1/\\lambda > 0$ and $\\langle u'', b\\rangle \\ge v^*$.\n  If $\\lambda = 0$, set $u' := u^0 + (\\mu + e_{i_0})$ for any\n  dual-optimal $u^0$: dual-feasible with $u'_{i_0} \\ge 1 > 0$ and\n  $\\langle u', b\\rangle = v^* + \\langle \\mu, b\\rangle + b_{i_0} \\ge v^*$.\n  In each case, combined with weak duality the new $u$ is dual-optimal,\n  and pair $(x^0, u)$ with any primal-optimal $x^0$ is the desired pair.\n\n**Per-column dichotomy.** Symmetric, exchanging roles of $x$ and $u$.\n\n**Averaging.** Take the witness pairs $(x^{(i)}, u^{(i)})$ for each\n$i \\in I$ and $(x^{(j)}, u^{(j)})$ for each $j \\in \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n$ — a\ntotal of $|I| + n$ optimal pairs. Define\n\n$$\n  x^* := \\frac{1}{|I| + n} \\sum_{\\text{indices}} x^{(\\cdot)}, \\qquad\n  u^* := \\frac{1}{|I| + n} \\sum_{\\text{indices}} u^{(\\cdot)}.\n$$\n\nEach set of optimal primal (resp. dual) solutions is convex (a polytope\nin the standard-form LP), so $x^*, u^*$ are optimal. For any fixed row\n$k$, at index $i_0 = k$ we picked a pair with\n$(Ax^{(k)} - b)_k + u^{(k)}_k > 0$. Hence\n\n$$\n  (A x^* - b)_k + u^*_k \\;=\\; \\frac{1}{|I|+n} \\sum (A x^{(\\cdot)} - b)_k + u^{(\\cdot)}_k\n  \\;\\ge\\; \\frac{1}{|I|+n} \\cdot \\big((A x^{(k)} - b)_k + u^{(k)}_k\\big) > 0,\n$$\n\nwith the other terms nonneg. Symmetric for columns. So $(x^*, u^*)$ is\nstrictly complementary on every row and column pair. By weak CS, exactly\none side of each complementary pair is positive — the desired\nbiconditional. $\\square$\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The proof is purely algebraic and constructive. The dual certificates\n  in the per-index step come from\n  [[node:math.linear_algebra.farkas_lemma]] (which in turn rests on\n  Fourier–Motzkin elimination, in `EconCSLib.LinearAlgebra`).\n- Works over any linearly ordered field — same generality as\n  [[node:math.linear_programming.strong_duality]].\n- The weak-CS direction (`exactly one of each pair is positive`) is\n  immediate; the strong content is the *existence of a pair where\n  every complementary pair has at least one strict side*.\n\n## Consequences\n\n- **Matrix-game strong complementarity** (downstream node\n  `zero_sum.minimax.strong_complementarity`, [MFoGT Prop. 2.4.1(c)]): in a\n  finite zero-sum matrix game, there is an optimal pair $(x^*, y^*)$\n  with the strict biconditional `x*_i > 0 ↔ row i is a best response to y*`\n  and dually. Obtained by applying this theorem to the matrix-game LP\n  (after shifting payoffs to be positive and rescaling).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 11] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Strong complementarity\n  for feasible primal-dual linear programs."

      "body": "# Strong Duality For Linear Programming\n\n## Setup\n\nFix a linearly ordered field $\\mathbb{K}$, a finite nonempty index type $I$,\nand $n \\in \\mathbb{N}$. Let $A \\colon I \\times \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n \\to \\mathbb{K}$,\n$b \\colon I \\to \\mathbb{K}$, $c \\colon \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n \\to \\mathbb{K}$.\nConsider the **standard-form linear programming pair**:\n\n- **Primal** $\\mathrm{P}$:  $\\min \\langle c, x\\rangle$ subject to\n  $A x \\ge b$ and $x \\ge 0$ (i.e. $x_j \\ge 0$ for every $j \\in \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n$).\n- **Dual** $\\mathrm{D}$:  $\\max \\langle u, b\\rangle$ subject to\n  $u^{\\mathsf T} A \\le c$ (componentwise, i.e. $\\sum_i u_i A_{ij} \\le c_j$ for\n  every $j$) and $u \\ge 0$.\n\n## Statements\n\n**Weak duality.** For every primal-feasible $x$ and dual-feasible $u$,\n$\\langle c, x\\rangle \\ge \\langle u, b\\rangle$.\n\n**Strong duality.** If the primal is feasible and bounded below by\n$d \\in \\mathbb{K}$ (i.e. $\\langle c, x\\rangle \\ge d$ for every primal-feasible\n$x$), then there exists a dual-feasible $u$ with $\\langle u, b\\rangle \\ge d$.\n\nCombining the two yields that the optimal primal and dual values coincide when\neither exists.\n\n## Proof\n\n### Weak duality\n\nLet $x$ be primal-feasible and $u$ dual-feasible. Weighting the primal\nconstraints by $u \\ge 0$:\n$$\n  \\langle u, A x\\rangle = \\langle u^{\\mathsf T} A, x\\rangle \\le \\langle c, x\\rangle\n$$\n(using $u^{\\mathsf T} A \\le c$ and $x \\ge 0$, so weighting term by term\npreserves $\\le$). And $\\langle u, A x\\rangle \\ge \\langle u, b\\rangle$ from\n$A x \\ge b$ and $u \\ge 0$. Hence $\\langle c, x\\rangle \\ge \\langle u, b\\rangle$.\n\n### Strong duality\n\nApply the Farkas lemma ([[node:math.linear_algebra.farkas_lemma]]) to the\n**augmented system** that combines $A x \\ge b$ and $x \\ge 0$. Concretely,\ndefine $A_{\\mathrm{aug}} \\colon (I \\sqcup \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n) \\times \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n\n\\to \\mathbb{K}$ and $b_{\\mathrm{aug}} \\colon I \\sqcup \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n \\to \\mathbb{K}$\nby\n\n- $A_{\\mathrm{aug}}(\\mathrm{inl}\\,i,\\, j) = A_{i,j}$,\n  $b_{\\mathrm{aug}}(\\mathrm{inl}\\,i) = b_i$ for $i \\in I$ (the original rows);\n- $A_{\\mathrm{aug}}(\\mathrm{inr}\\,j',\\, j) = [j = j']$\n  (Kronecker delta) and $b_{\\mathrm{aug}}(\\mathrm{inr}\\,j') = 0$ for\n  $j' \\in \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n$ (the unit rows $x_{j'} \\ge 0$).\n\nPrimal feasibility coincides with feasibility of $A_{\\mathrm{aug}}\\,x \\ge\nb_{\\mathrm{aug}}$. By hypothesis, the primal is feasible and bounded below by\n$d$. Farkas yields $u_{\\mathrm{aug}} \\colon I \\sqcup \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n \\to \\mathbb{K}$\nwith $u_{\\mathrm{aug}} \\ge 0$, $u_{\\mathrm{aug}}^{\\mathsf T} A_{\\mathrm{aug}} = c$,\nand $\\langle u_{\\mathrm{aug}}, b_{\\mathrm{aug}}\\rangle \\ge d$.\n\nDecompose $u_{\\mathrm{aug}} = (u, v)$ with $u \\colon I \\to \\mathbb{K}$ and\n$v \\colon \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n \\to \\mathbb{K}$. The column conditions read\n\n- For each $j \\in \\mathrm{Fin}\\,n$:\n  $\\sum_i u_i A_{i,j} + \\sum_{j'} v_{j'} [j = j'] = c_j$, i.e.\n  $u^{\\mathsf T} A\\, j + v_j = c_j$, i.e. $u^{\\mathsf T} A = c - v$. Since\n  $v \\ge 0$, $u^{\\mathsf T} A \\le c$.\n\nThe RHS condition reads\n$$\n  \\langle u_{\\mathrm{aug}}, b_{\\mathrm{aug}}\\rangle\n    = \\langle u, b\\rangle + \\langle v, 0\\rangle = \\langle u, b\\rangle \\ge d.\n$$\n\nSo $u \\ge 0$, $u^{\\mathsf T} A \\le c$ (dual feasibility), and\n$\\langle u, b\\rangle \\ge d$. This is the required dual-feasible point with\ndual objective at least $d$.\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The proof is purely algebraic and constructive: the dual certificate $u$ is\n  built explicitly from the Farkas certificate of the augmented system.\n- Works over any linearly ordered field (in particular $\\mathbb{Q}$).\n- \"Optimal value\" is not used as a primitive; instead, the theorem is phrased\n  for any lower bound $d$. The primal optimum is recovered by combining strong\n  duality with weak duality:\n  $$\n    \\sup_{u \\text{ dual-feasible}} \\langle u, b\\rangle\n      \\;\\ge\\; d \\quad\\text{whenever}\\quad d \\le \\inf_{x \\text{ primal-feasible}}\\langle c, x\\rangle,\n  $$\n  and weak duality gives the converse inequality.\n\n## Consequences\n\n- **Complementary slackness**: optimal primal-dual pairs satisfy strict slack\n  conditions on every variable (downstream from this theorem).\n- **Matrix-game value**: zero-sum value computed via row and column LPs\n  (downstream from this theorem).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 9] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Primal-dual strong duality for linear programming."

      "body": "# Antisymmetric Matrix Games Have Value\n\nLet $B$ be a real square matrix satisfying $B=-B^T$. Then the matrix game $B$ has\na value. Equivalently, there exists $x\\in\\Delta(I)$ such that\n$$\n  Bx\\le 0.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* The finite minimax theorem gives a mixed value for the square matrix\ngame. Since $B=-B^T$, every mixed strategy $z$ satisfies\n$$\n  zBz=0.\n$$\nFor any row mixed strategy $x$, the average of the column payoffs $xBe_j$ under\n$x$ is $xBx=0$, so some column gives payoff at most $0$ to player $1$ and the\nrow player cannot guarantee more than $0$. Dually, for any column mixed strategy\n$y$, the average of the row payoffs $e_iBy$ under $y$ is $yBy=0$, so some row\ngives payoff at least $0$ and the column player cannot hold the payoff below $0$.\nEquality of maxmin and minmax therefore forces the value to be $0$.\n\nIf $x$ is an optimal column strategy for player $2$, then it holds every row\npayoff to at most $0$, i.e. $(Bx)_i\\le0$ for all $i$. This is the displayed\nequivalent form.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 10(1)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Brown-von Neumann theorem for antisymmetric games."

      "body": "# Kakutani Fixed-Point Proof of the Minimax Theorem\n\nA proof of von Neumann's minimax theorem\n([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) via the **Kakutani\nfixed-point theorem**, complementing the Loomis induction proof\n([[math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]) and the LP-duality\nproof ([[math.minimax.lp_duality_minimax_proof]]).\n\nThis is the route Nash later generalised to obtain Nash equilibrium\nexistence in $N$-person finite games — the zero-sum minimax theorem\nfalls out as the 2-player zero-sum special case.\n\n## Proof plan\n\nFor a finite matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$:\n\n1. **Best-response correspondence.** Define\n   $$\n   \\mathrm{BR} : \\Delta(I) \\times \\Delta(J) \\;\\rightrightarrows\\; \\Delta(I) \\times \\Delta(J)\n   $$\n   by\n   $\\mathrm{BR}(x, y) = (\\arg\\max_{x'} x' A y) \\times (\\arg\\min_{y'} x A y')$.\n\n   Each component is a convex compact subset of the corresponding\n   simplex (set of maximisers / minimisers of a continuous linear\n   function on a compact convex set).\n\n2. **Kakutani hypotheses.** $\\mathrm{BR}$ has nonempty convex compact\n   values (linear optimisation on a compact convex set), and its graph\n   is closed by continuity of the bilinear $xAy$. The domain\n   $\\Delta(I) \\times \\Delta(J)$ is compact, convex, and nonempty.\n\n3. **Apply Kakutani.** $\\mathrm{BR}$ has a fixed point\n   $(x^*, y^*)$ — a profile that is its own best response.\n\n4. **Fixed point ⇒ saddle point.** At $(x^*, y^*)$:\n   - $x^*$ maximises $x A y^*$ over $x \\in \\Delta(I)$;\n   - $y^*$ minimises $x^* A y$ over $y \\in \\Delta(J)$.\n\n   So for every $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y \\in \\Delta(J)$:\n   $$\n   x A y^* \\;\\le\\; x^* A y^* \\;\\le\\; x^* A y.\n   $$\n\n   This is the **saddle-point inequality**\n   ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.saddle_point]]), equivalent to existence of value\n   and optimal strategies for both players (the minimax theorem).\n\n## Why this route matters\n\n- **Pedagogical**: gives a clean conceptual proof using a single\n  topological theorem (Kakutani), avoiding the combinatorial / LP-\n  duality machinery.\n- **Strategic**: this is the proof technique Nash generalised to\n  multi-player non-zero-sum games. Reading the minimax proof in this\n  shape clarifies why Nash equilibrium is the natural generalisation\n  of saddle point.\n- **Connections**: Kakutani follows from Brouwer; many minimax-style\n  results in continuous games (Sion's theorem\n  [[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.continuous.sion_minimax_theorem]]) similarly reduce to\n  Brouwer / Kakutani arguments.\n\n## Where Kakutani is missing in this library\n\nEconCSLib does not yet carry Kakutani in Lean. Until that infrastructure is\nimplemented, this proof exists only at blueprint level. The Lean proof of the matrix-game minimax\ntheorem currently uses Loomis ([[math.minimax.minimax_from_loomis]]) over ℝ,\nand `Minimax.minimax` ([[node:math.minimax.ordered_field_minimax]]) over any\nlinearly ordered field.\n\n## References\n\n- von Neumann, J. (1928). \"Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele\".\n  *Math. Ann.* 100: 295–320.\n- Nash, J. F. (1950). \"Equilibrium Points in N-Person Games\". *PNAS*.\n- Kakutani, S. (1941). \"A Generalization of Brouwer's Fixed Point\n  Theorem\". *Duke Math. J.* 8: 457–459.\n- [MSZ Chapter 5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*.\n- [MFoGT Chapter 2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Direct Induction Proof Of Loomis Theorem\n\nThis proof-plan closes [[node:math.minimax.loomis_theorem]] by induction\non $N := |I| + |J|$. The sub-lemmas it cites factor the argument into six\npieces.\n\n## Notation\n\nFix $A, B \\colon I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ with $B$ entrywise positive. Set\n$$\n  \\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x) = \\inf_{j \\in J} \\frac{(xA)_j}{(xB)_j},\n  \\qquad\n  \\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(y) = \\sup_{i \\in I} \\frac{(Ay)_i}{(By)_i},\n$$\n$$\n  \\lambda_0 = \\sup_{x \\in \\Delta(I)} \\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x),\n  \\qquad\n  \\mu_0 = \\inf_{y \\in \\Delta(J)} \\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(y).\n$$\nBoth ratios are well-defined by\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.positive_aggregate]]:\n$(xB)_j > 0$ and $(By)_i > 0$ for every $x \\in \\Delta(I)$, $y \\in \\Delta(J)$,\n$j \\in J$, $i \\in I$.\n\n## Proof structure\n\n*Step 1 — Existence of optimisers.* By\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.value_existence]], the\nfunctionals $\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}$ and $\\mu_\\mathrm{aux}$ are continuous on\nthe compact simplices $\\Delta(I)$ and $\\Delta(J)$, and attain their\nrespective $\\sup$ and $\\inf$. Let $x_0 \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y_0 \\in \\Delta(J)$\nbe attaining strategies, so that for every $j \\in J$ and every $i \\in I$\n$$\n  (x_0 A)_j \\ge \\lambda_0 \\,(x_0 B)_j,\n  \\qquad\n  (A y_0)_i \\le \\mu_0 \\,(B y_0)_i.\n$$\n\n*Step 2 — Weak duality.* By\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.weak_duality]],\n$\\lambda_0 \\le \\mu_0$, using positivity of $x_0 B y_0$.\n\n*Step 3 — Induction on $N = |I| + |J|$.* The base case $N = 2$ (i.e. $|I| =\n|J| = 1$) is handled by\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.base_case]]: the unique\nratio $A_{i_0, j_0} / B_{i_0, j_0}$ is simultaneously $\\lambda_0$ and\n$\\mu_0$.\n\n*Step 4 — Inductive step.* Assume $\\lambda_0' = \\mu_0'$ for every\npositive-$B$ pair on index types of total cardinality strictly less than\n$N$. Suppose, for contradiction, that $\\lambda_0 < \\mu_0$. The attainment\ninequalities above must contain at least one *strict* inequality: if every\ninequality were an equality then\n$$\n  x_0 A y_0 = \\lambda_0 \\,(x_0 B y_0) = \\mu_0 \\,(x_0 B y_0)\n$$\n(weighting the equalities by $y_0$ and $x_0$ respectively), and dividing by\nthe strictly positive quantity $x_0 B y_0$ gives $\\lambda_0 = \\mu_0$,\ncontradiction. Hence either some column $j_0$ satisfies\n$(x_0 A)_{j_0} > \\lambda_0 (x_0 B)_{j_0}$, or some row $i_0$ satisfies\n$(A y_0)_{i_0} < \\mu_0 (B y_0)_{i_0}$. The two cases are dual:\n\n- the column case is closed by\n  [[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.column_drop]];\n- the row case is closed by\n  [[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.row_drop]].\n\nEach case derives a contradiction from $\\lambda_0 < \\mu_0$, completing the\ninduction. Therefore $\\lambda_0 = \\mu_0 = v$, and $(x_0, y_0, v)$ witnesses\nthe Loomis inequalities of [[node:math.minimax.loomis_theorem]].\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Direct induction proof of\n  Loomis theorem, independent of von Neumann minimax."

      "body": "# Base Case of Loomis Induction\n\nThe base case of the induction in\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]: when $|I| + |J| = 2$ the\nmatrices are $1 \\times 1$ and the Loomis values reduce to a single ratio.\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $I$ and $J$ be finite nonempty index types with $|I| + |J| = 2$, so\n$|I| = |J| = 1$ with single elements $i_0 \\in I$ and $j_0 \\in J$. Let\n$A, B \\colon I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ with $B_{i_0, j_0} > 0$. Then\n$$\n  \\lambda_0 \\;=\\; \\mu_0 \\;=\\; \\frac{A_{i_0, j_0}}{B_{i_0, j_0}}.\n$$\n\n## Proof\n\nBoth simplices are singletons: $\\Delta(I) = \\{e_{i_0}\\}$ and\n$\\Delta(J) = \\{e_{j_0}\\}$, where $e_{i_0}$, $e_{j_0}$ are the unique unit\nmass strategies. For the unique $x = e_{i_0}$ and $j = j_0$ we have\n$(xA)_{j_0} = A_{i_0, j_0}$ and $(xB)_{j_0} = B_{i_0, j_0}$, so\n$$\n  \\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(e_{i_0}) = \\frac{A_{i_0, j_0}}{B_{i_0, j_0}}.\n$$\nTaking the supremum over the singleton $\\Delta(I)$ gives $\\lambda_0 = A_{i_0,\nj_0} / B_{i_0, j_0}$. The argument for $\\mu_0$ is identical. $\\square$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Base case of the Loomis induction."

      "body": "# Column-Drop Step of Loomis Induction\n\nThe first of the two symmetric inductive steps in\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]: a strict column inequality\nin the optimiser of $A$ forces a contradiction by mixing with the inductive\noptimiser of a column-restricted game.\n\n## Setup\n\nFix $A, B \\colon I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ with $B$ entrywise positive and\n$|I| + |J| \\ge 3$. Let $x_0 \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y_0 \\in \\Delta(J)$ be the\noptimisers from\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.value_existence]], and use\n$\\lambda_0, \\mu_0$ as defined there.\n\n**Induction hypothesis.** Every pair $(A', B')$ on smaller index types — in\nparticular on $(I, J')$ with $J' \\subsetneq J$ — satisfies the equality\n$\\lambda_0(A', B') = \\mu_0(A', B')$.\n\n## Statement\n\nSuppose $\\lambda_0 < \\mu_0$ and there exists $j_0 \\in J$ with\n$$\n  (x_0 A)_{j_0} \\;>\\; \\lambda_0 \\,(x_0 B)_{j_0}.\n$$\nThen a contradiction follows. (Symmetrically: this strict-column situation\ncannot coexist with $\\lambda_0 < \\mu_0$.)\n\n## Proof\n\n**Step 1: $|J| \\ge 2$.** If $|J| = 1$ then $j_0$ is the unique column and\n$$\n  \\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x_0) = \\frac{(x_0 A)_{j_0}}{(x_0 B)_{j_0}}\n  > \\lambda_0,\n$$\ncontradicting $\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x_0) \\le \\lambda_0$. So $|J| \\ge 2$ and\n$J' := J \\setminus \\{j_0\\}$ is nonempty.\n\n**Step 2: Restricted game.** Let $A', B' \\colon I \\times J' \\to \\mathbb{R}$\nbe the restrictions of $A, B$ to $J'$. Then $B'$ is still entrywise\npositive, and $|I| + |J'| = |I| + |J| - 1 < |I| + |J|$. By induction\nhypothesis, $\\lambda_0' = \\mu_0'$ where $\\lambda_0', \\mu_0'$ are the Loomis\nscalars of $(A', B')$.\n\n**Step 3: $\\mu_0 \\le \\mu_0'$.** For any $y' \\in \\Delta(J')$, define\n$\\tilde y \\in \\Delta(J)$ by extending $y'$ with $0$ at $j_0$. Then\n$$\n  (A \\tilde y)_i = \\sum_{j \\in J'} A_{ij}\\, y'_j = (A' y')_i,\n  \\qquad\n  (B \\tilde y)_i = (B' y')_i,\n$$\nso $\\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(\\tilde y) = \\mu_\\mathrm{aux}^{(A',B')}(y')$. In particular\n$\\mu_0 \\le \\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(\\tilde y) = \\mu_\\mathrm{aux}^{(A',B')}(y')$.\nTaking the infimum over $y' \\in \\Delta(J')$ gives $\\mu_0 \\le \\mu_0'$.\n\n**Step 4: $\\lambda_0 < \\lambda_0'$.** Combining Step 3 with the inductive\nequality and the hypothesis,\n$$\n  \\lambda_0 \\;<\\; \\mu_0 \\;\\le\\; \\mu_0' \\;=\\; \\lambda_0'.\n$$\n\n**Step 5: Inductive optimiser $x'$.** By\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.value_existence]] applied to\n$(A', B')$ there exists $x' \\in \\Delta(I)$ with\n$$\n  (x' A)_j \\ge \\lambda_0' \\,(x' B)_j\n  \\qquad\\text{for every } j \\in J'.\n$$\n(Strategies on $I$ for $(A', B')$ live in the same simplex $\\Delta(I)$.)\n\n**Step 6: Convex combination.** For $\\alpha \\in [0, 1]$ set\n$x_\\alpha = \\alpha x' + (1 - \\alpha) x_0 \\in \\Delta(I)$. By bilinearity of\n$(\\cdot, A)$ and $(\\cdot, B)$, for every $j \\in J$\n$$\n  (x_\\alpha A)_j = \\alpha (x' A)_j + (1 - \\alpha)(x_0 A)_j, \\qquad\n  (x_\\alpha B)_j = \\alpha (x' B)_j + (1 - \\alpha)(x_0 B)_j.\n$$\n\n*Sub-case $j \\in J'$.* Using Step 5 and the $x_0$-inequality at $\\lambda_0$:\n$$\n  (x_\\alpha A)_j\n  \\ge \\alpha \\lambda_0'(x'B)_j + (1 - \\alpha) \\lambda_0 (x_0 B)_j\n  = \\lambda_0 (x_\\alpha B)_j + \\alpha(\\lambda_0' - \\lambda_0)(x'B)_j.\n$$\nThe extra term $\\alpha(\\lambda_0' - \\lambda_0)(x'B)_j$ is strictly positive\nwhen $\\alpha > 0$ (Step 4 plus $(x'B)_j > 0$ by\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.positive_aggregate]]). So for\nevery $\\alpha \\in (0, 1]$ and every $j \\ne j_0$,\n$$\n  (x_\\alpha A)_j \\;>\\; \\lambda_0 (x_\\alpha B)_j. \\tag{*}\n$$\n\n*Sub-case $j = j_0$.* The function\n$\\alpha \\mapsto (x_\\alpha A)_{j_0} - \\lambda_0 (x_\\alpha B)_{j_0}$ is\naffine, hence continuous. At $\\alpha = 0$ it equals\n$(x_0 A)_{j_0} - \\lambda_0 (x_0 B)_{j_0}$, which is strictly positive by\nhypothesis. Therefore there exists $\\alpha^* > 0$ such that the inequality\nremains strict for every $\\alpha \\in [0, \\alpha^*)$. Pick any $\\alpha \\in\n(0, \\min(\\alpha^*, 1))$.\n\n**Step 7: Contradiction.** For the chosen $\\alpha$, $(*)$ holds for every\n$j \\in J$. Hence\n$$\n  \\frac{(x_\\alpha A)_j}{(x_\\alpha B)_j} > \\lambda_0\n  \\quad\\text{for every } j \\in J,\n$$\nwhich gives $\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x_\\alpha) > \\lambda_0$, contradicting the\ndefinition $\\lambda_0 = \\sup_x \\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x)$. $\\square$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Column-drop inductive step in the direct Loomis proof."

      "body": "# Positive Aggregates xB and By\n\nA bookkeeping lemma used throughout the direct Loomis induction proof: an\nentrywise-positive matrix $B$ stays positive after weighting by a\nprobability vector on either side.\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $I$ and $J$ be finite nonempty index types, and let\n$B \\colon I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $B_{ij} > 0$ for every\n$(i, j) \\in I \\times J$. Then:\n\n1. For every $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and every $j \\in J$,\n   $(xB)_j = \\sum_i x_i B_{ij} > 0$.\n2. For every $y \\in \\Delta(J)$ and every $i \\in I$,\n   $(By)_i = \\sum_j B_{ij}\\, y_j > 0$.\n3. For every $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and every $y \\in \\Delta(J)$,\n   $x B y = \\sum_{i, j} x_i B_{ij} y_j > 0$.\n\n## Proof\n\n(i) Fix $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $j \\in J$. Each summand $x_i B_{ij}$ is\nnonnegative because $x_i \\ge 0$ and $B_{ij} > 0$. Since $\\sum_i x_i = 1$,\nthere is some $i^* \\in I$ with $x_{i^*} > 0$; for that index\n$x_{i^*} B_{i^* j} > 0$ strictly. Adding the nonnegative remaining terms\nkeeps the sum strictly positive.\n\n(ii) Symmetric in $y$ and the column variable.\n\n(iii) Weight (ii) by $x \\ge 0$ with $\\sum_i x_i = 1$. The argument of (i)\napplied to the strictly positive function $i \\mapsto (By)_i$ gives\n$\\sum_i x_i (By)_i > 0$, which is exactly $x B y$. $\\square$\n\n## Use\n\nUsed wherever the Loomis ratios $\\frac{(xA)_j}{(xB)_j}$ and\n$\\frac{(Ay)_i}{(By)_i}$ appear: the denominators are strictly positive, so\nthe ratios are well-defined real numbers and continuous in their simplex\narguments. In particular it underwrites the value-existence and\nweak-duality lemmas of the direct Loomis induction proof.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations\n  of Game Theory*. Aggregate\n  positivity used to define the Loomis ratios."

      "body": "# Row-Drop Step of Loomis Induction\n\nDual to [[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.column_drop]]: a\nstrict row inequality in the optimiser of $A$ forces a contradiction by\nmixing with the inductive optimiser of a row-restricted game.\n\n## Setup\n\nFix $A, B \\colon I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ with $B$ entrywise positive and\n$|I| + |J| \\ge 3$. Use $x_0, y_0, \\lambda_0, \\mu_0$ as in\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.value_existence]].\n\n**Induction hypothesis.** Every pair $(A', B')$ on $(I', J)$ with\n$I' \\subsetneq I$ satisfies $\\lambda_0(A', B') = \\mu_0(A', B')$.\n\n## Statement\n\nSuppose $\\lambda_0 < \\mu_0$ and there exists $i_0 \\in I$ with\n$$\n  (A y_0)_{i_0} \\;<\\; \\mu_0 \\,(B y_0)_{i_0}.\n$$\nThen a contradiction follows.\n\n## Proof\n\nThe argument is dual to\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.column_drop]]. We sketch the\ncorrespondences and record the sign flips:\n\n- $|I| \\ge 2$: if $|I| = 1$ then $i_0$ is the unique row and\n  $\\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(y_0) = (A y_0)_{i_0} / (B y_0)_{i_0} < \\mu_0$,\n  contradicting $\\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(y_0) \\ge \\mu_0$. So $I' := I \\setminus\n  \\{i_0\\}$ is nonempty.\n\n- Restricted game $(A', B')$ on $(I', J)$. $B'$ stays entrywise positive\n  and $|I'| + |J| < |I| + |J|$, so the induction hypothesis applies:\n  $\\lambda_0' = \\mu_0'$.\n\n- Extending $x' \\in \\Delta(I')$ by $0$ at $i_0$ yields $\\tilde x \\in\n  \\Delta(I)$ with\n  $$\n    (\\tilde x A)_j = (x' A')_j,\\qquad\n    (\\tilde x B)_j = (x' B')_j.\n  $$\n  So $\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(\\tilde x) = \\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}^{(A',B')}(x')$ and\n  $\\lambda_0' \\le \\lambda_0$.\n\n- Combined with the inductive equality and the hypothesis,\n  $\\mu_0' = \\lambda_0' \\le \\lambda_0 < \\mu_0$, so $\\mu_0' < \\mu_0$.\n\n- Let $y' \\in \\Delta(J)$ be the inductive optimiser of $(A', B')$, so\n  $(A' y')_i \\le \\mu_0' (B' y')_i$ for every $i \\in I'$. Set\n  $y_\\alpha = \\alpha y' + (1 - \\alpha) y_0 \\in \\Delta(J)$.\n\n  *For $i \\in I'$:*\n  $$\n    (A y_\\alpha)_i\n    \\le \\alpha \\mu_0'(B y')_i + (1 - \\alpha)\\mu_0 (B y_0)_i\n    = \\mu_0 (B y_\\alpha)_i - \\alpha (\\mu_0 - \\mu_0')(B y')_i.\n  $$\n  The subtracted term is strictly positive when $\\alpha > 0$ (using\n  $\\mu_0 > \\mu_0'$ and $(By')_i > 0$ by\n  [[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.positive_aggregate]]), so\n  $(A y_\\alpha)_i < \\mu_0 (B y_\\alpha)_i$.\n\n  *For $i = i_0$:* the affine function\n  $\\alpha \\mapsto (A y_\\alpha)_{i_0} - \\mu_0 (B y_\\alpha)_{i_0}$ is\n  continuous and strictly negative at $\\alpha = 0$, so it remains strictly\n  negative on a neighborhood $[0, \\alpha^*)$. Pick any\n  $\\alpha \\in (0, \\min(\\alpha^*, 1))$.\n\n- For the chosen $\\alpha$, $(A y_\\alpha)_i < \\mu_0 (B y_\\alpha)_i$ for every\n  $i \\in I$, giving $\\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(y_\\alpha) < \\mu_0$ and contradicting\n  the definition of $\\mu_0$ as an infimum.\n\n$\\square$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Row-drop inductive step in the direct Loomis proof."

      "body": "# Existence of Loomis Optimisers\n\nCompactness and continuity step for the Loomis induction\n([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]): the Loomis ratios are\ncontinuous on the simplices, and their extrema are attained.\n\n## Setup\n\nFix $A, B \\colon I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ with $B$ entrywise positive\n(see [[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.positive_aggregate]]).\nDefine\n$$\n  \\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x) = \\inf_{j \\in J} \\frac{(xA)_j}{(xB)_j},\n  \\qquad\n  \\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(y) = \\sup_{i \\in I} \\frac{(Ay)_i}{(By)_i},\n$$\nand\n$$\n  \\lambda_0 = \\sup_{x \\in \\Delta(I)} \\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x),\n  \\qquad\n  \\mu_0 = \\inf_{y \\in \\Delta(J)} \\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(y).\n$$\n\n## Statement\n\n(i) **Continuity.** The maps $\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux} \\colon \\Delta(I) \\to\n\\mathbb{R}$ and $\\mu_\\mathrm{aux} \\colon \\Delta(J) \\to \\mathbb{R}$ are\ncontinuous.\n\n(ii) **Boundedness.** $\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}$ is bounded above and\n$\\mu_\\mathrm{aux}$ is bounded below on their respective simplices.\n\n(iii) **Attainment.** There exist $x_0 \\in \\Delta(I)$ and\n$y_0 \\in \\Delta(J)$ such that\n$\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x_0) = \\lambda_0$ and $\\mu_\\mathrm{aux}(y_0) = \\mu_0$.\nEquivalently, for every $j \\in J$ and every $i \\in I$,\n$$\n  (x_0 A)_j \\ge \\lambda_0\\,(x_0 B)_j,\n  \\qquad\n  (A y_0)_i \\le \\mu_0\\,(B y_0)_i.\n$$\n\n## Proof\n\n(i) Each coordinate $x \\mapsto (xA)_j$ and $x \\mapsto (xB)_j$ is a continuous\nlinear functional on $\\Delta(I)$. Their quotient is continuous because the\ndenominator is strictly positive\n([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.positive_aggregate]]). The\nfinite infimum of continuous functions over the finite set $J$ is continuous.\nThe argument for $\\mu_\\mathrm{aux}$ is dual.\n\n(ii) Each ratio $(xA)_j / (xB)_j$ is bounded above by the obvious extreme\n$M_A / m_B$, where $M_A := \\max_{i, j} A_{ij}$ and $m_B := \\min_{i, j} B_{ij}\n> 0$. So $\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux} \\le M_A / m_B$. Symmetrically,\n$\\mu_\\mathrm{aux} \\ge m_A / M_B$ where $m_A := \\min_{i, j} A_{ij}$ and\n$M_B := \\max_{i, j} B_{ij}$.\n\n(iii) $\\Delta(I)$ is compact in $\\mathbb{R}^{|I|}$, and the continuous\nfunction $\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}$ attains its supremum on a compact set\n(extreme-value theorem). Let $x_0$ be a maximiser; then\n$\\lambda_\\mathrm{aux}(x_0) = \\lambda_0$, which by definition of the\ninfimum-over-$j$ gives $(x_0 A)_j / (x_0 B)_j \\ge \\lambda_0$ for every $j$,\ni.e. $(x_0 A)_j \\ge \\lambda_0 (x_0 B)_j$ (multiplying by the strictly\npositive $(x_0 B)_j$). The $\\mu_0$ side is dual.\n\nThe compact/continuous building blocks ([[node:math.simplex.continuity]]\nand [[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]]) live in the core simplex\nlayer; this lemma extends the $B = \\mathbf{1}$ case\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.lam_mu_existence]]) to general positive $B$ by composing\nwith positive division. $\\square$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations\n  of Game Theory*. Compactness\n  step for the Loomis ratios."

      "body": "# Weak Duality For Loomis Values\n\nThe \"easy\" direction of the Loomis theorem: any maxmin Loomis ratio is\nbounded by any minmax Loomis ratio. Used by the direct Loomis induction\nproof to set up the sandwich $\\lambda_0 \\le \\mu_0$.\n\n## Statement\n\nFix $A, B \\colon I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ with $B$ entrywise positive.\nWith $\\lambda_0$ and $\\mu_0$ defined in\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.value_existence]],\n$$\n  \\lambda_0 \\;\\le\\; \\mu_0.\n$$\n\n## Proof\n\nLet $x_0 \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y_0 \\in \\Delta(J)$ be the optimisers supplied\nby [[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.value_existence]], so that\nfor every $j \\in J$ and every $i \\in I$\n$$\n  (x_0 A)_j \\ge \\lambda_0\\,(x_0 B)_j,\n  \\qquad\n  (A y_0)_i \\le \\mu_0\\,(B y_0)_i.\n$$\nWeight the first family by $y_{0,j} \\ge 0$ and sum over $j$:\n$$\n  \\sum_j y_{0,j} (x_0 A)_j \\;\\ge\\; \\lambda_0 \\sum_j y_{0,j} (x_0 B)_j,\n$$\ni.e. $x_0 A y_0 \\ge \\lambda_0 \\cdot (x_0 B y_0)$. Symmetrically, weight the\nsecond family by $x_{0,i} \\ge 0$ and sum over $i$:\n$$\n  x_0 A y_0 \\;\\le\\; \\mu_0 \\cdot (x_0 B y_0).\n$$\nCombining,\n$$\n  \\lambda_0 \\cdot (x_0 B y_0) \\;\\le\\; x_0 A y_0 \\;\\le\\; \\mu_0 \\cdot (x_0 B y_0).\n$$\nBy [[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.positive_aggregate]] the\nquantity $x_0 B y_0$ is strictly positive, so dividing gives $\\lambda_0 \\le\n\\mu_0$. $\\square$\n\n## Use\n\nThis is the first half of the Loomis sandwich. The reverse direction\n$\\mu_0 \\le \\lambda_0$ is established by ruling out the strict inequality\n$\\lambda_0 < \\mu_0$ via the column-drop and row-drop steps of the direct\nLoomis induction.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations\n  of Game Theory*. Weak duality\n  for the Loomis ratios."

      "body": "# Loomis Theorem (Positive B)\n\n## Setup\n\nFix finite nonempty index types $I$ and $J$. Let $A, B \\colon I \\times J \\to\n\\mathbb{R}$ be two real matrices, and assume $B$ is **entrywise positive**:\n$B_{ij} > 0$ for every $(i, j) \\in I \\times J$.\n\nFor $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y \\in \\Delta(J)$ define the row- and column-vector\nproducts\n$$\n  (xA)_j = \\sum_i x_i A_{ij}, \\qquad (Ay)_i = \\sum_j A_{ij}\\, y_j,\n$$\nand similarly $(xB)_j$, $(By)_i$. Positivity of $B$ implies $(xB)_j > 0$ for\nevery $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and every $j$, and $(By)_i > 0$ for every\n$y \\in \\Delta(J)$ and every $i$ — recorded as\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.positive_aggregate]].\n\n## Statement\n\n**Theorem (Loomis).** There exist $x \\in \\Delta(I)$, $y \\in \\Delta(J)$, and\n$v \\in \\mathbb{R}$ such that\n$$\n  xA \\ge v \\cdot xB, \\qquad Ay \\le v \\cdot By,\n$$\nwhere the inequalities are componentwise. Equivalently, for every $j \\in J$\nand every $i \\in I$,\n$$\n  \\sum_i x_i A_{ij} \\ge v \\sum_i x_i B_{ij}, \\qquad\n  \\sum_j A_{ij}\\, y_j \\le v \\sum_j B_{ij}\\, y_j.\n$$\n\nThe common ratio level $v$ is the **Loomis value** of the pair $(A, B)$. The\nscalar form of the same statement is\n$$\n  \\lambda_0 \\;=\\; \\mu_0 \\;=\\; v,\n$$\nwhere\n$$\n  \\lambda_0\n  \\;=\\; \\sup_{x \\in \\Delta(I)} \\inf_{j \\in J} \\frac{(xA)_j}{(xB)_j},\n  \\qquad\n  \\mu_0\n  \\;=\\; \\inf_{y \\in \\Delta(J)} \\sup_{i \\in I} \\frac{(Ay)_i}{(By)_i}.\n$$\nThe denominators are strictly positive by positivity of $B$, so both\nexpressions are well-defined.\n\n## Discussion\n\nMFoGT presents Loomis as an extension of von Neumann's minimax theorem. The\ncanonical blueprint route in this library is the opposite: Loomis is proved\ndirectly by induction on $|I| + |J|$ (see the proof-plan\n[[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]). Finite minimax is then the\n$B = \\mathbf{1}$ specialisation\n([[node:math.minimax.minimax_from_loomis]]): for any probability vectors\n$x, y$ and the all-ones matrix $B = \\mathbf{1}$, both $xB$ and $By$ are\nidentically $1$, so the Loomis inequalities collapse to\n$\\min_j (xA)_j \\ge v \\ge \\max_i (Ay)_i$.\n\nThe library's Lean development formalises the general positive-$B$ Loomis\ntheorem in `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.Loomis`, and re-derives the\n$B = \\mathbf{1}$ specialisation (the finite von Neumann minimax) as the\ncorollary `Loomis.minmax_from_general`. The original inlined\ninduction at $B = \\mathbf{1}$ in `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.MinimaxLoomis`\nis retained as an independent witness.\n\n*Proof.* See the induction-on-$|I|+|J|$ proof-plan\n*Direct Induction Proof Of Loomis Theorem*, which decomposes the argument\ninto:\n\n1. positivity of the aggregates $xB$ and $By$\n   ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.positive_aggregate]]);\n2. existence of optimisers attaining $\\lambda_0$ and $\\mu_0$\n   ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.value_existence]]);\n3. weak duality $\\lambda_0 \\le \\mu_0$\n   ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.weak_duality]]);\n4. the base case $|I| + |J| = 2$\n   ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.base_case]]);\n5. the column-drop induction step\n   ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.column_drop]]);\n6. the row-drop induction step\n   ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof.row_drop]]).\n\nSteps 1–3 give $\\lambda_0 \\le \\mu_0$ and existence of attaining strategies\n$x_0, y_0$. Step 4 closes the base case. Steps 5–6 rule out the strict\ninequality $\\lambda_0 < \\mu_0$ by induction on $|I| + |J|$, leaving the\nequality $\\lambda_0 = \\mu_0 = v$, witnessed by $(x_0, y_0)$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 2.5.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations\n  of Game Theory*. Loomis\n  theorem for matrices $A$ and positive $B$.\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 1] Same. Direct induction proof of Loomis,\n  independent of von Neumann minimax."

      "body": "# Minimax via the All-Ones Specialization of Loomis\n\nThis proof-plan node records the **selected** route the library uses to close\nthe finite von Neumann minimax theorem\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]): take the Loomis theorem\n([[node:math.minimax.loomis_theorem]]) and specialise the positive matrix\n$B$ to the all-ones matrix $\\mathbf{1}$. It produces\n$x \\in \\Delta(I)$, $y \\in \\Delta(J)$, and $v \\in \\mathbb{R}$ with\n$$\n  xA \\ge v \\cdot xB \\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad Ay \\le v \\cdot By.\n$$\nFor every probability vector $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y \\in \\Delta(J)$ the\nall-ones vectors $xB$ and $By$ are identically $1$. Weak duality $\\lambda_0 \\le \\mu_0$\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.maximin_le_minimax]]) closes the sandwich:\n$\\lambda_0 = \\mu_0 = v$, with $(x, y)$ the asserted optimisers.\n\n*Lean implementation note.* The Lean development now formalises the general\npositive-$B$ Loomis theorem in `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.Loomis` and\nre-derives finite minimax as the one-line corollary\n`Loomis.minmax_from_general`, which calls `loomis_value_eq` at the\nall-ones matrix `B = fun _ _ => 1` and uses the bridge lemmas\n`lamB0_one` and `muB0_one` to translate `lamB0 A 1` back to\n`MinimaxLoomis.lam0 A` (resp. `muB0`/`mu0`). That module\nnow contributes only the shared foundational scaffold reused by the general\nproof — the aggregates, the existence + weak-duality step\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.lam_mu_existence]]), and the\ncolumn/row drop-extend infrastructure — built on the core simplex layer\n([[node:math.simplex.pure]], [[node:math.simplex.continuity]],\n[[node:math.simplex.mix]], and [[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3, Thm. 2.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Ordered-Field Minimax Statement\n\nThe finite minimax theorem admits an ordered-field form: if the payoff\nmatrix has entries in an ordered field and the proof is carried out\nalgebraically through finitely many weak linear inequalities, then the\nvalue and optimal mixed strategies can be taken over that ordered field.\n\n*Proof.* Use an algebraic proof route for finite minimax, such as the\nlinear-programming route, whose steps are finite systems of weak\nlinear inequalities, pivot operations, and normalisations by positive\nelements. These operations make sense over any ordered field. The terminal\ninequalities are precisely the two minimax optimality systems, so the\nextracted mixed strategies and value lie in the same ordered field as the\nmatrix entries.\n\nThe Lean theorem is `Minimax.minimax`, polymorphic in\n`[Field 𝕜] [LinearOrder 𝕜] [IsStrictOrderedRing 𝕜]`, proved **sorry-free**\n(axioms: `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`). The route is von\nNeumann symmetrisation: shift the game positive, embed it in the\nskew-symmetric matrix on `I ⊕ J ⊕ Unit`, and read the optimal `(x, y, v)`\noff the value-0 optimal strategy of that skew game — which exists by the\nTheorem of the Alternative (`SkewSymmetric.optimal`), a pure feasibility\nstatement needing no LP optimum / order-completeness. The ℝ-specialisation\nalso follows from the Loomis route\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3, paragraph after the proof of Thm. 2.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Ordered-field generalization via finite weak linear inequalities."

      "body": "# Strong Complementarity\n\n## Statement\n\nFor a finite zero-sum matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$, there\nexists an optimal pair $(x^*, y^*) \\in X(A) \\times Y(A)$ such that\n\n- for every row $i$: $x^*_i > 0 \\iff A.\\mathrm{Ei}\\,i\\,y^* = A.\\mathrm{value}$\n  (i.e. row $i$ is a best response to $y^*$);\n- for every column $j$: $y^*_j > 0 \\iff A.\\mathrm{Ej}\\,x^*\\,j = A.\\mathrm{value}$\n  (i.e. column $j$ is a best response to $x^*$).\n\n## Proof\n\n*The forward direction* of each biconditional is\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.support_complementarity]] (Prop. 2.4.1(b)) and\nholds for every optimal pair: if $x^*_i > 0$, then row $i$ obtains the\nvalue against $y^*$; dually for columns.\n\n*The reverse direction — existence of an optimal pair where every\nbest-response row has positive probability* — comes from\n[[node:math.linear_programming.strong_complementarity]] applied to the\nmatrix-game LP. The Lean implementation\n(`MatrixGame.exists_strong_complementary_pair`) carries out:\n\n### Step 1 — Shift to make payoffs strictly positive\n\nChoose $K := 1 + |A.\\mathrm{value}| + \\max_{i,j} |A_{ij}|$. Then\n$A'_{ij} := A_{ij} + K > 0$ for every $i, j$, and the shifted value\n$v' := A.\\mathrm{value} + K > 0$. The shift is required because the\nstandard-form LP we apply expects nonneg variables and finite\noptimum; with positive payoffs the value-LP has a clean primal form.\n\n### Step 2 — Encode the row LP in standard form\n\nThe shifted row LP is\n\n$$\n  \\min \\sum_i x'_i \\quad\n  \\text{s.t.} \\quad (A'^{\\mathsf T} x')_j \\ge 1\\ (\\forall j \\in J),\n  \\quad x'_i \\ge 0\\ (\\forall i \\in I).\n$$\n\nOptimal $x'$ rescales to a mixed strategy via $x_i = x'_i \\cdot v'$\n(since $\\sum_i x'_i = 1/v'$ at optimum).\n\n### Step 3 — Build LP-feasible primal and dual from a matrix-game optimal pair\n\nFrom an existing matrix-game optimal pair $(x^0, y^0)$ (via\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.matrix_game_nash_equilibrium]]), define\n$x'^0 := x^0 / v'$ and $u'^0 := y^0 / v'$. Both have LP objective\n$1/v'$, hence are LP-optimal by weak duality.\n\n### Step 4 — Apply LP strong complementarity\n\nInvoke [[node:math.linear_programming.strong_complementarity]] to obtain a\nstrong-CS optimal LP pair $(x'^*, u'^*)$.\n\n### Step 5 — Rescale back and translate the biconditional\n\nSet $x^*_i := x'^*(e\\,i) \\cdot v'$ and $y^*_j := u'^*_j \\cdot v'$\n(where $e : I \\simeq \\mathrm{Fin}\\,(\\#I)$ is the standard equivalence\nused so the LP variables fit `Fin n → \\mathbb{R}`). Verify:\n\n- $(A^{\\mathsf T} x^*)_j = A.\\mathrm{Ej}\\,x^*\\,j$ and\n  $(A^{\\mathsf T} x^* + K)_j = (A'^{\\mathsf T} x^*)_j = (A'^{\\mathsf T} x'^*)_j \\cdot v'\n  \\ge 1 \\cdot v' = v'$,\n  so $A.\\mathrm{Ej}\\,x^*\\,j \\ge A.\\mathrm{value}$ — i.e. $x^*$ is\n  row-optimal. Symmetrically $y^*$ is column-optimal.\n\nThe LP strict complementarity at the column index $i$ (in the strong\npair) is the assertion\n$x'^*(e\\,i) + (1 - \\sum_j u'^*_j \\cdot A'_{i,j}) > 0$. Multiplying\nthrough by $v'$ and using $v' = A.\\mathrm{value} + K$, this becomes\n\n$$\n  x^*_i + (A.\\mathrm{value} - A.\\mathrm{Ei}\\,i\\,y^*) > 0.\n$$\n\nBoth summands are non-negative (by primal/dual feasibility), so at\nleast one is strictly positive: $x^*_i > 0$ **or**\n$A.\\mathrm{Ei}\\,i\\,y^* < A.\\mathrm{value}$. The contrapositive is\nexactly the missing direction: if $A.\\mathrm{Ei}\\,i\\,y^* = A.\\mathrm{value}$\nthen $x^*_i > 0$. Symmetric argument for columns. $\\square$\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The shift in Step 1 is essential for the standard-form LP reduction;\n  without it the value LP \"max $v$\" has $v$ free, which doesn't fit\n  the `min ⟨c, x⟩ s.t. Ax ≥ b, x ≥ 0` form of\n  [[node:math.linear_programming.strong_complementarity]].\n- The Lean implementation restricts `I J : Type` (= `Type 0`) so the\n  `Fintype.sum_equiv` adapter that bridges `I` and `Fin (#I)` lines up\n  with the LP theorem's universe ($\\mathbb{R} : \\mathrm{Type}\\,0$).\n- Combined with [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.support_complementarity]] this\n  produces a *fully two-sided* biconditional in the strong pair: every\n  best-response row has positive probability and every positive-probability\n  row is a best response.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(c)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Existence of a strongly complementary optimal pair."

      "body": "# Field-Generic Value Predicates\n\nFor a finite matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{K}$ with payoff in any\nlinearly ordered field $\\mathbb{K}$, the maxmin / minmax / saddle-value\nnotions admit the following predicate characterisations that do **not**\ninvoke any `sSup` / `sInf`:\n\n**Maximin (predicate form).** $v$ is a *maximin value* of $A$ when\n\n$$\n  \\bigl(\\exists x \\in \\Delta(I),\\ \\forall j \\in J,\\ v \\le \\sum_i x_i\\, A(i,j)\\bigr)\n  \\quad\\text{and}\\quad\n  \\bigl(\\forall w,\\ (\\exists x \\in \\Delta(I),\\ \\forall j,\\ w \\le \\sum_i x_i\\, A(i,j)) \\Rightarrow w \\le v\\bigr).\n$$\n\nThat is: some row strategy guarantees at least $v$ against every column\n(existence), and no strictly larger value is achievable (maximality).\n\n**Minimax (predicate form).** Dual: $v$ is a *minimax value* when some\ncolumn strategy caps player I's payoff at $v$, and no strictly smaller\ncap is achievable.\n\n**Value (saddle-point form).** $v$ is *the value* of $A$ when there are\nrow and column strategies $x, y$ with\n\n$$\n  \\forall j,\\ v \\le \\sum_i x_i\\, A(i,j)\n  \\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad\n  \\forall i,\\ \\sum_j y_j\\, A(i,j) \\le v.\n$$\n\nThe saddle-point form is the existential combination of the two one-sided\nguarantee statements; it is equivalent to \"value exists and equals $v$\"\nwithout invoking $\\sup$ / $\\inf$.\n\n## Relationship to `sSup`-based definitions\n\nWhen $\\mathbb{K}$ admits order completeness (e.g. $\\mathbb{K} = \\mathbb{R}$\nvia `Real.instConditionallyCompleteLinearOrder`), the `sSup`-based\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.maximin_minimax]] definitions are available, and:\n\n- `IsMaximin A v ↔ v = A.maximin` (assuming the supremum is attained),\n- `IsMinimax A v ↔ v = A.minimax`,\n- `IsValue A v` is equivalent to the conjunction of the above when the\n  minimax theorem ([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) holds.\n\nThe Lean library realises `IsMaximin`, `IsMinimax`, `IsValue` in\n`EconCSLib.StrategicGame.Minimax`. The bridge lemmas between the\npredicate and `sSup` forms are tracked as Phase 2 follow-up of #54.\n\n## Why this matters\n\nAn ordered-field-generic value route constructs the value as a witness over\nany linearly ordered field, not as a supremum, so it is naturally phrased via\n`IsValue` rather than via `value`. The symmetrisation route `Minimax.minimax`\n([[node:math.minimax.ordered_field_minimax]]) is exactly this: it delivers the\noptimal value and strategies over any\n`[Field 𝕜] [LinearOrder 𝕜] [IsStrictOrderedRing 𝕜]` without requiring order\ncompleteness, so the predicate forms are the natural interface for it.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Saddle-point characterisation of value."

      "body": "# Ville Theorem By Discretization\n\nLet $X=Y=[0,1]$ and let $f:X\\times Y\\to\\mathbb R$ be continuous. For each\n$n\\ge1$, form the finite grid\n$$\n  X_n=Y_n=\\{0,1,\\ldots,2^n\\}\n$$\nand the finite matrix game\n$$\n  G_n(i,j)=f(i/2^n,j/2^n).\n$$\nLet $v_n$ be the mixed value of $G_n$.\n\n*Proof.* The proof of Ville's theorem has two steps.\n\nFirst, use uniform continuity of $f$ to transfer guarantees from sufficiently fine\ngrid games to the original continuous game. If player 1 plays an optimal mixed\nstrategy on a fine grid, interpreted as a finitely supported Borel probability\nmeasure on $[0,1]$, then player 1 guarantees $\\limsup_n v_n$ up to any prescribed\n$\\varepsilon>0$. Dually, player 2 guarantees $\\liminf_n v_n$ from above. These\ntwo inequalities force existence of a value.\n\nSecond, regard optimal grid strategies as Borel probability measures on the\ncompact interval $[0,1]$. By compactness of probability measures in the weak\ntopology, extract weakly convergent subsequences. Continuity of $f$ lets the\npayoff functional pass to the limit, and the limiting measures are optimal\nstrategies. The finite grid strategies also give the finite-support\n$\\varepsilon$-optimal strategies.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Proof of Ville's theorem by finite discretizations and weak convergence."

      "body": "# Ville Theorem\n\nLet $I=J=[0,1]$ and let $f:I\\times J\\to\\mathbb{R}$ be continuous.  The mixed\nextension over Borel probability measures on $[0,1]$ has a value, and each\nplayer has an optimal strategy.  Moreover, for every $\\varepsilon>0$, each\nplayer has an $\\varepsilon$-optimal strategy with finite support.\n\nThe mixed payoff is\n$$\n  f(\\sigma,\\tau)=\\int_{[0,1]\\times[0,1]} f(x,y)\\,d\\sigma(x)\\,d\\tau(y),\n$$\nwhere $\\sigma$ and $\\tau$ are Borel probability measures on $[0,1]$.\n\n*Proof.* One discretizes the square\n$[0,1]\\times[0,1]$ by finer and finer grids, applies finite minimax to each\nmatrix game, and then extracts weakly convergent subsequences of optimal\nprobability measures. Uniform continuity transfers the finite-grid guarantees to\nthe continuous game. The finite-support $\\varepsilon$-optimal strategies come\nfrom the same grid approximations.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 2.5.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Continuous zero-sum game on [0,1] has a value in mixed strategies."

      "body": "# Zero-Sum Nash Equilibria As Saddle Points\n\nIn a zero-sum game, a pair of mixed strategies is a Nash equilibrium exactly\nwhen it is a saddle point of the matrix payoff.\n\n*Proof.* Write $u(x,y)=xAy$ for player I's payoff and $-u(x,y)$ for player\nII's payoff. A mixed pair $(x^*,y^*)$ is a Nash equilibrium exactly when\n$$\n  u(x,y^*)\\le u(x^*,y^*)\\quad\\text{for all }x\n$$\nand\n$$\n  -u(x^*,y)\\le -u(x^*,y^*)\\quad\\text{for all }y.\n$$\nThe second inequality is equivalent to $u(x^*,y^*)\\le u(x^*,y)$ for all\n$y$. Together these are precisely the saddle-point inequalities.\n\nIn the Lean formalisation this equivalence is *definitional*: the predicate\n`MatrixGame.IsSaddlePoint` is an `abbrev` for `MatrixGame.IsMixedNashEq`, so\n`isMixedNashEq_iff_isSaddlePoint` is closed by `Iff.rfl`.  The\nstrategic-game-level form ([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.matrix_game_nash_equilibrium]])\nfollows from the same definitional identity combined with the profile\nexpansion lemmas.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(d), proof paragraph] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Saddle points express the identity between optimal strategies and Nash equilibria."

      "body": "# Pointwise Bounds Are Simplex Bounds\n\nFor a finite index `I`, strictly ordered field `𝕜`, value `v ∈ 𝕜`, and\nfunction `f : I → 𝕜`,\n$$\n  (\\forall i,\\; v \\le f(i)) \\;\\Longleftrightarrow\\;\n  (\\forall x \\in \\operatorname{stdSimplex} \\mathbb{K}\\, I,\\; v \\le \\operatorname{wsum} x\\, f).\n$$\n\nThe symmetric `le_iff_simplex_le` gives the analogous statement for upper\nbounds. Both directions are short:\n\n- pointwise $\\Rightarrow$ simplex uses `wsum_const` plus `wsum_le_wsum`;\n- simplex $\\Rightarrow$ pointwise specializes to the point-mass simplex\n  element `stdSimplex.pure i` and applies `wsum_pure_apply`.\n\nThese bridges are the workhorses of Loomis-style minimax arguments: they\nreduce a quantification over the entire mixed-strategy simplex to a\nquantification over pure strategies, where finiteness of `I` makes the\nremaining argument elementary.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Reduction of mixed-strategy quantifiers to\n  pure-strategy quantifiers in zero-sum analyses."

      "body": "# Continuity on the Real Standard Simplex\n\nSpecialized to the field $\\mathbb{R}$, the standard simplex carries the\nsubspace topology from $\\mathbb{R}^I$, and two basic continuity facts are\nneeded by every existence-via-compactness argument:\n\n- `stdSimplex.continuous_coord i` -- the `i`-th coordinate projection\n  $x \\mapsto x_i$ is continuous on `stdSimplex ℝ I`.\n- `wsum_continuous f` -- for any `f : I → ℝ`, the map\n  $x \\mapsto \\operatorname{wsum} x\\, f$ is continuous on `stdSimplex ℝ I`.\n\nCombined with Mathlib's compactness of the real standard simplex\n(`stdSimplex.instCompactSpace_coe`), these continuity facts deliver the\nexistence of optimal mixed strategies via the extreme-value theorem. This\nis the analytic ingredient of the Loomis route to the minimax theorem and\nof Brouwer-based proofs of Nash existence.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Continuity of the expected payoff in the\n  mixed-strategy profile."

      "id": "math.simplex.mix",
      "title": "Convex Combination of Simplex Points",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "formalized",

      "body_refs": {

      "body": "# Convex Combination of Simplex Points\n\nThe basic vocabulary for blending two mixed strategies. Given\n$x, y \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $\\alpha \\in [0, 1]$, the *mixed* point\n\n$$\n  \\mathrm{mix}(\\alpha; x, y) \\;=\\; \\alpha \\cdot x + (1 - \\alpha) \\cdot y\n$$\n\nis again a simplex point. This is the substrate for compound lotteries (MSZ\nAxiom 2.16), the inductive perturbation step in Loomis-style minimax proofs,\nand any algorithm that interpolates between two distributions (fictitious\nplay, no-regret dynamics, Sion-style continuity arguments).\n\n## Statement\n\nFor a finite index `I`, a strictly ordered field `𝕜`, and `α ∈ [0, 1]`:\n\n- `stdSimplex.mix α hα₀ hα₁ x y` is the element of `stdSimplex 𝕜 I` whose\n  `i`-th coordinate is $\\alpha \\cdot x_i + (1 - \\alpha) \\cdot y_i$.\n- **Bilinearity of `wsum`** (`wsum_mix`): for any `f : I → 𝕜`,\n  $$\n    \\operatorname{wsum}(\\mathrm{mix}(\\alpha; x, y), f)\n    \\;=\\; \\alpha \\cdot \\operatorname{wsum}(x, f)\n        + (1 - \\alpha) \\cdot \\operatorname{wsum}(y, f).\n  $$\n- **Strict-monotonicity over a convex combination** (`linear_comb_gt_of_ge_gt`,\n  `linear_comb_lt_of_le_lt`, and their `wsum` versions `wsum_mix_gt_of_ge_gt`\n  and `wsum_mix_lt_of_le_lt`): if one endpoint of the combination satisfies\n  a non-strict bound and the other a strict bound, the combination remains\n  strict for any `α < 1`.\n- **Neighborhood-of-1 existential** (`mix_gt_of_gt_nbh` and dual\n  `mix_lt_of_lt_nbh`): if `c < x`, there is an interior `t ∈ (0, 1)` with\n  `c < t · x + (1 - t) · y`. The proof appeals to continuity of\n  $s \\mapsto s \\cdot x + (1 - s) \\cdot y$ at $s = 1$.\n\n## Hypothesis convention\n\nHypotheses for `α` are passed as plain `(α : 𝕜) (hα₀ : 0 ≤ α) (hα₁ : α ≤ 1)`\nrather than via a unit-interval subtype, matching Mathlib idioms and avoiding\na Core-level subtype declaration that would not pay for itself. The legacy\n`Interval := { t : ℝ // 0 ≤ t ∧ t ≤ 1 }` subtype, previously defined in\n`StrategicGame/MinimaxLoomis.lean`, has been retired in favor of this\nconvention.\n\n## Use\n\n- `EconCSLib.Utility.Lottery`: `Lottery.mix` is a definitional alias of\n  `stdSimplex.mix`; `Lottery.expectedValue_mix` is a one-line wrapper around\n  `wsum_mix`.\n- `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.MinimaxLoomis` (simplified Loomis induction) and\n  `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.Loomis` (general-`B` Loomis): the\n  inductive step \"blend the existing optimiser with the optimiser of the\n  smaller restricted game\" is the canonical consumer of `stdSimplex.mix`,\n  `wsum_mix`, `wsum_mix_*_of_*`, and `mix_*_nbh`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*, Axiom 2.16 and the surrounding\n  discussion of compound lotteries.\n- [MFoGT] Laraki, Renault, Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*,\n  Section 2.5 (Loomis induction)."
    },

      "body": "# Point Mass on the Standard Simplex\n\nFor a finite index `I` with decidable equality and a chosen vertex `i₀ ∈ I`,\nthe *point mass* `stdSimplex.pure i₀` is the simplex element that puts unit\nweight on `i₀`:\n$$\n  (\\operatorname{pure} i_0)_i \\;=\\;\n  \\begin{cases} 1 & i = i_0,\\\\ 0 & i \\ne i_0. \\end{cases}\n$$\n\nThe two key facts:\n\n- `stdSimplex.pure_apply` -- the coordinate formula above (rfl-true).\n- `wsum_pure_apply` -- weighted-sum collapse:\n  $\\operatorname{wsum}\\,(\\operatorname{pure} i_0)\\, f \\;=\\; f(i_0)$.\n\nA legacy version `wsum_pure` is also exposed for code that builds the point\nmass inline as an anonymous-structure simplex element; new code should\nprefer `stdSimplex.pure` together with `wsum_pure_apply`.\n\nThe point mass is the bridge between pure and mixed strategies: it embeds\nany pure action into the mixed-strategy simplex without disturbing its\nweighted-sum semantics. This embedding is what justifies \"pure strategies\nare a special case of mixed strategies\".\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Pure strategies as Dirac mixed strategies."

      "body": "# Weighted Sum over the Standard Simplex\n\nFor a finite index `I`, a strictly ordered field `𝕜`, an element\n`x ∈ stdSimplex 𝕜 I`, and a function `f : I → 𝕜`, the *weighted sum* is\n$$\n  \\operatorname{wsum} x \\, f \\;=\\; \\sum_{i \\in I} x_i \\cdot f(i).\n$$\n\nThis is the operator that turns a mixed strategy into an expected payoff and\na lottery into an expected utility. It is definitionally equal to Mathlib's\nfinite dot product `x ⬝ᵥ f`, but receives a dedicated name because the\nsimplex-specific algebraic lemmas below depend on the constraints\n$\\sum_i x_i = 1$ and $x_i \\ge 0$ and have no generic `dotProduct`\nanalogue.\n\nThe core algebra:\n\n- `wsum_const`  -- `wsum x (fun _ => c) = c`\n- `wsum_le_wsum`  -- pointwise `f ≤ g` implies `wsum x f ≤ wsum x g`\n- `wsum_nonneg`  -- pointwise `0 ≤ f` implies `0 ≤ wsum x f`\n- `wsum_ge_wsum`  -- the symmetric `≥` version of monotonicity\n- `wsum_add`  -- `wsum x (f + g) = wsum x f + wsum x g`\n- `wsum_smul`  -- `wsum x (c • f) = c · wsum x f`\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of\n  Game Theory*. Mixed-strategy\n  weighted sums.\n\n## Provenance\n\n- Adapted from `GameTheory/Simplex.lean` in\n  [math-xmum/gametheory](https://github.com/math-xmum/gametheory)."

      "body": "# Iterated Weighted Sums Commute\n\nFor finite indices `I` and `J`, simplex elements `x ∈ stdSimplex 𝕜 I` and\n`y ∈ stdSimplex 𝕜 J`, and a payoff matrix `A : I → J → 𝕜`,\n$$\n  \\sum_{i \\in I} x_i \\!\\left( \\sum_{j \\in J} y_j \\, A_{ij} \\right)\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\sum_{j \\in J} y_j \\!\\left( \\sum_{i \\in I} x_i \\, A_{ij} \\right).\n$$\n\nIn `wsum`-notation:\n$$\n  \\operatorname{wsum} x \\, (\\lambda i.\\; \\operatorname{wsum} y\\, A_{i\\,\\cdot})\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\operatorname{wsum} y \\, (\\lambda j.\\; \\operatorname{wsum} x\\, A_{\\cdot\\, j}).\n$$\n\nThis is the finite-sum Fubini fact that lets matrix-game expected payoffs be\ncomputed in either order. It is the algebraic backbone of the minimax-style\nmanipulations (Loomis) on the value of a mixed extension.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Expected payoff of a matrix game evaluated as a\n  bilinear form in the two players' mixed strategies."

      "body_refs": {

      "body": "# Balanced Collection Of Coalitions\n\nA finite collection of coalitions $\\mathcal{D}$ is **balanced** if its\ncoalitions can be assigned positive weights $\\delta_S>0$ so that every\nplayer is covered with total weight one:\n$$\n  \\sum_{\\substack{S \\in \\mathcal{D}\\\\ i \\in S}} \\delta_S = 1\n  \\quad\\text{for every } i \\in N.\n$$\n\nThe condition says that the weighted incidence vectors of the coalitions in\n$\\mathcal{D}$ add up to the incidence vector of the grand coalition.\n\nBalanced collections are the combinatorial input to the\nBondareva-Shapley theorem ([[game_theory.cooperative_game.bondareva_shapley]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.17, Def 17.11] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.balanced_game",
      "title": "Balanced Coalitional Game",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "staged",
      "evidence": "non-admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.cooperative_game",
      "topics": [
        "game_theory.cooperative_game",

      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/staged/cooperative_game/balanced_game.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Balanced Coalitional Game\n\nA coalitional game is **balanced** if every balanced collection of\ncoalitions satisfies the weighted worth inequality\n$$\n  \\sum_{S \\in \\mathcal{D}} \\delta_S v(S) \\le v(N),\n$$\nwhenever the positive weights $\\delta_S$ cover each player with total\nweight one.\n\nIntuitively, if a fractional schedule of coalitions uses each player once\nin total, then the weighted value of that schedule cannot exceed the worth\nof the grand coalition.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.17, Thm 17.14] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*. Balancedness condition in the\n  Bondareva-Shapley theorem."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.bondareva_shapley",
      "title": "Bondareva-Shapley Theorem",
      "kind": "theorem",
      "status": "staged",
      "evidence": "non-admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.cooperative_game",
      "topics": [

      ],
      "uses": [

      ],
      "used_by": [
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.convex_game_core_nonempty"
      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/staged/cooperative_game/bondareva_shapley.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Bondareva-Shapley Theorem\n\n**Theorem.** A finite transferable-utility coalitional game has nonempty\ncore if and only if it is balanced:\n$$\n  \\operatorname{Core}(v) \\ne \\varnothing\n  \\quad\\Longleftrightarrow\\quad\n  v \\text{ is balanced}.\n$$\n\n## Proof Route\n\nThe standard proof is a theorem-of-the-alternative or linear-programming\nduality argument. Core nonemptiness is feasibility of the linear system\nconsisting of efficiency and the coalition inequalities\n$$\n  \\sum_{i \\in S} x_i \\ge v(S).\n$$\nThe dual certificates for infeasibility are exactly balanced collections\nwhose weighted worth exceeds $v(N)$. Therefore no such certificate exists\nprecisely when all balanced collections satisfy the balanced-game\ninequality.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nThe Lean module defines the core and balanced-game predicates. This theorem\nremains a blueprint target with an LP-duality proof route.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.17, Thm 17.14 and Thm 17.19] Maschler, Solan, Zamir,\n  *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.convex_game",
      "title": "Convex Coalitional Game",
      "kind": "definition",

      "topics": [

      ],
      "uses": [

      "used_by": [
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.convex_game_core_nonempty",
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.shapley_in_core_convex"
      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/staged/cooperative_game/convex_game.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Convex Coalitional Game\n\nA coalitional game is **convex** when its characteristic function is\nsupermodular:\n$$\n  v(S \\cup T) + v(S \\cap T) \\ge v(S) + v(T)\n$$\nfor all coalitions $S,T \\subseteq N$.\n\nEquivalently, a player's marginal contribution weakly increases as the\ncoalition they join becomes larger. Convexity is a strong regularity\ncondition: convex games have nonempty core, and their Shapley value lies in\nthe core.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nLean defines convexity as `CoalitionalGame.IsConvex` and proves the basic\nfact `CoalitionalGame.IsConvex.isSuperadditive`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.17, Def 17.51 and Thm 17.54] Maschler, Solan, Zamir,\n  *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.convex_game_core_nonempty",
      "title": "Convex Games Have Nonempty Core",
      "kind": "theorem",

      "body_refs": {

      "body": "# Convex Games Have Nonempty Core\n\n**Theorem.** If a finite TU game is convex, then its core is nonempty.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nConvexity implies the balancedness inequalities required by\nBondareva-Shapley. Applying\n[[game_theory.cooperative_game.bondareva_shapley]] then gives\nnonemptiness of the core.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nThe Lean module defines the relevant core and convex-game predicates. This\ntheorem remains a blueprint target depending on the Bondareva-Shapley route.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.17, Thm 17.55] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.core",
      "title": "Core Of A Coalitional Game",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "staged",
      "evidence": "non-admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.cooperative_game",
      "topics": [
        "game_theory.cooperative_game",
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.core"
      ],
      "uses": [
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.imputation"
      ],
      "used_by": [
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.bondareva_shapley",
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.core_subset_imputations",
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.shapley_in_core_convex"
      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/staged/cooperative_game/core.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Core Of A Coalitional Game\n\nThe **core** is the set of payoff vectors that no coalition can block.\nFor a TU game $(N,v)$, a payoff vector $x$ is in the core if:\n$$\n  \\sum_{i \\in N} x_i = v(N)\n$$\nand, for every coalition $S \\subseteq N$,\n$$\n  \\sum_{i \\in S} x_i \\ge v(S).\n$$\n\nThe first condition allocates the worth of the grand coalition. The second\ncondition is coalitional rationality: every coalition receives at least the\nworth it can secure on its own.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nThe Lean predicate `CoalitionalGame.Core` uses the efficient payoff\ncondition plus the coalition-by-coalition inequality above.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.17, Def 17.2] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.core_subset_imputations",
      "title": "Core Payoffs Are Imputations",
      "kind": "theorem",
      "status": "staged",
      "evidence": "non-admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.cooperative_game",
      "topics": [
        "game_theory.cooperative_game",
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.core"
      ],
      "uses": [
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.core",
        "game_theory.cooperative_game.imputation"
      ],
      "used_by": [],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/staged/cooperative_game/core_subset_imputations.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Core Payoffs Are Imputations\n\nEvery payoff vector in the core is an imputation.\n\nIndeed, the core definition already contains efficiency:\n$$\n  \\sum_{i \\in N} x_i = v(N).\n$$\nFor individual rationality, apply the core's coalitional rationality\ncondition to the singleton coalition $\\{i\\}$:\n$$\n  x_i = \\sum_{j \\in \\{i\\}} x_j \\ge v(\\{i\\}).\n$$\n\nThus core membership implies both efficiency and individual rationality.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.17, Def 17.1-17.2] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.imputation",
      "title": "Imputation",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "staged",
      "evidence": "non-admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.cooperative_game",
      "topics": [

      ],

      ],
      "used_by": [
