        "game_theory.cooperative_game.core_subset_imputations"
      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/staged/cooperative_game/imputation.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Imputation\n\nAn **imputation** is a payoff vector that distributes all worth of the grand\ncoalition and gives every player at least their singleton worth.\n\nFor a TU game $(N,v)$, a payoff vector $x : N \\to \\mathbb{R}$ is an\nimputation when:\n$$\n  \\sum_{i \\in N} x_i = v(N)\n$$\nand, for every player $i \\in N$,\n$$\n  x_i \\ge v(\\{i\\}).\n$$\n\nThe first condition is **efficiency**; the second is **individual\nrationality**.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nLean separates the two predicates as `CoalitionalGame.IsEfficient` and\n`CoalitionalGame.IsIndividuallyRational`, then combines them in\n`CoalitionalGame.IsImputation`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.17, Def 17.1] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.marginal_contribution",
      "title": "Marginal Contribution",
      "kind": "definition",

      "body": "# Marginal Contribution\n\nThe **marginal contribution** of player $i$ to a coalition $S$ not\ncontaining $i$ is\n$$\n  v(S \\cup \\{i\\}) - v(S).\n$$\n\nThis is the payoff increment created by adding $i$ to $S$. Shapley-value\nformulae average this quantity over all possible predecessor coalitions.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.18, §18.2] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.monotonic_game",
      "title": "Monotonic Coalitional Game",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "staged",
      "evidence": "non-admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.cooperative_game",

      "used_by": [],

      "body_refs": {

      "body": "# Monotonic Coalitional Game\n\nA coalitional game is **monotonic** if enlarging a coalition cannot reduce\nits worth. For coalitions $S \\subseteq T \\subseteq N$,\n$$\n  v(S) \\le v(T).\n$$\n\nThis property is weaker than superadditivity in many standard settings but\ncaptures the same basic direction: adding players should not make a\ncoalition worse off.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.16, Def 16.10] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.payoff_vector",
      "title": "Payoff Vector",

      "evidence": "non-admitted",

      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Payoff Vector\n\nGiven a coalitional game on player set $N$, a **payoff vector** is a function\n$$\n  x : N \\to \\mathbb{R}.\n$$\nIt specifies the final payoff allocated to each individual player.\n\nThe total payoff assigned to a coalition $S \\subseteq N$ is\n$$\n  x(S) = \\sum_{i \\in S} x_i.\n$$\nCoalitional-game solution concepts compare this allocated amount with the\ncoalition worth $v(S)$.\n\n## Role In The Blueprint\n\nThis is the common input object for imputations\n([[game_theory.cooperative_game.imputation]]), the core\n([[game_theory.cooperative_game.core]]), and the Shapley value\n([[game_theory.cooperative_game.shapley_value]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.16, Def 16.1 and Def 16.13-16.16] Maschler, Solan, Zamir,\n  *Game Theory*."
    },
    {
      "id": "game_theory.cooperative_game.shapley_axioms",

      "body": "# Shapley Axioms\n\nThe Shapley-value characterization uses four axioms for a single-valued\nsolution concept $\\varphi$ assigning each game a payoff vector:\n\n- **Efficiency:** $\\sum_{i \\in N} \\varphi_i(v)=v(N)$.\n- **Symmetry:** symmetric players receive equal payoffs.\n- **Null player:** a player who never changes any coalition's worth receives\n  payoff zero.\n- **Additivity:** $\\varphi(v+w)=\\varphi(v)+\\varphi(w)$.\n\nLean also defines the supporting predicates for symmetric players and null\nplayers. These are the hypotheses of Shapley's uniqueness theorem\n([[game_theory.cooperative_game.shapley_uniqueness]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.18, Def 18.2, Def 18.4, Def 18.6, Def 18.8] Maschler, Solan,\n  Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Shapley Value Lies In The Core Of A Convex Game\n\n**Theorem.** If a TU game is convex, then its Shapley value belongs to the\ncore.\n\nConvexity means marginal contributions are increasing with coalition size.\nThis increasing-marginal-returns property makes the Shapley average satisfy\nevery coalitional rationality inequality:\n$$\n  \\sum_{i \\in S}\\operatorname{Sh}_i(v) \\ge v(S)\n  \\quad\\text{for every } S \\subseteq N.\n$$\nTogether with Shapley efficiency, this places the Shapley payoff vector in\nthe core.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nThe Lean module defines the Shapley value and core predicates. This theorem\nremains a blueprint target.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.18, Thm 18.32] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Shapley Uniqueness Theorem\n\n**Theorem.** The Shapley value is the unique single-valued solution concept\nthat satisfies efficiency, symmetry, the null-player property, and\nadditivity.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nThe usual proof expands arbitrary games in a basis of unanimity games.\nThe four axioms determine the value uniquely on unanimity games: players in\nthe winning coalition receive equal shares and players outside it are null.\nAdditivity then extends the determination to every game.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nThe Lean module defines the Shapley value and its axioms. Uniqueness remains a\nblueprint target with the unanimity-game proof route.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.18, Thm 18.13 and Thm 18.15] Maschler, Solan, Zamir,\n  *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Shapley Value\n\nThe **Shapley value** assigns to each player their average marginal\ncontribution over all possible orders in which the grand coalition can form.\nEquivalently,\n$$\n  \\operatorname{Sh}_i(v)\n  =\n  \\sum_{S \\subseteq N\\setminus\\{i\\}}\n  \\frac{|S|!(|N|-|S|-1)!}{|N|!}\n  \\bigl(v(S \\cup \\{i\\})-v(S)\\bigr).\n$$\n\nThe factorial coefficient is the probability that exactly the players in\n$S$ precede $i$ in a uniformly random ordering of $N$.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nLean defines this formula as `CoalitionalGame.shapleyValue`. The main\nproperties of the formula are separate theorem nodes: efficiency,\nuniqueness, and convex-core membership.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.18, Def 18.14 and Thm 18.17] Maschler, Solan, Zamir,\n  *Game Theory*."
    },

      "home_topic": "game_theory.cooperative_game",

      "body_refs": {

      "body": "# Shapley Value Is Efficient\n\n**Theorem.** The Shapley value distributes the worth of the grand coalition:\n$$\n  \\sum_{i \\in N} \\operatorname{Sh}_i(v)=v(N).\n$$\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nExpand the Shapley formula and exchange the sums over players and predecessor\ncoalitions. Each coalition marginal contribution appears with the number of\norders in which it is the relevant predecessor set. The resulting telescoping\nover permutations leaves exactly $v(N)-v(\\varnothing)=v(N)$.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nThe Lean module defines the Shapley value. Efficiency remains a blueprint\ntarget with a combinatorial proof route.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.18, Thm 18.18] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."
    },

      "body": "# Simple Game\n\nA **simple game** is a coalitional game whose coalitions are classified as\nlosing or winning. In characteristic-function form,\n$$\n  v(S) \\in \\{0,1\\}\n$$\nfor every coalition $S \\subseteq N$, and the grand coalition is winning:\n$$\n  v(N)=1.\n$$\n\nA coalition $S$ is **winning** when $v(S)=1$.\n\nSimple games model yes/no collective decision rules. Later refinements such\nas weighted majority games add an explicit quota-and-weight representation.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.16, Def 16.2] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Superadditive Coalitional Game\n\nA coalitional game is **superadditive** if disjoint coalitions can do at\nleast as well by merging. Formally, for disjoint coalitions\n$S,T \\subseteq N$,\n$$\n  v(S \\cup T) \\ge v(S) + v(T).\n$$\n\nSuperadditivity is a basic economic compatibility condition: it says there\nis no loss of worth merely from allowing two non-overlapping coalitions to\ncoordinate as one larger coalition.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.16, Def 16.8] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Transferable-Utility Coalitional Game\n\nA **transferable-utility coalitional game** consists of a finite player set\n$N$ and a characteristic function\n$$\n  v : 2^N \\to \\mathbb{R}\n$$\nwith $v(\\varnothing)=0$. For each coalition $S \\subseteq N$, the number\n$v(S)$ is the total payoff that members of $S$ can secure by coordinating\namong themselves.\n\nFor a payoff vector $x : N \\to \\mathbb{R}$, the payoff assigned to a\ncoalition is\n$$\n  x(S) = \\sum_{i \\in S} x_i.\n$$\nThis derived coalition payoff is the quantity compared with $v(S)$ in\nimputation, core, and balancedness conditions.\n\n## Lean Status\n\nThe Lean structure `CoalitionalGame N U` is intentionally parameterized by\nthe utility type `U`; real-valued assumptions are introduced only for\ntheorems such as Bondareva-Shapley and Shapley-value results. The declaration\n`CoalitionalGame.coalitionPayoff` supplies the finite sum\n$\\sum_{i \\in S} x_i$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.16, Def 16.1] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Game Tree\n\nThe tree of a finite perfect-information extensive game is a finite connected\ndirected acyclic graph with a distinguished origin $\\theta$. Every non-origin node\nhas a unique predecessor, and iterating predecessors eventually reaches $\\theta$.\n\nTerminal nodes are those with no successors. Decision positions are nonterminal\nnodes. Each decision position has a nonempty successor set.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.2.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Tree of nodes, origin, predecessor map, terminal nodes, and successors."

      "body": "# Completely Mixed Nash Is Subgame Perfect\n\nLet $\\Gamma$ be an extensive-form game. Every Nash equilibrium in completely\nmixed strategies, whether behavior strategies or mixed strategies in the\ntextbook statement, is a subgame-perfect equilibrium.\n\n## Lean Scope\n\nThe current Lean theorem\n`ExtensiveGame.IsBehaviorNashEq.toSubgamePerfect_of_isCompletelyMixed`\nformalizes the behavior-strategy side in the same finite-fuel, Arena-based\ninterface used for [MSZ, Theorem 7.5]. Complete mixing is represented by\n`ExtensiveGame.BehaviorProfile.IsCompletelyMixed`, and the bridge from complete\nmixing to positive reach of every subgame root is packaged as\n`ExtensiveGame.BehaviorProfile.IsCompletelyMixedWithPositiveReach`.\n\nUnder that positive-reach interface and the existing affine\n`ExtensiveGame.ReachedSubgamePayoffTransfer` hypothesis for every subgame root,\nthe proof is a direct universal application of\n`ExtensiveGame.IsBehaviorNashEq.restrictSubgame_of_reachProb_pos`.\n\nThe mixed-strategy version and a concrete derivation of positive reach from\nfinite histories with explicit chance probabilities remain future\nstrengthenings.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Cor. 7.7] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. A completely mixed Nash equilibrium is subgame-perfect."

      "body": "# Reached Subgame Nash Restriction\n\nLet $\\Gamma$ be an extensive-form game, let $\\sigma^\\ast$ be a Nash equilibrium\nin mixed strategies or behavior strategies, and let $\\Gamma(x)$ be a subgame.\nIf the probability of reaching $x$ under $\\sigma^\\ast$ is positive, then the\nrestriction of $\\sigma^\\ast$ to $\\Gamma(x)$ is a Nash equilibrium of the subgame\n$\\Gamma(x)$.\n\n## Lean Scope\n\nThe Lean target should reuse `ExtensiveGame.subgameAt` for $\\Gamma(x)$. A faithful\nformalization also needs behavior strategies, reach probabilities, expected\npayoffs, profile restriction to a subgame, and a lifting lemma showing that a\nprofitable deviation in a positive-probability subgame induces a profitable\ndeviation in the original game.\n\nThe current Lean theorem\n`ExtensiveGame.IsBehaviorNashEq.restrictSubgame_of_reachProb_pos` proves the\nNash-restriction step from an affine payoff-transfer interface. The root-subgame\nspecial case `ExtensiveGame.IsBehaviorNashEq.restrictSubgame_init` is proved\nwithout this interface. The supporting API now also includes\n`ExtensiveGame.reachableSubgameAt`, a subtype subgame whose states are exactly\nthose reachable from the subgame root, together with local lift lemmas that keep\nthe original profile unchanged outside that reachable subgame. A later\nstrengthening can derive the affine payoff-transfer interface for arbitrary\npositively reached subgames from finite-history reach probabilities and expected\npayoffs.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Thm. 7.5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. A Nash equilibrium restricted to a subgame reached with positive probability remains a Nash equilibrium of that subgame."
    },

      "body": "# Backward And Forward Induction Can Conflict\n\nMFoGT Figure 6.21 adds an initial stage before the battle-of-the-sexes game with\noutside option. The continuation subgame has the forward-induction outcome\n$(T,L)$ with payoff $(3,1)$.\n\nBackward induction then says player 2 should stop at the first stage and obtain\npayoff $2$. But if player 2 continues, forward-induction reasoning interprets the\ncontinuation as evidence that player 2 expects more than $2$, which changes the\nbeliefs used in the later subgame.\n\nThis illustrates why forward-induction refinements are usually applied only when\nthe rationality interpretation is coherent.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.7 and Figure 6.21] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Example where backward-induction and forward-induction reasoning are incompatible."

      "body": "# Chomp Strategy Stealing\n\nFor finite $n,m\\ge 1$, the $n\\times m$ Chomp game is a finite perfect-information\ngame. The first player has a winning strategy.\n\nWhen $n=m$, an explicit winning strategy is:\n\n- first choose square $(2,2)$;\n- after the opponent chooses $(1,k)$, choose $(k,1)$;\n- after the opponent chooses $(k,1)$, choose $(1,k)$.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nBy Zermelo determinacy, one of the two players has a winning strategy. If the\nsecond player had one, the first player could make a harmless initial move and\nthen imitate the second player's winning response, contradicting the assumed\nsecond-player win.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Exercise 6.8.1 and Hints for Chapter 6, Exercise 1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Finite Chomp first-player win and square-board explicit mirror strategy."

      "body": "# Rubinstein Bargaining Subgame Perfect Equilibrium\n\nIn the ultimatum game with amount $M>0$, the unique subgame-perfect equilibrium\nhas player 1 offer $0$ to player 2 and player 2 accept every positive offer.\n\nIn the finite alternating-offer game with discount factor $\\delta\\in(0,1)$, let\n$a_n$ be the fraction of the current surplus kept by the current proposer when\nthere are $n$ rounds remaining. Then\n$$\n  a_1=1,\n  \\qquad\n  a_n=1-\\delta a_{n-1}.\n$$\nThus\n$$\n  a_n=\\frac{1-(-\\delta)^n}{1+\\delta}.\n$$\n\nIn the infinite discounted alternating-offer game, the unique subgame-perfect\nequilibrium has each proposer offer the other player the fraction\n$$\n  \\frac{\\delta}{1+\\delta}\n$$\nof the current surplus, and the offer is accepted. The proposer keeps\n$1/(1+\\delta)$ of the current surplus.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Exercise 6.8.4 and Hints for Chapter 6, Exercise 4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Ultimatum, finite alternating-offer, and infinite discounted bargaining SPE formulas."

      "body": "# Action At An Information Set\n\nFor an information set $P^i_k$, successors of nodes in $P^i_k$ are grouped into\nequivalence classes representing the same physical action. The action set available\nto player $i$ at $P^i_k$ is denoted\n$$\n  A_i(P^i_k).\n$$\nA strategy at imperfect information must choose an action in $A_i(P^i_k)$, not a\nnode-specific successor.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Behavioral Equilibrium\n\nLet $\\Gamma$ be a finite extensive form game with perfect recall. A mixed\nequilibrium of $\\Gamma$ is a Nash equilibrium of its mixed normal-form extension.\nA behavioral equilibrium of $\\Gamma$ is a Nash equilibrium of the compact\ncontinuous game whose strategy sets are behavioral strategy spaces $B_i$ and whose\npayoffs are expected payoffs in $\\Gamma$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.3.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Mixed and behavioral equilibria of a finite extensive game with perfect recall."

      "body": "# Existence Of Behavioral Equilibrium\n\nFor every finite extensive form game with perfect recall, any mixed equilibrium is\noutcome equivalent to a behavioral equilibrium and conversely. In particular,\nbehavioral equilibria always exist.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nNash's theorem gives a mixed equilibrium of the associated finite normal form.\nKuhn's perfect-recall theorem converts each player's mixed strategy to an\noutcome-equivalent behavioral strategy. If the behavioral profile admitted a\nprofitable behavioral deviation, Isbell's theorem would convert that deviation into\nan outcome-equivalent mixed deviation, contradicting mixed equilibrium. The reverse\ndirection is analogous.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.3.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. In every finite perfect-recall extensive game, mixed and behavioral equilibria are outcome-equivalent and behavioral equilibria exist."

        "refs": [],

      "body": "# Forward Induction\n\nForward induction is a refinement principle for extensive form games. Unlike\nbackward induction, which evaluates future optimality at each information set,\nforward induction also uses past play to restrict beliefs: when possible, a\ndeviation from the equilibrium path should be interpreted as a rational signal\nrather than as a mere mistake.\n\nIn the battle-of-the-sexes game with outside option in MFoGT Figure 6.20, player\n1 can stop and receive payoff $2$. If player 1 instead enters, player 2 should\ninfer, when possible, that player 1 expects more than $2$. Since one continuation\nchoice of player 1 is strictly dominated by stopping, the forward-induction\noutcome selects the continuation equilibrium $(T,L)$ with payoff $(3,1)$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.7 and Figure 6.20] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Forward induction restricts off-path beliefs by interpreting deviations as rational when possible."

      "body": "# Information Set Refinement And Equilibrium\n\nLet $G'$ be obtained from a finite perfect-recall extensive game $G$ by refining\nsome information sets. If $\\sigma$ is a pure Nash equilibrium of $G$ and there are\nno chance moves, then $\\sigma$ is also a Nash equilibrium of $G'$.\n\nThe conclusion does not extend to mixed equilibria or to games with chance moves.\nMFoGT gives two counterexamples: matching pennies in extensive form after player\n2 observes player 1's move, and a variant where player 1 is replaced by Nature.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nA pure strategy profile without chance moves induces a unique play. Any profitable\ndeviation at a reached refined information set would also be a profitable deviation\nin the coarser game.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Exercise 6.8.5 and Hints for Chapter 6, Exercise 5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Pure no-chance equilibria survive information-set refinement; mixed or chance cases need not."

      "body": "# Isbell Behavioral-To-Mixed Equivalence\n\nIf an extensive game is linear for player $i$, then for every behavioral strategy\n$\\beta_i$ of player $i$ there exists a mixed strategy $\\sigma_i$ such that, against\nevery general strategy of the other players, the induced probability distributions\non terminal nodes coincide.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nGiven $\\beta_i$, define a product distribution on pure strategies by multiplying\nthe probabilities assigned by $\\beta_i$ at all information sets. Since each\ninformation set can occur at most once along a play, the probability of any terminal\nhistory factors through exactly the behavioral probabilities used on that history;\nall unused information-set probabilities sum to one. Hence the mixed strategy and\nbehavioral strategy induce the same outcome distribution.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.3.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. In a game linear for player i, every behavioral strategy is outcome equivalent to a mixed strategy."

      "body": "# Linear Extensive Game\n\nAn extensive game is linear for player $i$ if no play intersects any information\nset of player $i$ more than once.\n\nLinearity rules out repeated visits to the same information set along a single play,\nwhich is enough to compare behavioral and mixed strategies in one direction.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Linearity for a player means no play crosses one of that player's information sets more than once."

      "body": "# Local Characterization Of Behavioral Equilibrium\n\nFor a finite extensive form game with perfect recall, a behavioral profile $\\beta$\nis a behavioral equilibrium if and only if, for every player $i$ and every reached\ninformation set $Q_i\\in Rch(\\beta)$, the behavioral action $\\beta_i(Q_i)$ is a best\nresponse in the local continuation game starting at $Q_i$, with Nature choosing a\nnode of $Q_i$ according to $\\nu_\\beta(Q_i)$ and future play following $\\beta$.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nIf a behavioral profile is not an equilibrium, then some profitable deviation can be\nlocalized to a reached information set, because changing off-path behavior alone\ndoes not affect payoffs. Conversely, a profitable local deviation at a reached\ninformation set can be inserted into the full behavioral strategy to obtain a\nprofitable global deviation.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.3.8] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Behavioral equilibrium iff prescribed actions are best responses at reached information sets."
    },

      "body": "# Mertens Stable Sets\n\nMFoGT describes Mertens stable sets as essential components obtained using a\nSelten-style topology of strategy perturbations. For each $\\epsilon>0$ and fully\nmixed $\\sigma\\in\\operatorname{int}\\Sigma$, one considers the perturbed game\n$G(\\sigma;\\epsilon)$ in which every player is restricted to a perturbed simplex\nclose to the original mixed simplex.\n\nMertens proved that the resulting stable sets are connected, BR-invariant,\nadmissible, and compatible with backward-induction and forward-induction\nrequirements.\n\nThe text notes that a complete uniqueness characterization of Mertens stable sets\nfrom these desirable properties remains open in general.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.7] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Mertens stable sets from Selten-style strategy perturbation topology."

      "body": "# Mixed Behavioral And General Strategies\n\nIn an extensive game, player $i$ has three common randomized strategy spaces:\n\n1. a mixed strategy is a probability distribution on pure strategies, denoted\n   $\\Sigma_i=\\Delta(S_i)$;\n2. a behavioral strategy chooses independently at each information set, assigning\n   $\\beta^i_k\\in\\Delta(A_i(P^i_k))$;\n3. a general strategy is a probability distribution over behavioral strategies,\n   denoted $G_i=\\Delta(B_i)$.\n\nThese three randomization models need not induce the same distributions over\nterminal outcomes unless additional recall conditions hold.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.3.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Three kinds of randomized strategies in extensive form games."

      "body": "# Perfect Recall\n\nAn extensive game has perfect recall for player $i$ if, whenever two nodes $x$ and\n$y$ lie in the same information set of player $i$, the earlier information sets of\nplayer $i$ encountered on histories leading to $x$ and $y$ match, and the player's\nown earlier actions also match as actions in the corresponding equivalence classes.\n\nInformally, player $i$ never forgets what they knew or which actions they\npreviously chose.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.3.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. A player remembers what they knew and did in the past."

      "body": "# Kuhn Mixed-To-Behavioral Equivalence\n\nIf an extensive game has perfect recall for player $i$, then for every mixed\nstrategy $\\sigma_i$ there exists a behavioral strategy $\\beta_i$ such that, against\nevery general strategy of the other players, the induced probability distributions\non terminal nodes coincide.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nFor each information set reached with positive probability under $\\sigma_i$, define\nthe behavioral probability of an action by conditioning $\\sigma_i$ on pure\nstrategies that reach the information set and choose that action. Perfect recall\nmakes the probabilities along a reached history telescope: reaching the next\ninformation set is determined by the previous remembered action. Thus the\nbehavioral strategy reproduces the same terminal probabilities as the original\nmixed strategy.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.3.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. With perfect recall, every mixed strategy is outcome equivalent to a behavioral strategy."

      "body": "# Proper Equilibrium Induces Sequential Equilibrium\n\nLet $G$ be a finite normal-form game and let $\\Gamma$ be any perfect-recall\nextensive form game whose normal form is $G$. If $\\sigma$ is a proper equilibrium\nof $G$, then $\\sigma$ induces a sequential equilibrium $(\\beta,\\mu)$ of $\\Gamma$.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nWrite $\\sigma$ as the limit of completely mixed $\\epsilon_n$-proper profiles\n$\\sigma^n$. By Kuhn's theorem, each $\\sigma^n$ generates an equivalent interior\nbehavioral strategy $\\beta^n$. Since every information set is reached with positive\nprobability under $\\beta^n$, Bayes' rule gives beliefs $\\mu^n$.\n\nAfter passing to a convergent subsequence, $(\\beta^n,\\mu^n)\\to(\\beta,\\mu)$. If an\naction in the support of $\\beta$ were not optimal at some information set, the\n$\\epsilon_n$-proper inequalities would force its probability to vanish, a\ncontradiction. Hence $(\\beta,\\mu)$ is sequential.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.6.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. A proper equilibrium of a finite normal form induces a sequential equilibrium in every perfect-recall extensive form with that normal form."

      "body": "# Reached Information Set\n\nAn information set $Q$ is reached by a behavioral strategy profile $\\beta$ if the\nprobability of reaching $Q$ under $\\beta$ is positive. The set of reached\ninformation sets is denoted $Rch(\\beta)$.\n\nWhen $Q\\in Rch(\\beta)$, Bayes' rule defines a conditional probability\n$\\nu_\\beta(Q)$ on the nodes of $Q$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.3.7] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. An information set is reached by a behavioral strategy profile if it has positive probability."

      "body": "# Sequential Equilibrium\n\nA pair $(\\beta,\\mu)$ is a sequential equilibrium if it is weak Bayesian perfect and\nthere exists a sequence of completely mixed behavioral profiles $\\beta^n$ converging\nto $\\beta$ such that the Bayes-rule beliefs $\\nu_{\\beta^n}$ converge to $\\mu$.\n\nThus off-path beliefs must arise as limits of beliefs generated by fully mixed\ntrembling strategies.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.4.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Sequential equilibrium as weak Bayesian perfection plus consistency from completely mixed trembles."

      "body": "# Existence Of Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium With Perfect Recall\n\nEvery finite extensive form game with perfect recall admits a subgame-perfect\nequilibrium.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nInduct on the number of subgames. If there is no proper subgame, behavioral\nequilibrium existence gives the result. Otherwise, solve all proper subgames by\nthe induction hypothesis, replace each subgame root by its equilibrium payoff, and\nsolve the reduced game by behavioral equilibrium existence. Concatenating the\nreduced-game equilibrium with the equilibria of the proper subgames gives a\nsubgame-perfect equilibrium.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.4.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Every finite extensive form game with perfect recall admits an SPE."

      "body": "# Strategic Stability\n\nA subset $C$ of Nash equilibria of an extensive or normal form game $\\Gamma$ is\nstrategically stable if:\n\n- $C$ is connected;\n- for any normal-form game $G$ with the same reduced normal form as $\\Gamma$;\n- for any sufficiently nearby perturbation $G^\\epsilon$ of $G$;\n\nthere is a Nash equilibrium $\\sigma^\\epsilon$ of $G^\\epsilon$ close to $C$.\n\nMFoGT presents this after the Kohlberg-Mertens axioms. A stable solution should\ndepend only on the reduced normal form, form a connected set of non-weakly\ndominated equilibria, contain a proper equilibrium, and survive deletion of\nweakly dominated strategies.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.7] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Kohlberg-Mertens strategic stability and stable sets of Nash equilibria."

      "body": "# Subroot And Subgame In Imperfect-Information Games\n\nIn a perfect-recall extensive game, a node $x$ is a subroot if:\n\n1. $x$ is the unique node in its information set;\n2. for every information set $Q$, either every node of $Q$ follows $x$, or no node\n   of $Q$ follows $x$.\n\nThe followers of a subroot, together with inherited information sets and payoffs,\ndefine a subgame.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.4.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Subroot definition for subgames in perfect-recall extensive games."

      "body": "# Weak Bayesian Perfect Equilibrium\n\nA pair $(\\beta,\\mu)$ of a behavioral strategy profile and a belief system is weak\nBayesian perfect if:\n\n1. at every information set $Q_i$, $\\beta_i(Q_i)$ is a best response in the\n   continuation game starting at $Q_i$ under belief $\\mu(Q_i)$ and continuation\n   play $\\beta$;\n2. on every reached information set $Q\\in Rch(\\beta)$, beliefs are Bayes-compatible:\n   $$\n     \\mu(Q)=\\nu_\\beta(Q).\n   $$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.4.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Weak Bayesian perfect equilibrium as sequential rationality plus Bayes compatibility on path."

      "body": "# Agent Normal Form\n\nFor a perfect-recall extensive form game $\\Gamma$, the agent normal form\n$\\Gamma^a$ replaces each information set $Q$ of $\\Gamma$ by a distinct agent\n$i(Q)$.\n\nThe agent at $Q$ has the same payoff function as the original player who moves at\n$Q$. Thus a single original player is duplicated into a team of agents, one for\neach information set, all with common interests.\n\nSince each agent moves at most once, mixed and behavioral strategies coincide in\nthe agent normal form.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.6.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Agent normal form of a perfect-recall extensive form game."

      "body": "# Normal Form Invariance Of Extensive Representations\n\nTwo extensive forms can have the same normal form even when their trees and\ninformation sets look different. MFoGT records that extensive forms with the same\nnormal form can be linked by chains of elementary transformations: interchange of\nsimultaneous moves, coalescing of consecutive moves, and addition of superfluous\nmoves.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nThe statement is structural rather than an equilibrium theorem. Each elementary\ntransformation preserves the pure strategy sets up to canonical identification and\npreserves the outcome induced by every strategy profile. Chains of these moves\ntherefore preserve the normal form.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.3.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Extensive forms with the same normal form are related by elementary transformations."
    },

      "body": "# Normal Form Reduction\n\nThe normal form reduction of a perfect-information extensive game is the map\n$$\n  F:\\prod_{i\\in I} S_i\\to R\n$$\nthat sends each pure strategy profile to the unique terminal outcome it induces.\nComposing $F$ with terminal payoff functions gives an ordinary strategic game in\nnormal form.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.2.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Semi-Reduced Normal Form\n\nTwo strategies $s_i,t_i$ of player $i$ are payoff-equivalent if for every\n$s_{-i}$ and every player $j$,\n$$\n  g_j(s_i,s_{-i})=g_j(t_i,s_{-i}).\n$$\nThe semi-reduced normal form identifies payoff-equivalent strategies. This removes\ndifferences that occur only at positions excluded by the strategy itself.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Semi-reduced normal form identifies payoff-equivalent strategies."

      "body": "# Existence Of Sequential Equilibrium\n\nEvery finite extensive form game with perfect recall has at least one sequential\nequilibrium.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nMFoGT defers the proof to the following normal-form refinement section. The\nstrategy is to use fully mixed perturbations and compactness: perturbed games have\nequilibria, limits of perturbed behavioral profiles give sequentially rational\nstrategies, and the limiting beliefs are obtained as limits of Bayes-rule beliefs\nfrom the fully mixed profiles.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.4.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. The set of sequential equilibria of a finite perfect-recall extensive game is nonempty.\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.6.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Existence proof via Selten perturbations of the agent normal form."

      "body": "# Backward Induction Value\n\nFor a finite perfect-information game tree, the **backward-induction value** is\nthe payoff vector $\\operatorname{value} : \\texttt{GameTree} \\to (\\iota \\to U)$\ncomputed bottom-up:\n\n- at a leaf, the value is its payoff vector;\n- at a decision node with mover $m$, the value is that of the child the mover\n  prefers, i.e. the child maximizing coordinate $m$.\n\nThe only structural requirement on the payoff type $U$ is a total preorder\n(reflexivity, transitivity, totality); neither antisymmetry nor decidability is\nused. The mover's own coordinate dominates every child's value\n(`value_Node_ge`), and the chosen value is realized by some child\n(`value_Node_eq_some_child_value`). This value function and its optimality\nlemmas are the machinery behind Zermelo determinacy\n([[node:game_theory.extensive_game.perfect_information.subgame_perfect_equilibrium]])\nand Kuhn's subgame-perfect existence theorem.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 3] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Backward induction on finite perfect-information games."
    },

      "body": "# Determined Game\n\nA simple two-player game is determined if one of the two players has a winning\nstrategy.\n\nBecause the winning sets $R_1$ and $R_2$ are disjoint, both players cannot have\nwinning strategies simultaneously.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.2.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. A game is determined if one player has a winning strategy."

      "body": "# Generic Uniqueness Of Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium\n\nA finite perfect-information game, with or without Nature, with $K$ terminal nodes\nand $I$ players has generically a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium with respect\nto Lebesgue measure on the terminal payoff space.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nAfter excluding payoff parameters that create indifference during backward\ninduction, every decision point has a unique optimal continuation. The excluded\nparameters lie in lower-dimensional equality sets. Therefore, for generic terminal\npayoffs, backward induction selects a unique continuation at every node and hence\na unique subgame-perfect equilibrium.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 6.2.8] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Finite perfect-information games generically have a unique SPE."
    },

      "body": "# Kuhn Existence Of Pure Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium (No-Chance)\n\nEvery finite perfect-information game **without chance moves** has a\nsubgame-perfect equilibrium in pure strategies.\n\nFormally, on `GameTree N U` with `[TotalPreorder U]`, the strategy\n`optStrategy` produced by backward induction is subgame-perfect.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nBackward induction solves all terminal predecessor positions first. Replace each\nsuch position by the payoff generated by an optimal successor choice. The reduced\ntree is shorter, so induction gives a subgame-perfect strategy profile there.\nCombining the reduced-game strategy with the locally optimal choices at removed\npositions yields a pure strategy profile that is Nash in every subgame.\n\nThe Lean proof in `GameTreeSPE.lean` follows exactly this pattern, with the\n`GameTree.strong_induction` principle providing the size-decreasing induction\nhypothesis.\n\n## Scope\n\nThis node is the no-chance specialization of the MFoGT theorem cited below\n(stated there in \"with or without Nature\" form). The variant that allows\nchance/Nature nodes is tracked by [[kuhn_spe_existence_with_chance]] and the\nLean implementation is gated on the vNM theorem in\n`EconCSLib/Utility/Lottery.lean` (see\n[EG-L3 / #181](https://github.com/gametheoryinlean/EconCSLib/issues/181)).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.2.7] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Stated in the more general with-or-without-Nature form; the no-chance specialization is what is formalized here.\n- [MSZ, Thm. 3.13] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*.\n- Kuhn, H. W. (1953). \"Extensive Games and the Problem of Information.\" In *Contributions to the Theory of Games, Vol. II*."
    },

      "body": "# Kuhn Existence Of Pure Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium (With Chance)\n\nEvery finite perfect-information game **with Nature / chance moves** has a\nsubgame-perfect equilibrium in pure strategies. At a chance node the value is\nthe probability-weighted average of the successor subgame values under any\nfixed strategy profile.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nSame backward-induction skeleton as [[kuhn_spe_existence_no_chance]], extended\nto handle Nature nodes: at a chance position the player payoffs at that node\nare defined as the probability-weighted expectation of the successor payoffs,\nand the induction step is unchanged.\n\nThe expectation step requires von Neumann–Morgenstern utility theory so that\n\"expected payoff\" is meaningful for a general preference relation. With cash /\nℝ-valued payoffs the expectation is well-defined directly.\n\n## Lean status\n\nNot yet implemented. The\ntarget Lean module is `EconCSLib.ExtensiveGame.StochasticGameTree`; current\nstate is a type definition + `fairCoinGame` example, no general theorem.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.2.7] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Original \"with or without Nature\" form.\n- [MSZ, Thm. 3.13] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Finite Extensive Game With Perfect Information\n\nA finite extensive form game with perfect information consists of:\n\n1. a finite nonempty player set $I$;\n2. a finite tree of nodes $Z$ with origin $\\theta$ and predecessor map;\n3. terminal nodes $R$ and decision positions $P=Z\\setminus R$;\n4. a successor set $S(p)$ for each decision position $p$;\n5. a partition $(P_i)_{i\\in I}$ of decision positions by the player who moves;\n6. payoff functions $g_i:R\\to\\mathbb R$.\n\nPlay starts at $\\theta$, follows successor choices at decision positions, stops at a\nterminal node $r\\in R$, and gives player $i$ payoff $g_i(r)$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.2.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Description of a finite extensive form game with perfect information."

      "body": "# Strategy In A Perfect-Information Game\n\nFor a player $i$, a pure strategy is a function on $P_i$ that assigns to each\nposition $p\\in P_i$ a successor in $S(p)$. Thus a strategy specifies what the\nplayer would do at every position where that player might move, including\npositions that are not reached by the realized play.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.2.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. A strategy selects a successor at each position controlled by the player."

      "body": "# Simple Perfect-Information Game\n\nA two-player perfect-information game is simple if its terminal outcomes are\npartitioned into winning sets $(R_1,R_2)$, where reaching a terminal node in $R_i$\nmeans player $i$ wins and the other player loses.\n\nA winning strategy for player $i$ is a strategy $\\sigma_i$ such that, for every\nopponent strategy $\\sigma_{-i}$,\n$$\n  F(\\sigma_i,\\sigma_{-i})\\in R_i.\n$$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 6.2.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Two-player simple game with terminal outcomes partitioned into winners."

      "body": "# Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium Implies Nash Equilibrium\n\nIn a perfect-information game, every subgame-perfect equilibrium is a Nash\nequilibrium of the whole game.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nThe whole game is the subgame rooted at the origin. Since subgame perfection\nrequires the continuation profile to be Nash in every subgame, applying the\ndefinition at the origin gives the Nash condition for the original game.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.2.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Strictly Competitive Perfect-Information Determinacy\n\nEvery finite strictly competitive game with perfect information is determined.\n\nEquivalently, when terminal outcomes are interpreted as player 1 payoffs and\nplayer 2 has the opposite preference order, the game has a pure-strategy value.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nOrder outcomes by player 1's preference. Let $R_k$ be the smallest initial segment\nof outcomes that player 1 can guarantee. Player 1 can guarantee $R_k$, while by\nZermelo determinacy player 2 can guarantee the complement of $R_{k-1}$. This\nidentifies the threshold outcome and gives determinacy.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Cor. 6.2.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Every finite strictly competitive perfect-information game is determined."

      "body": "# Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium In Perfect-Information Games\n\nA strategy profile $\\sigma$ is subgame-perfect if for every position $p$, the\ncontinuation strategy profile $\\sigma[p]$ induced by $\\sigma$ is a Nash equilibrium\nof the subgame $G[p]$.\n\nThis strengthens Nash equilibrium by requiring optimality after every possible\nhistory, including histories not reached by the equilibrium play.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 6.2.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. A strategy profile is subgame-perfect if every continuation strategy is Nash in every subgame."

      "body": "# Zermelo Determinacy For Finite Perfect-Information Games\n\nEvery simple finite game with perfect information is determined.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nThe proof is by induction on the length of the tree. Each successor of the origin\ndefines a shorter subgame. By the induction hypothesis, each such subgame is\ndetermined and has value $+1$ or $-1$ according to which player can force a win.\nThe player who moves at the origin chooses a successor with the best value; if that\nvalue is favorable, that player wins, otherwise the opponent's winning strategy in\neach successor subgame wins.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 6.2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Every simple finite game with perfect information is determined."
    },

      "body": "# Value In Finite Zero-Sum Perfect-Information Games (No-Chance)\n\nEvery finite zero-sum perfect-information game **without chance moves** has a\nvalue, and both players have pure optimal strategies. On `GameTree (Fin 2) ℚ`\nsatisfying `IsZeroSum`, the player-0 root value (obtained via backward\ninduction) coincides with the max-min / min-max value, and player-1's value is\nits negation.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nBackward induction over the tree. If player 1 moves at a node, the value there\nis the maximum over successor values; if player 2 moves, the minimum. Leaves\ncontribute their payoff directly. Optimal pure strategies are obtained by\nchoosing an optimal successor at each own-move node and then following optimal\nstrategies in the selected subgame.\n\nThe Lean theorem `zermelo_determinacy` makes the value/optimality precise:\nplaying `optStrategy`, player 0 secures at least `value₀ g` and player 1 holds\nplayer 0 to at most `value₀ g`, so `value₀ g` is the (max-min = min-max) value\nattained by a pure strategy on both sides. The packaging lemma\n`value₀_eq_outcome_and_zeroSum` records that `optStrategy` realizes `value₀ g`\nand that the value vector is zero-sum (`value g 1 = -value₀ g`).\n\n## Scope\n\nThis is the no-chance specialization of the MFoGT proposition cited below\n(stated there in \"with or without Nature\" form). The variant with chance /\nNature nodes lives at [[zero_sum_perfect_information_value_with_chance]] and is\ngated on [EG-L3 / #181](https://github.com/gametheoryinlean/EconCSLib/issues/181).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 6.2.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Stated in the more general with-or-without-Nature form.\n- [Zermelo 1913] *Über eine Anwendung der Mengenlehre auf die Theorie des Schachspiels*."
    },

      "body": "# Value In Finite Zero-Sum Perfect-Information Games (With Chance)\n\nEvery finite zero-sum perfect-information game **with Nature / chance moves**\nhas a value, and both players have pure optimal strategies. At a chance node,\nthe value equals the probability-weighted average of the successor subgame\nvalues.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nSame forward / backward induction as\n[[zero_sum_perfect_information_value_no_chance]], with one extra case: at a\nNature node the value is the probability-weighted expectation over the\nsuccessor values. The minimax / maximin equality at player nodes is unaffected\nbecause expectation is linear and player choice still optimizes over a finite\nset.\n\n## Lean status\n\nImplemented in `EconCSLib.ExtensiveGame.ZeroSumGameTreeWithChance` (EG-L6, #220).\nThe key declarations are:\n\n- `ZeroSumChance.GameTree` — binary game tree with `Leaf`, `Pnode`, `Nnode`.\n- `ZeroSumChance.GameTree.value` — backward-induction value (computable).\n- `ZeroSumChance.GameTree.DStrategy` — A's dominant strategy.\n- `ZeroSumChance.GameTree.outcome` — payoff under a strategy pair.\n- `ZeroSumChance.GameTree.value_prop` — `t.value ≤ t.outcome DStrategy SB`.\n\nThe ℚ-valued port requires no vNM theorem; rational arithmetic handles chance\naveraging directly. The fully general n-player + arbitrary utility version\nremains in `EconCSLib.ExtensiveGame.StochasticGameTree` and is blocked on\nvNM (EG-L3 #181).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 6.2.5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Original \"with or without Nature\" form."

Each row links to the dedicated knowledge node and\nthe module that contains the proof.\n\nFor the analogous strategic-game / zero-sum catalog see\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.finite_game_catalog]].\n\n---\n\n## Catalog\n\n### 1.       "body": "# Discounted Repeated Game\n\nFor discount rate $\\lambda\\in(0,1]$, the discounted repeated game $G^\\lambda$\nevaluates player $i$ by\n$$\n  \\gamma_\\lambda^i(\\sigma)\n  =\n  \\mathbb E_\\sigma\\left[\n    \\lambda\\sum_{t=1}^\\infty (1-\\lambda)^{t-1}g_i(a_t)\n  \\right].\n$$\n\nSmall $\\lambda$ corresponds to patient players. MFoGT uses normalized discounted\npayoffs, so a constant stream $c$ has value $c$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 8, Def. 8.3.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Infinite repeated game with normalized discount rate."
    },

      "body": "# Repeated Feasible Individually Rational Payoffs\n\nFor a finite stage game, the repeated-game feasible payoff set is the convex hull\nof pure action payoff vectors:\n$$\n  \\operatorname{co} g(A)=g(\\Delta(A)).\n$$\n\nFor each player $i$, the independent minmax level is\n$$\n  v_i=\n  \\min_{x_{-i}\\in\\prod_{j\\ne i}\\Delta(A_j)}\n  \\max_{x_i\\in\\Delta(A_i)}g_i(x_i,x_{-i}).\n$$\nThe feasible and individually rational set is\n$$\n  E=\\{u\\in\\operatorname{co} g(A):u_i\\ge v_i\\text{ for every }i\\}.\n$$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 8, Definitions 8.4.1 to 8.4.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Feasible payoffs, independent minmax levels, and individually rational payoffs."
    },

      "body": "# Finitely Repeated Game\n\nFor $T\\ge 1$, the $T$-stage repeated game $G^T$ evaluates a strategy profile by\nthe expected average payoff\n$$\n  \\gamma_T^i(\\sigma)\n  =\n  \\mathbb E_\\sigma\\left[\n    \\frac1T\\sum_{t=1}^T g_i(a_t)\n  \\right].\n$$\n\nBecause only the first $T$ stages matter, $G^T$ may be treated as a finite\nextensive-form game.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 8, Def. 8.3.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. T-stage repeated game with average payoff."

      "id": "game_theory.repeated_game.core.history",
      "title": "Repeated Game History",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "staged",
      "evidence": "non-admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.repeated_game",
      "topics": [
        "game_theory.repeated_game",

        "game_theory.repeated_game.core.repeated_game"

      "used_by": [
        "game_theory.repeated_game.core.payoff_aggregation"
      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/staged/repeated_game/history.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Repeated Game History\n\nFor a repeated game with stage action profile space $A = \\prod_i A_i$\n([[game_theory.repeated_game.core.repeated_game]]), a **length-$t$ history** is a\nsequence of $t$ past action profiles:\n$$\nh_t = (a_0, a_1, \\dots, a_{t-1}) \\in A^t.\n$$\n\nThe empty history $h_0 = \\emptyset$ corresponds to stage 0 before any\nplay occurs.\n\n## Strategy spaces over histories\n\n- A **pure strategy** for player $i$ is a function\n  $\\sigma_i : \\bigcup_t A^t \\to A_i$ that picks an action for every\n  possible history.\n- A **behavioural strategy** is\n  $\\sigma_i : \\bigcup_t A^t \\to \\Delta(A_i)$.\n\nThe set of all possible histories $\\bigcup_t A^t$ is countably infinite\neven for finite $A$, so the strategy space is enormous. Equilibrium\narguments typically restrict to:\n\n- **Automaton strategies**: strategies implementable by a finite-state\n  automaton reading $h_t$ — the standard tool for folk-theorem\n  constructions (grim trigger, tit-for-tat, etc.).\n- **Markovian / Markov-1 strategies**: depend only on the last action\n  profile $a_{t-1}$ (or short-memory variants).\n\n## Observability variants\n\nThe \"public history\" assumption above gives every player the entire\n$h_t$. Other observability structures yield different games:\n\n- *Private monitoring*: each player observes only their own action and\n  a private signal correlated with the action profile.\n- *Public-imperfect monitoring*: all players observe the same public\n  signal, but not the underlying action profile.\n\nThese are central to dynamic mechanism design and reputation theory; the\nfolk theorem changes form in the imperfect-monitoring setting\n(Fudenberg-Levine-Maskin 1994).\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Chapter 13] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*.\n- Mailath, G. and Samuelson, L. (2006). *Repeated Games and Reputations.* Oxford.\n- [MFoGT Chapter 8] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*."
    }

        "refs": [

        "missing_from_uses": []

      "body": "# Antisymmetric Matrix Game Has Value Zero\n\nA square matrix $B : I \\times I \\to \\mathbb{R}$ is **antisymmetric** if\n$B = -B^{\\mathsf{T}}$, i.e. $B_{ij} = -B_{ji}$ for all $i,j$ (so in particular\n$B_{ii} = 0$). The matrix game $B$ then has value $0$, and there exists\n$x \\in \\Delta(I)$ such that $(Bx)_i \\le 0$ for every row $i$.\n\n*Proof.* By the minimax theorem\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) the game has a\nvalue $v$. Antisymmetry gives $z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z = 0$ for every mixed $z$, since\n$z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z = -z^{\\mathsf{T}} B^{\\mathsf{T}} z = -(z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z)$.\nApplying this to an optimal $x^\\ast$ for player I,\n$0 = \\sum_j x^\\ast_j (e_j B x^\\ast)$ while each $e_j B x^\\ast \\ge v$, forcing\n$v \\le 0$; the symmetric argument gives $v \\ge 0$, so $v = 0$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 10(1)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Antisymmetric matrix games have value zero."
    },

      "used_by": [],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/zero_sum/applications/markov_stationary_as_zero_sum_value.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []

      "body": "# Markov Stationary Distribution as Zero-Sum Game Value\n\n**Lemma.** Let $A : I \\times I \\to \\mathbb{R}$ be a row-stochastic\nmatrix (entries $\\ge 0$, every row sums to 1), and consider the\n*displacement game* with payoff matrix $B := A - \\operatorname{Id}$.\nThen:\n\n1. The displacement game has value $\\operatorname{val}(B) = 0$.\n2. Every row-optimal mixed strategy $x^* \\in X(B)$ for player 1 is a\n   **stationary distribution** of $A$:\n   $x^* A = x^*$.\n\nThis is the proof structure underlying\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.applications.stochastic_matrix_invariant_distribution]] —\nthe classical von Neumann construction translating\n\"Markov stationary distribution exists\" into \"an optimal mixed\nstrategy in a particular zero-sum game\".\n\n## Why this is a useful framing\n\nThe standard textbook proof of Markov stationary-distribution existence\nuses Brouwer's fixed-point theorem on $\\Delta(I)$. The\nzero-sum-game-theoretic proof bypasses Brouwer entirely:\n\n- Apply the minimax theorem\n  ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) to the displacement game\n  $B = A - \\operatorname{Id}$ — this gives existence of optimal\n  strategies for free.\n- Reduce stationarity to the *saddle-point characterisation* of those\n  optimal strategies (player 1's guarantee inequality, summed across\n  columns, forces equality on every column).\n\nThe whole argument is purely algebraic / combinatorial once minimax is\nin hand, which is itself proved by Loomis induction\n([[math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]) — no topology required.\nThis is a satisfying application of zero-sum theory to elementary\nMarkov-chain theory.\n\n## Bridge to the main theorem\n\nThe detailed argument lives in\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.applications.stochastic_matrix_invariant_distribution]]\n(MFoGT Cor. 2.5.2): the three-step proof there is\n\n1. Show $\\operatorname{val}(B) = 0$ (this lemma's statement 1) by\n   exhibiting matching upper and lower bounds.\n2. Take any $x^* \\in X(B)$; saddle-point inequality gives\n   $x^* A \\ge x^*$ componentwise.\n3. Sum across $j$ and use row-stochasticity: total mass forces\n   $x^* A = x^*$ pointwise.\n\nThis node is the *conceptual restatement* of that argument — the\nunderlying meta-pattern is \"minimax theorem + saddle-point\ncharacterisation + a counting / mass-balance step ⇒ existence of a\nmatrix-algebraic object\".\n\n## References\n\n- von Neumann's original 1928 paper already contains this technique.\n- [MFoGT Cor. 2.5.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.\n- Owen, G. (1995). *Game Theory*. Ch. 3."
    },

      "title": "Perron-Frobenius For Positive Matrices",
      "kind": "theorem",
      "status": "proved",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.zero_sum",
      "topics": [
        "game_theory.zero_sum",
        "game_theory.zero_sum.applications"
      ],
      "uses": [
        "math.minimax.loomis_theorem"
      ],
      "used_by": [],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/zero_sum/applications/perron_frobenius_positive_matrix.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [
          {
            "target_id": "math.minimax.loomis_theorem",
            "known": true,
            "in_uses": true
          }
        ],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Perron-Frobenius For Positive Matrices\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $M \\in \\mathbb{R}^{n \\times n}$ be a square matrix whose entries are\nstrictly positive: $M_{ij} > 0$ for every $i, j$. Then there exist\n$x \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, $y \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, and\n$\\lambda > 0$ such that\n\n- $x$ and $y$ have **strictly positive components**;\n- $xM = \\lambda\\, x$ (so $x$ is a left eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\\lambda$);\n- $My = \\lambda\\, y$ (so $y$ is a right eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\\lambda$).\n\nThe Loomis value $v$ of the pair $(I, M)$ (identity matrix vs. $M$)\nprovides $\\lambda = 1/v$.\n\n## Proof\n\nApply the general-$B$ Loomis theorem\n([[node:math.minimax.loomis_theorem]]) with $A := I$ (the $n \\times n$\nidentity matrix) and $B := M$. Since $M_{ij} > 0$, the hypothesis\n`IsPositive M` is satisfied. Loomis produces\n$x \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, $y \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, and\n$v \\in \\mathbb{R}$ such that\n\n- $(1)\\quad \\forall j,\\quad v \\cdot (xM)_j \\le x_j$  (from $xI \\ge v \\cdot xM$,\n  using $xI = x$);\n- $(2)\\quad \\forall i,\\quad y_i \\le v \\cdot (My)_i$  (from $Iy \\le v \\cdot My$,\n  using $Iy = y$).\n\n**Step 1: $v > 0$.** Pick $i_0$ with $y_{i_0} > 0$ (which exists because\n$\\sum y_i = 1$). Inequality (2) at $i_0$ gives\n$y_{i_0} \\le v \\cdot (My)_{i_0}$. Since $M > 0$ entrywise and $y \\ge 0$ has\n$y_{i_0} > 0$ (hence $\\sum y_j M_{i_0, j} > 0$), $(My)_{i_0} > 0$.\nTherefore $0 < y_{i_0} \\le v \\cdot (My)_{i_0}$ forces $v > 0$.\n\n**Step 2: $x$ and $y$ are strictly positive.** For every $j$,\n$(xM)_j = \\sum_i x_i M_{ij} > 0$ because $x \\in \\Delta$ has at least one\npositive entry and $M > 0$ entrywise. Combined with (1), $x_j \\ge v \\cdot\n(xM)_j > 0$. So $x_j > 0$ for all $j$. By the same argument applied to (2)\nand $y$, $(My)_i > 0$ and $y_i > 0$ for all $i$.\n\n**Step 3: Tight inner-product sandwich.** Compute\n$$\n  \\langle x, y\\rangle - v\\cdot \\langle xM, y\\rangle\n  = \\sum_j (x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j) \\cdot y_j \\ge 0\n$$\n(each summand is nonneg by (1) and $y_j \\ge 0$). And by\n$\\langle xM, y\\rangle = \\sum_j \\sum_i x_i M_{ij} y_j = \\langle x, My\\rangle$,\n$$\n  v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle - \\langle x, y\\rangle\n  = v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle - \\langle x, y\\rangle.\n$$\nWeighting (2) by $x \\ge 0$ and summing,\n$\\langle x, y\\rangle \\le v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle$. Therefore\n$$\n  \\langle x, y\\rangle \\;\\ge\\; v \\cdot \\langle xM, y\\rangle \\;=\\; v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle \\;\\ge\\; \\langle x, y\\rangle,\n$$\nso both inequalities are tight.\n\n**Step 4: Componentwise equality.** From Step 3,\n$\\sum_j (x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j) \\cdot y_j = 0$. Each summand is nonneg (by\n(1)) and $y_j > 0$ strict (by Step 2). For the nonneg sum to vanish, each\nsummand must vanish, so $x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j = 0$, i.e., $x_j = v \\cdot\n(xM)_j$ for every $j$. As a row-vector identity, $xM = (1/v) \\cdot x$.\n\nDually, $\\sum_i (v \\cdot (My)_i - y_i) \\cdot x_i = 0$ with each summand\nnonneg and $x_i > 0$ strict, so $y_i = v \\cdot (My)_i$, i.e.,\n$My = (1/v) \\cdot y$.\n\nSetting $\\lambda := 1/v > 0$, we have $xM = \\lambda \\cdot x$ (left\neigenvector) and $My = \\lambda \\cdot y$ (right eigenvector), both with\n$x, y$ strictly positive. $\\square$\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The argument is purely algebraic and works over $\\mathbb{R}$ (where\n  general-$B$ Loomis is formalised in `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.Loomis`).\n- Strict positivity of $x$ and $y$ is automatic given strict positivity of\n  $M$, **without** needing a separate \"irreducibility\" argument.\n- The same Loomis instance simultaneously produces the **left** eigenvector\n  $x$ and the **right** eigenvector $y$ at the same eigenvalue $\\lambda\n  = 1/v$. This eigenvalue is the **Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue** of $M$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 1(2)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Application of Loomis theorem\n  to positive matrices."
    },

      "body": "# Stochastic Matrix Has An Invariant Distribution\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $A : I \\times I \\to \\mathbb{R}$ be a (row-)stochastic matrix: every\nentry is non-negative and every row sums to $1$. Then there exists a\nmixed strategy $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ such that\n\n$$\n  \\forall j,\\quad \\sum_i x_i \\, A_{ij} = x_j\n$$\n\n— i.e. $x A = x$, an **invariant distribution** of $A$.\n\n## Proof\n\nLet $B := A - \\operatorname{Id}$, i.e. $B_{ij} = A_{ij} - [i=j]$, and\nconsider the matrix game with payoff matrix $B$.\n\n### Step 1 — The displacement game has value $0$\n\n**Upper bound $v \\le 0$.** Take Player 2's uniform mixed strategy\n$y_{\\mathrm{unif}}$ with $y_j = 1 / |I|$. For every pure row $i$:\n$$\n  E_i(i, y_{\\mathrm{unif}}) = \\sum_j B_{ij} \\cdot \\tfrac{1}{|I|}\n    = \\tfrac{1}{|I|} \\big(\\!\\sum_j A_{ij}\\big) - \\tfrac{1}{|I|}\n    = \\tfrac{1}{|I|} - \\tfrac{1}{|I|} = 0,\n$$\nusing $\\sum_j A_{ij} = 1$. Hence Player 2's guarantee under\n$y_{\\mathrm{unif}}$ is $\\sup_i E_i(i, y_{\\mathrm{unif}}) = 0$. Since\n$\\mathrm{value} = \\mathrm{minimax} = \\inf_y \\mathrm{guarantee}_{II}(y)$,\nwe get $\\mathrm{value} \\le 0$.\n\n**Lower bound $v \\ge 0$.** For any column strategy $y$, pick\n$i_0 \\in \\arg\\min_j y_j$. Since $A_{i_0 j} \\ge 0$, $y_j \\ge y_{i_0}$,\nand $\\sum_j A_{i_0 j} = 1$:\n$$\n  (A y)_{i_0} \\;=\\; \\sum_j A_{i_0 j}\\, y_j\n                \\;\\ge\\; \\sum_j A_{i_0 j}\\, y_{i_0}\n                \\;=\\; y_{i_0} \\cdot 1 \\;=\\; y_{i_0}.\n$$\nTherefore $E_i(i_0, y) = (Ay)_{i_0} - y_{i_0} \\ge 0$, and\n$\\mathrm{guarantee}_{II}(y) = \\sup_i E_i(i, y) \\ge 0$ for every $y$.\nHence $\\mathrm{minimax} = \\inf_y \\mathrm{guarantee}_{II}(y) \\ge 0$.\n\nCombining, $\\mathrm{value} = 0$.\n\n### Step 2 — A row-optimal strategy is invariant\n\nTake any row-optimal $x^* \\in X(A)$ — existence via\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.matrix_game_nash_equilibrium]] combined with\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.optimal_strategy_sets]]. Then for every pure column $j$,\n$$\n  E_j(x^*, j) \\;\\ge\\; \\mathrm{value} \\;=\\; 0.\n$$\nExpanding $E_j(x^*, j) = (x^* A)_j - x^*_j$, we get\n$(x^* A)_j \\ge x^*_j$ for every $j$, i.e. $x^* A \\ge x^*$\ncomponentwise.\n\n### Step 3 — Total mass forces componentwise equality\n\nSum over $j$. Using $\\sum_j A_{ij} = 1$ and $\\sum_i x^*_i = 1$:\n$$\n  \\sum_j (x^* A)_j = \\sum_i x^*_i \\!\\sum_j A_{ij} = \\sum_i x^*_i = 1\n    = \\sum_j x^*_j.\n$$\nHence $\\sum_j ((x^* A)_j - x^*_j) = 0$, with every term $\\ge 0$, so\nevery term is exactly $0$:\n$$\n  \\forall j,\\quad (x^* A)_j = x^*_j.\n$$\n\nSo $x^*$ is an invariant distribution. $\\square$\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The argument is constructive once an optimal pair is given by\n  the minimax existence theorem ([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]).\n- The choice $B = A - \\operatorname{Id}$ converts \"$x A = x$\" into the\n  saddle-point condition for the matrix game with payoff $B$.\n- The Lean implementation lives in\n  `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.StochasticMatrix` and consists of:\n  - `IsStochasticMatrix` — predicate (rows sum to 1, entries ≥ 0).\n  - `uniformDist` — uniform mixed strategy on a `Nonempty` `Fintype`.\n  - `MatrixGame.exists_invariant_distribution` — main theorem.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Cor. 2.5.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Invariant distribution of a stochastic matrix from minimax."
    },

      "body": "# Strict Domination And Never Best Response\n\nIn a finite strategic game, a mixed strategy $m_i\\in\\Delta(S_i)$ is strictly\ndominated if and only if it is never a best response against any correlated\nstrategy of the opponents.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nIf $m_i$ is strictly dominated by $\\sigma_i$, linearity of expected payoff extends\nthe strict inequality to every correlated strategy of the opponents, so $m_i$\ncannot be a best response.\n\nConversely, form the two-player zero-sum game in which player $i$ compares the\npayoff of a pure action $t_i$ with the payoff of the fixed mixed strategy $m_i$.\nThe hypothesis that $m_i$ is never a best response implies that the auxiliary\nzero-sum game has strictly positive value. An optimal strategy in that game then\nstrictly dominates $m_i$ in the original game.\n\n## Why this lives under `zero_sum.applications`\n\nThis proposition is a strategic-game result, but the MFoGT proof route\nis structural in [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]: the\n\"$m_i$ is never a best response $\\Rightarrow$ strictly dominated\"\ndirection is established by constructing an auxiliary two-player\nzero-sum game and extracting a dominating strategy from its\nminimax-optimal strategy. Filing the node under `zero_sum.applications`\nreflects the proof technique and keeps the top-level `strategic_games`\ntopic from depending back on `zero_sum`. A separation-theorem proof à\nla Pearce 1984 is available as an alternative and would substitute a\nTheorem-of-the-Alternative citation in `math.linear_algebra`; the\nMFoGT route is chosen here for alignment with the rest of the library's\nzero-sum infrastructure.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 4.3.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Strict domination is equivalent to never being a best response against a correlated strategy."

      "body": "# Weak Domination And Completely Mixed Tests\n\nIn a finite strategic game, a mixed strategy $m_i\\in\\Delta(S_i)$ is weakly\ndominated if and only if it is never a best response against a completely\ncorrelated strategy of the opponents.\n\nHere \"completely correlated\" means a correlated strategy in the relative interior\nof $\\Delta(S_{-i})$, assigning positive probability to every opponent profile.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nWeak domination gives a strict expected-payoff improvement against every\nfull-support correlated opponent strategy, so $m_i$ is not a best response to any\nof them. For the converse, MFoGT reduces to an auxiliary finite zero-sum game. If\nthe value is positive then strict domination follows. If the value is zero, optimal\nsupport and best-response complementarity identify an opponent pure profile\nagainst which an optimal strategy gives a strict improvement while never lowering\nthe payoff elsewhere.\n\n## Why this lives under `zero_sum.applications`\n\nThis proposition is a strategic-game result, but the MFoGT 4.3.6 proof\nroute is structural in [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.support_complementarity]]:\nthe converse uses both the value of the auxiliary zero-sum game and\nsupport/best-response complementarity to extract a separating opponent\nprofile. Filing the node under `zero_sum.applications` reflects the\nproof technique and keeps the top-level `strategic_games` topic from\ndepending back on `zero_sum`. A separation-theorem proof à la Pearce\n1984, which would let the result live under\n`strategic_games.dominance` while citing only\n`math.linear_algebra.theorem_of_alternative`, is an alternative route.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 4.3.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Weak domination is equivalent to never being a best response against a completely correlated strategy."

      "body": "# Compact Mixed Versus Finite-Support Minimax\n\nLet $(S,T,g)$ be a zero-sum game such that $S$ is compact Hausdorff and\n$g(\\cdot,t)$ is upper semicontinuous for every $t\\in T$. Then the mixed game\n$$\n  (\\Delta(S),\\Delta_f(T),g)\n$$\nhas a value, and player 1 has an optimal strategy.\n\n*Proof.* The space $\\Delta(S)$ is compact in the weak-star topology, and integration\npreserves upper semicontinuity of $g(\\cdot,t)$. The payoff is bilinear on\n$\\Delta(S)\\times\\Delta_f(T)$. Thus the one-sided compact convex minimax theorem\napplies.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 3.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. The game (Delta(S), Delta_f(T), g) has a value under compactness and upper semicontinuity."

      "body": "# Finite-Opponent Separation Minimax\n\nAssume:\n\n1. $S$ is a measurable space and $X$ is a nonempty convex set of probability\n   measures over $S$;\n2. $T$ is a finite nonempty set;\n3. $g:S\\times T\\to\\mathbb R$ is measurable and bounded.\n\nThen the game $(X,\\Delta(T),g)$ has a value, and player 2 has an optimal strategy.\n\n*Proof.* Let $v=\\sup_X\\inf_T g(x,t)$. Consider the convex payoff-vector set\n$$\n  D=\\{(g(x,t))_{t\\in T}:x\\in X\\}\\subseteq\\mathbb R^T\n$$\nand the upper orthant $C=\\{a:a_t\\ge v+\\epsilon\\text{ for all }t\\}$. These two\nconvex sets are disjoint. A separating hyperplane gives nonnegative weights on\n$T$, normalized to a mixed strategy $y\\in\\Delta(T)$, such that\n$g(x,y)\\le v+\\epsilon$ for all $x\\in X$. Letting $\\epsilon\\downarrow0$ gives the\nvalue, and compactness of $\\Delta(T)$ gives an optimal strategy for player 2.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 3.3.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Separation proof of minimax when the minimizing player's pure strategy set is finite."

      "body": "# General Mixed Minimax Theorem\n\nLet $G=(S,T,g)$ be a zero-sum game such that:\n\n1. $S$ and $T$ are compact Hausdorff topological spaces;\n2. for each $t\\in T$, $g(\\cdot,t)$ is upper semicontinuous, and for each $s\\in S$,\n   $g(s,\\cdot)$ is lower semicontinuous;\n3. $g$ is bounded and measurable for the product Borel sigma-algebra.\n\nThen the mixed extension\n$$\n  (\\Delta(S),\\Delta(T),g)\n$$\nhas a value. Each player has a mixed optimal strategy, and for every\n$\\epsilon>0$ each player has an $\\epsilon$-optimal strategy with finite support.\n\n*Proof.* Apply the compact mixed-versus-finite-support minimax proposition twice: once to\n$(\\Delta(S),\\Delta_f(T),g)$ and once dually to $(\\Delta_f(S),\\Delta(T),g)$. Let\n$v^+$ and $v^-$ be the resulting values. Optimal strategies $\\sigma$ and $\\tau$\nfor the two one-sided games satisfy inequalities against all pure opponent\nstrategies. Fubini's theorem gives\n$$\n  v^+\\le \\int g\\,d(\\sigma\\otimes\\tau)\\le v^-.\n$$\nSince always $v^-\\le v^+$, equality follows.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 3.3.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Mixed minimax theorem for compact Hausdorff strategy spaces."

      "body_refs": {

      "body": "# Intersection Lemma\n\nLet $C_1,\\ldots,C_n$ be nonempty convex compact subsets of a Euclidean space.\nAssume that $\\bigcup_{i=1}^n C_i$ is convex and that every intersection of\n$n-1$ of the sets is nonempty:\n$$\n  \\bigcap_{i\\ne j} C_i\\ne\\emptyset\n  \\quad\\text{for every }j=1,\\ldots,n.\n$$\nThen\n$$\n  \\bigcap_{i=1}^n C_i\\ne\\emptyset.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* The proof is by induction on $n$. The case $n=2$ uses strict separation of two\ndisjoint compact convex sets: if $C_1$ and $C_2$ were disjoint, their convex union\nwould have to cross the separating hyperplane, contradiction. For the induction\nstep, separate $C_n$ from $\\bigcap_{i<n}C_i$ and intersect the other sets with the\nseparating hyperplane. The induction hypothesis applied in the hyperplane gives a\npoint that contradicts strict separation.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Lem. 3.2.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Convex compact intersection lemma used in Sion's theorem."

      "body": "# Monotone Decreasing Values Limit\n\nLet $G_n=(S,T,f_n)$ be a family of zero-sum games such that:\n\n1. $(f_n)$ is a weakly decreasing sequence of uniformly bounded functions\n   $S\\times T\\to\\mathbb R$;\n2. each $f_n$ is upper semicontinuous in the first variable;\n3. each $G_n$ has a value $v_n$;\n4. $S$ is compact.\n\nLet $f=\\inf_n f_n$. Then the game $G=(S,T,f)$ has value\n$$\n  v=\\inf_n v_n,\n$$\nand player 1 has an optimal strategy in $G$.\n\n*Proof.* The values $v_n$ form a decreasing bounded sequence, so\n$v=\\inf_n v_n$ exists. For each $n$, let $S_n(\\varepsilon)$ be the closed set of\nstrategies in $S$ that guarantee at least $v_n-\\varepsilon$ in game $G_n$.\nUpper semicontinuity in the first variable and compactness of $S$ make these\nsets compact, and monotonicity of the payoffs makes them nested after replacing\n$\\varepsilon$ by a summable sequence. Compactness gives a common limit strategy\n$s^*$. Since $f=\\inf_n f_n$, this strategy guarantees at least $v$ in the limit\ngame. Conversely, every strategy's guarantee in $f$ is bounded above by its\nguarantee in each $f_n$, hence by $v_n$; taking the infimum over $n$ gives an\nupper bound $v$. Thus $G$ has value $v$ and $s^*$ is optimal for player $1$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Limit of values for a decreasing family of upper-semicontinuous zero-sum games."

      "body": "# Monotone Family Assumption Counterexamples\n\nMFoGT Exercise 3.5.3(2) gives two one-player examples showing why the hypotheses\nin the monotone-family value theorem are not cosmetic.\n\nIn the first example,\n$$\n  S=[0,+\\infty),\\qquad f_n(s)=\\mathbf 1_{s\\ge n}.\n$$\nFor each $n$, the value is $v_n=1$, but the pointwise infimum has value $0$.\nThe failure is that $S$ is not compact.\n\nIn the second example, $S=[0,1]$ is compact and $f_n$ is continuous and\npiecewise linear with\n$$\n  f_n(0)=f_n(2/n)=f_n(1)=0,\\qquad f_n(1/n)=1.\n$$\nAgain $v_n=1$ for each $n$, while the limiting value is $0$. The failure is that\nthe sequence $(f_n)$ is not monotone decreasing.\n\nThese examples explain the role of compactness of $S$ and monotone decrease of\nthe payoff sequence in `zero_sum.continuous.monotone_decreasing_values_limit`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 3(2)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Examples showing why compactness and monotonicity assumptions matter in the monotone-family value theorem.\n- [MFoGT, Section 9.3, Exercise 3 hints] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Both examples have v_n=1 and limiting value 0."

      "body": "# One-Sided Compact Convex Minimax\n\nLet $G=(S,T,g)$ be a zero-sum game. Assume:\n\n1. $S$ is convex and compact;\n2. $T$ is convex;\n3. for each $t\\in T$, $g(\\cdot,t)$ is quasi-concave and upper semicontinuous;\n4. for each $s\\in S$, $g(s,\\cdot)$ is convex.\n\nThen\n$$\n  \\sup_{s\\in S}\\inf_{t\\in T}g(s,t)\n  =\n  \\inf_{t\\in T}\\sup_{s\\in S}g(s,t),\n$$\nand player 1 has an optimal strategy.\n\n*Proof.* Assume a strict gap around $v$.       "body": "# Quasi-Concavity And Semicontinuity\n\nLet $E$ be a convex subset of a vector space. A function $f:E\\to\\mathbb R$ is\nquasi-concave if every upper section\n$$\n  \\{x\\in E:f(x)\\ge\\lambda\\}\n$$\nis convex. It is quasi-convex if $-f$ is quasi-concave.\n\nIf $E$ is a topological space, $f$ is upper semicontinuous if every upper section is\nclosed. It is lower semicontinuous if $-f$ is upper semicontinuous.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 3.2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Sion Boundary Counterexample\n\nLet $S=T=[0,1]$ and define $f:S\\times T\\to\\{0,-1\\}$ by\n$$\n  f(s,t)=\n  \\begin{cases}\n    -1, & t=0\\text{ and }s<1/2,\\\\\n    -1, & t=1\\text{ and }s\\ge 1/2,\\\\\n    0, & \\text{otherwise}.\n  \\end{cases}\n$$\nThis game has no value in pure strategies, while Sion's hypotheses fail only at\nthe boundary point $t=1$.\n\nThe pure quantities are\n$$\n  \\sup_s\\inf_t f(s,t)=-1,\\qquad \\inf_t\\sup_s f(s,t)=0.\n$$\nNevertheless, the mixed extension does have a value, equal to $-1/2$. Player 1\ncan guarantee this by playing uniformly on $[0,1]$, or by mixing equally between\n$0$ and $1$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Counterexample satisfying Sion hypotheses except at one boundary point.\n- [MFoGT, Section 9.3, Exercise 2 hints] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Sion Minimax Theorem\n\nLet $G=(S,T,g)$ be a zero-sum game where $S$ and $T$ are subsets of Hausdorff\ntopological real vector spaces. Assume:\n\n1. $S$ and $T$ are convex;\n2. at least one of $S,T$ is compact;\n3. for each $t\\in T$, $g(\\cdot,t)$ is quasi-concave and upper semicontinuous in\n   $s$;\n4. for each $s\\in S$, $g(s,\\cdot)$ is quasi-convex and lower semicontinuous in\n   $t$.\n\nThen $G$ has a value:\n$$\n  \\sup_{s\\in S}\\inf_{t\\in T}g(s,t)\n  =\n  \\inf_{t\\in T}\\sup_{s\\in S}g(s,t).\n$$\nMoreover, if $S$ is compact then player 1 has an optimal strategy, and if $T$ is\ncompact then player 2 has an optimal strategy.\n\n*Proof.* Assume, for example, that $S$ is compact and suppose the two sides are separated\nby a real number $v$. Open-cover compactness first reduces to finite subsets of\nstrategies, then to compact convex hulls. Minimality of the finite reduction and the\nintersection lemma produce a point $t_0$ against which all reduced player-1\nstrategies yield payoff greater than $v$, and symmetrically a point $s_0$ against\nwhich all reduced player-2 strategies yield payoff less than $v$. The value\n$g(s_0,t_0)$ gives a contradiction.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 3.2.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Pure-strategy minimax theorem under convexity, compactness, and semicontinuity hypotheses."
    },

      "body": "# Sion-Wolfe Game Has No Mixed Value\n\nLet $S=T=[0,1]$ with the Borel sigma-algebra and define\n$$\n  f(s,t)=\n  \\begin{cases}\n    -1, & s<t<s+1/2,\\\\\n    0, & t=s\\text{ or }t=s+1/2,\\\\\n    1, & \\text{otherwise}.\n  \\end{cases}\n$$\nFor the mixed extension over $\\Delta(S)$ and $\\Delta(T)$, MFoGT's exercise states\nthat\n$$\n  \\sup_{\\sigma\\in\\Delta(S)}\\inf_{t\\in T} f(\\sigma,t)=\\frac13,\n$$\nand asks to prove that the mixed game has no value.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 7] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body_refs": {
