      "body": "# Duality Gap In A Matrix Game\n\nFor a finite matrix game with bilinear payoff $g(x,y)=xAy$, define\n$$\n  L(y)=\\max_{x'\\in\\Delta(I)} g(x',y),\n  \\qquad\n  M(x)=\\min_{y'\\in\\Delta(J)} g(x,y').\n$$\nThe **point-wise duality gap** at $(x,y)$ is\n$$\n  W(x,y)=L(y)-M(x)\\ge 0.\n$$\n\nThe gap is zero exactly when $x$ and $y$ are optimal strategies: $W(x,y)=0$\nsays the best payoff player I can obtain against $y$ equals the worst payoff\nplayer I can secure with $x$, so the two one-sided guarantees meet at the\nvalue.\n\nThe Lean development uses the finite-mixed-strategy specialisation\n`L(y) = A.guarantee_II y` (maximum over pure rows) and\n`M(x) = A.guarantee_I x` (minimum over pure columns); the Loomis-style\norder-characterisation lemmas turn this into the full bilinear gap.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.7, proof of Prop. 2.7.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. L(y), M(x), and W(x,y)=L(y)-M(x) used for continuous fictitious play."
    },

      "body": "# Epsilon-Optimal Strategy\n\nGiven $\\varepsilon>0$, a row strategy $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ is **maxmin\n$\\varepsilon$-optimal** if its guarantee meets at least\n$\\operatorname{val}(A) - \\varepsilon$:\n$$\n  \\min_{j \\in J} E_A(x, j) \\ge \\operatorname{val}(A) - \\varepsilon.\n$$\nA $0$-optimal strategy is an optimal strategy. The dual definition (a column\nstrategy $y$ is $\\varepsilon$-optimal when\n$\\max_{i \\in I} E_A(i, y) \\le \\operatorname{val}(A) + \\varepsilon$) applies to\nplayer 2.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 2.2.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Epsilon-optimal and optimal strategies."

Its payoff is the bilinear\nextension\n$$\n  g(x,y)=\\sum_{i \\in I}\\sum_{j \\in J} x_i y_j A_{ij}.\n$$\nPure strategies are identified with Dirac measures in the corresponding\nsimplex.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Mixed Strategy Simplex\n\nFor a finite set $S$, the mixed strategy simplex $\\Delta(S)$ is the set of\nprobability vectors on $S$:\n$$\n  \\Delta(S)=\\{x \\in \\mathbb{R}^S : x_s \\ge 0 \\text{ for all } s,\\ \n  \\sum_{s \\in S} x_s = 1\\}.\n$$\nThe Lean library uses Mathlib's `stdSimplex ℝ S` for this set, with\n`stdSimplex.pure i` for the Dirac point mass at $i$ and `wsum x f` (a\ndefinitional abbreviation for the dot product `x ⬝ᵥ f`) for the weighted\nsum of a function $f \\colon S \\to \\mathbb{R}$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Delta(S) is the simplex of probabilities on a finite set S."

      "body": "# Optimal Pairs Are Exactly Saddle Points\n\nFor a finite matrix game $A$, the product $X(A)\\times Y(A)$ of\noptimal-strategy sets is exactly the set of saddle points of $A$.\n\n*Proof.* Let $v=\\operatorname{val}(A)$. If $x\\in X(A)$ and $y\\in Y(A)$, then\n$xAy'\\ge v$ for every mixed column $y'$ and $x'Ay\\le v$ for every mixed row\n$x'$. Applying these inequalities to $y$ and $x$ gives $xAy=v$, so\n$$\n  x'Ay\\le xAy\\le xAy'\n$$\nfor all $x'$ and $y'$. Thus $(x,y)$ is a saddle point. Conversely, if\n$(x,y)$ is a saddle point, then taking $x'$ and $y'$ as pure strategies and\napplying the simplex-side order characterisations\n([[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]]) gives\n$$\n  E_A(x,y)\\le \\operatorname{guarantee}_I(x), \\qquad\n  \\operatorname{guarantee}_{II}(y)\\le E_A(x,y).\n$$\nWeak duality [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.maximin_le_minimax]] sandwiches both quantities\nbetween $v$ on the appropriate side, forcing equality. Hence $x\\in X(A)$ and\n$y\\in Y(A)$.\n\nThe Lean formalisation factors through two characterisation iff-theorems\n(`mem_optimalRowStrategies_iff_E_ge` and `mem_optimalColumnStrategies_iff_E_le`),\nwhich then combine into `MatrixGame.optimal_pairs_iff_saddle_point`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(d)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. X(A) x Y(A) is the set of saddle points."

      "body": "# Optimal Strategy Sets Are Polytopes\n\nFor every finite matrix game $A$, the optimal strategy sets $X(A)$ and $Y(A)$\nare nonempty polytopes.\n\n*Proof.* By the minimax theorem, at least one mixed row $x$ and one mixed column\n$y$ attain the common value $v=\\operatorname{val}(A)$, so $X(A)$ and $Y(A)$ are\nnonempty. The row player's optimal set is\n$$\n  X(A)=\\{x\\in\\Delta(I): xAe_j\\ge v\\text{ for every }j\\in J\\}.\n$$\nThis is the intersection of the simplex $\\Delta(I)$ with finitely many closed\nhalf-spaces, hence a polytope. Similarly,\n$$\n  Y(A)=\\{y\\in\\Delta(J): e_iAy\\le v\\text{ for every }i\\in I\\},\n$$\nagain an intersection of the simplex with finitely many closed half-spaces.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(a)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Nonemptiness and polytope structure of optimal strategy sets."

      "body": "# Player Guarantee\n\nIn the finite mixed-strategy version, $w$ is a **guarantee for player I**\nwhen some $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ achieves $E_A(x, j) \\ge w$ for every pure\n$j \\in J$. Symmetrically, $w$ is a **guarantee for player II** when some\n$y \\in \\Delta(J)$ achieves $E_A(i, y) \\le w$ for every pure $i \\in I$.\nEquivalently, $w$ is a player I guarantee iff $w \\le \\operatorname{val}(A)$\n(the maximin), and dually for player II with $\\operatorname{val}(A) \\le w$\n(the minimax).\n\nThe abstract pure-strategy version ($\\exists i, \\forall j, g(i, j) \\ge w$)\ncollapses on finite mixed extensions to the same scalar bound via the\nsimplex-side order characterisation\n([[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 2.2.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Guarantees for both players in a zero-sum game."

      "body": "# Strong Complementarity\n\nFor a finite zero-sum matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ there exists an\noptimal pair $(x^\\ast, y^\\ast) \\in X(A) \\times Y(A)$ that is **strongly\ncomplementary**:\n\n$$\n  x^\\ast_i > 0 \\iff e_i A y^\\ast = \\operatorname{val}(A),\n  \\qquad\n  y^\\ast_j > 0 \\iff x^\\ast A e_j = \\operatorname{val}(A).\n$$\n\nThe forward implications ($\\Rightarrow$) hold for *every* optimal pair and are\nexactly [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.support_complementarity]].\nThe strengthening here is the existence of a pair for which the reverse\nimplications ($\\Leftarrow$) also hold simultaneously.\n\n*Proof.* Shift the payoffs by a constant $K$ so the value becomes positive, and\nread off the row/column linear programs of the shifted game. LP strong\ncomplementary slackness supplies an optimal LP pair satisfying strict\ncomplementarity; rescaling back by the shifted value yields an optimal\nmatrix-game pair satisfying the biconditional above.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(c)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Strong complementarity of optimal strategies via LP strong complementary slackness."

      "body": "# Support Complementarity\n\nLet $x \\in X(A)$ and $y \\in Y(A)$. If $i \\in \\operatorname{supp}(x)$, then\nthe pure row $i$ obtains the value against $y$. If\n$j \\in \\operatorname{supp}(y)$, then the mixed strategy $x$ obtains the\nvalue against the pure column $j$.\n\n*Proof.* Let $v=\\operatorname{val}(A)$. Since $y$ is optimal for player II,\neach pure row payoff satisfies $e_iAy\\le v$. Since $x$ is optimal for player\nI, the average of these row payoffs under $x$ is\n$$\n  xAy=\\sum_i x_i(e_iAy)=v.\n$$\nAn average of numbers all bounded above by $v$ can equal $v$ only if every\nterm with positive weight is equal to $v$. Hence $e_iAy=v$ for\n$i\\in\\operatorname{supp}(x)$. The column statement is dual: optimality of\n$x$ gives $xAe_j\\ge v$ for every $j$, while optimality of $y$ gives\n$$\n  xAy=\\sum_j y_j(xAe_j)=v.\n$$\nThus every positively weighted column in $y$ satisfies $xAe_j=v$.\n\nThe Lean formalisation provides separate theorems for the two directions:\n`MatrixGame.support_complementarity_row` (rows in $\\operatorname{supp}(x)$\nhit the value) and `MatrixGame.support_complementarity_column` (columns in\n$\\operatorname{supp}(y)$ hit the value).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(b)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Complementarity on supports of optimal strategies."

      "body": "# Silent Versus Noisy One-Bullet Duel Value\n\nConsider the one-bullet duel where player 1's gun is silent and player 2's gun\nis noisy, with $p_1(t)=p_2(t)=t$. MFoGT Exercise 3.5.1(4) states that the game\nhas a mixed value\n$$\n  v=1-2a,\\qquad a=\\sqrt 6-2.\n$$\n\nPlayer 1 guarantees this value by using the density\n$$\n  f(x)=\n  \\begin{cases}\n    0, & 0\\le x<a,\\\\\n    \\frac{\\sqrt{2a}}{(x^2+2x-1)^{3/2}}, & a\\le x\\le 1.\n  \\end{cases}\n$$\nPlayer 2 guarantees the same bound with cumulative distribution function\n$$\n  G(y)=\\frac{2}{2+a}\\int_0^y f(x)\\,dx\n       +\\frac{a}{2+a}I_1(y),\n$$\nwhere $I_1$ is the distribution function of a Dirac mass at $1$.\n\nThe example records an asymmetric timing game where the informational difference\nbetween silent and noisy shots changes the mixed value and optimal distributions.\n\n*Proof.* The pure payoff to player 1 is\n$$\n  g(x,y)=\n  \\begin{cases}\n    x-y+xy, & x<y,\\\\\n    0, & x=y,\\\\\n    1-2y, & x>y.\n  \\end{cases}\n$$\nThe displayed density for player 1 and distribution function for player 2 are\nprobability distributions when $a=\\sqrt6-2$. Substituting them into the three\npieces of $g$ and integrating on $[a,1]$ gives\n$$\n  \\int g(x,y)\\,f(x)\\,dx\\ge 1-2a\n  \\quad\\text{for every pure }y,\n$$\nwith equality on the support of player 2's mixed strategy. The dual computation\nwith $G$ gives\n$$\n  \\int g(x,y)\\,dG(y)\\le 1-2a\n  \\quad\\text{for every pure }x,\n$$\nwith equality on the support of $f$. Hence the displayed pair is a saddle point\nand the value is $1-2a$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 1(4)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. One silent gun versus one noisy gun, with p1(t)=p2(t)=t.\n- [MFoGT, Section 9.3, Exercise 1(4) hints] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Confirms the displayed strategies form a saddle point."

      "body": "# Three-By-Two Matrix Game Computation\n\nMFoGT Exercise 2.8.5 asks for the value and optimal strategies of\n$$\n  A=\n  \\begin{pmatrix}\n    3 & -1\\\\\n    0 & 0\\\\\n    -2 & 1\n  \\end{pmatrix}.\n$$\n\nThe middle row is strictly dominated by the mixed row\n$0.49\\,a_1+0.51\\,a_3$, so the computation reduces to the two-row game using\nrows $a_1$ and $a_3$:\n$$\n  \\begin{pmatrix}\n    3 & -1\\\\\n    -2 & 1\n  \\end{pmatrix}.\n$$\n\nThe value is\n$$\n  \\operatorname{val}(A)=\\frac17.\n$$\nAn optimal strategy for player 1 plays rows $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ with probabilities\n$$\n  \\left(\\frac37,0,\\frac47\\right),\n$$\nand an optimal strategy for player 2 plays columns $(b_1,b_2)$ with\nprobabilities\n$$\n  \\left(\\frac27,\\frac57\\right).\n$$\n\nThis example is a useful small test case for dominance elimination,\nequalizing-strategy computations, and matrix-game value formulas.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 5] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Compute the value and optimal strategies of a displayed 3 by 2 matrix game.\n- [MFoGT, Section 9.2, Exercise 5 hints] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Gives the reduced game and the optimal strategies."

      "body": "# Diagonal Matrix Game Value\n\nLet $A$ be the diagonal $n\\times n$ matrix with diagonal entries\n$a_i>0$. Then\n$$\n  \\operatorname{val}(A)=\n  \\left(\\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^{-1}\\right)^{-1}.\n$$\nBoth players have the same optimal mixed strategy $p\\in\\Delta(\\{1,\\ldots,n\\})$\ngiven by\n$$\n  p_i=\n  \\frac{a_i^{-1}}{\\sum_{k=1}^n a_k^{-1}}.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* Let\n$$\n  c=\\left(\\sum_{k=1}^n a_k^{-1}\\right)^{-1}\n  \\quad\\text{and}\\quad\n  p_i=ca_i^{-1}.\n$$\nThen $p$ is a probability vector. Against any pure column $j$, the row player's\npayoff from $p$ is $p_ja_j=c$, so $p$ guarantees $c$. Against any pure row $i$,\nthe column player's mixed strategy $p$ gives payoff $a_ip_i=c$, so $p$ holds the\nrow player to $c$. By weak duality, the value is $c$ and $p$ is optimal for both\nplayers.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Compute value and optimal strategies for a positive diagonal matrix game."

      "body": "# Noisy Duel With Multiple Bullets\n\nIn the noisy duel with $m$ bullets for player 1 and $n$ bullets for player 2,\nassuming $p_1(t)=p_2(t)=t$, the game has value\n$$\n  \\frac{m-n}{m+n}.\n$$\nIt is optimal for the player with $\\max\\{m,n\\}$ bullets to shoot the first bullet\nat time\n$$\n  t_0=\\frac1{m+n}.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* The proof is by induction on $m+n$. The one-bullet case is the noisy\none-bullet duel. Assume the statement known for all pairs with total bullet\ncount at most $K$, and consider $(m+1,n)$ with $m+n+1=K+1$.\n\nIf player 1 has more bullets, player 1 shoots first at time\n$1/(m+n+1)$. If player 2 has not shot before then and player 1 misses, the\ncontinuation is the already solved $(m,n)$ game. If player 2 shoots first and\nmisses, the continuation is the already solved $(m+1,n-1)$ game. If both shoot\nat that time and miss, the continuation is the $(m,n-1)$ game. Substituting the\ninduction values of these continuation games gives the guarantee\n$$\n  \\frac{m+1-n}{m+n+1}.\n$$\nThe column player uses the dual strategy: randomize the first shot in a small\ninterval immediately after $1/(m+n+1)$ and then switch to the corresponding\noptimal continuation game. Letting the interval length tend to $0$ gives the\nmatching upper bound. The equal-bullet case is symmetric and gives value $0$;\nthe case where player 2 has more bullets is the same argument with the players\ninterchanged. Thus the induction proves the value formula and the stated first\nshot time.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 1(2)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Noisy duel with m bullets versus n bullets."

      "body": "# Noisy One-Bullet Duel Value\n\nIn the noisy duel where each player has one bullet and the kill probabilities\n$p_1,p_2:[0,1]\\to[0,1]$ are strictly increasing continuous functions with\n$p_1(0)=p_2(0)=0$ and $p_1(1)=p_2(1)=1$, the game has a value in pure strategies.\n\nThe optimal pure strategy of each player is to shoot at the unique time $t_0$\nsatisfying\n$$\n  p_1(t_0)+p_2(t_0)=1.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* Continuity and monotonicity of $p_1+p_2$ give a unique\n$t_0\\in[0,1]$ with $p_1(t_0)+p_2(t_0)=1$. If player $1$ shoots before $t_0$,\nthen player $2$ can wait until $t_0$; the early shot has hit probability below\n$p_1(t_0)$, while player $2$'s later shot has hit probability $p_2(t_0)$, so\nplayer $1$ cannot improve past the payoff at $t_0$. If player $1$ waits past\n$t_0$, player $2$ shoots at $t_0$ and again player $1$ cannot improve. The same\nargument with the players interchanged shows that shooting at $t_0$ is optimal\nfor player $2$. Thus $(t_0,t_0)$ is a pure saddle point, so the game has a\npure-strategy value.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 1(1)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Noisy duel with one bullet for each player."

      "body": "# Silent One-Bullet Duel Has No Pure Value\n\nIn the silent one-bullet duel, each player chooses a shooting time\n$x\\in[0,1]$, but a player does not observe whether the opponent has already\nshot. Assume $p_1(t)=p_2(t)=t$.\n\nThe pure-strategy game has no value. However, player 1 can guarantee a\nnon-negative payoff by using a mixed strategy supported on $[1/3,1]$ with\ndensity\n$$\n  f(y)=\\frac14 y^{-3}\\mathbf 1_{y\\ge 1/3}.\n$$\nBy symmetry, player 2 can guarantee the opposite bound. Thus the silent\none-bullet duel has mixed value $0$ even though it has no pure value.\n\nThis exercise is a useful warning that pure values can fail in timing games even\nwhen a natural mixed guarantee exists.\n\n*Proof.* For pure shooting times $x,y$, the symmetric silent-duel payoff is\n$$\n  g(x,y)=\n  \\begin{cases}\n    x-(1-x)y, & x<y,\\\\\n    0, & x=y,\\\\\n    x-(1+x)y, & x>y.\n  \\end{cases}\n$$\nIf $y>0$, player 1 can shoot just before $y$ and obtain payoff arbitrarily close\nto $y^2$. If $y<1$, player 1 can shoot at $1$ and obtain $1-2y$. Hence\n$$\n  \\inf_y\\sup_x g(x,y)>0.\n$$\nBut the game is symmetric and zero-sum, so a pure value, if it existed, would\nhave to be $0$. Therefore there is no pure value.\n\nNow let $\\sigma$ have density $f(y)=\\frac14y^{-3}$ on $[1/3,1]$. This is a\nprobability density because\n$$\n  \\int_{1/3}^1 \\frac14y^{-3}\\,dy=1.\n$$\nFor $y\\ge 1/3$, direct integration gives\n$$\n  \\int g(x,y)\\,d\\sigma(x)=0.\n$$\nFor $y<1/3$, every $x$ in the support satisfies $x>y$, so\n$$\n  \\int g(x,y)\\,d\\sigma(x)\n  =(1-y)\\int x\\,d\\sigma(x)-y\n  =(1-y)\\frac12-y\n  =\\frac{1-3y}{2}\\ge0.\n$$\nThus player 1 guarantees at least $0$. By symmetry the same distribution lets\nplayer 2 hold player 1 to at most $0$, so the mixed value is $0$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 1(3)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Silent one-bullet duel with p1(t)=p2(t)=t.\n- [MFoGT, Section 9.3, Exercise 1(3) hints] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Constructs a mixed strategy with density C y^{-3} on [a,1]."
    },

      "body": "# Three-Player Minimax Failure\n\nMFoGT Exercise 2.8.2 considers a three-player zero-sum interaction where players\n1 and 2 are maximizers using independent mixed actions, and player 3 is the\nminimizer. Player 1 chooses $T$ or $B$, player 2 chooses $L$ or $R$, and player\n3 chooses $W$ or $E$. The payoff to the maximizing side is\n$$\n  g(T,L,W)=1,\\qquad g(B,R,E)=1,\n$$\nand all other pure outcomes have payoff $0$.\n\nWriting $x$ for the probability of $T$ and $y$ for the probability of $L$, the\ntwo payoff components seen by player 3 are\n$$\n  xy,\\qquad (1-x)(1-y).\n$$\nThus\n$$\n  \\max_{x,y\\in[0,1]}\\min\\{xy,(1-x)(1-y)\\}=\\frac14,\n$$\nattained at $x=y=1/2$.\n\nOn the other hand, if player 3 mixes with probability $z$ on $W$, then the\nmaximizers can choose between the two matching corners, giving\n$$\n  \\min_{z\\in[0,1]}\\max\\{z,1-z\\}=\\frac12.\n$$\nHence the natural minimax equality fails:\n$$\n  \\max_{x,y}\\min_z g(x,y,z)=\\frac14\n  <\\frac12\n  =\\min_z\\max_{x,y}g(x,y,z).\n$$\nThe point of the example is that the joint strategy set of players 1 and 2 is\nrestricted to product distributions.       "body": "# Existence of Optimal Mixed Strategies (Loomis Foundations)\n\nFor a finite matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$, the row player's\nguarantee function is\n$$\\lambda_{\\mathrm{aux}}(x) = \\min_{j \\in J} \\sum_{i \\in I} x_i A(i,j),$$\nand the column player's loss-cap function is\n$$\\mu_{\\mathrm{aux}}(y) = \\max_{i \\in I} \\sum_{j \\in J} y_j A(i,j).$$\nThe two scalar values\n$$\\lambda_0 = \\sup_{x \\in \\Delta(I)} \\lambda_{\\mathrm{aux}}(x) \\quad \\text{and} \\quad\n  \\mu_0 = \\inf_{y \\in \\Delta(J)} \\mu_{\\mathrm{aux}}(y)$$\nare the maxmin and minmax values of the game.\n\nThis node packages four facts that hold *before* the inductive minimax\nidentity is established:\n\n1. **Continuity.** Both $\\lambda_{\\mathrm{aux}}$ and $\\mu_{\\mathrm{aux}}$ are\n   continuous on the (compact) mixed-strategy simplices.\n2. **Boundedness.** $\\lambda_{\\mathrm{aux}}$ is bounded above and\n   $\\mu_{\\mathrm{aux}}$ is bounded below by the obvious extremes of $A$.\n3. **Achievement.** There exist mixed strategies $x^\\ast$ and $y^\\ast$ such\n   that $\\sum_i x^\\ast_i A(i,j) \\ge \\lambda_0$ for every column $j$ and\n   $\\sum_j y^\\ast_j A(i,j) \\le \\mu_0$ for every row $i$.\n4. **Weak duality.** $\\lambda_0 \\le \\mu_0$.\n\n*Proof.* Continuity of $\\lambda_{\\mathrm{aux}}$ is the finite infimum of\ncontinuous weighted sums (`Continuous.finset_inf'_apply`); the proof for\n$\\mu_{\\mathrm{aux}}$ is dual. Boundedness follows because each weighted sum\nis bounded by the extreme matrix entry. The supremum\n$\\lambda_0$ is achieved by the extreme-value theorem applied to the compact\nmixed-strategy simplex (`IsCompact.exists_isMaxOn`), and the optimiser\nrealises $\\lambda_0$ on every pure column by the infimum definition; the\n$\\mu_0$ side is symmetric. Weak duality combines the two optimisers in the\nbilinear payoff:\n$$\\lambda_0 \\le \\sum_{i,j} x^\\ast_i y^\\ast_j A(i,j) \\le \\mu_0,$$\nusing the pointwise-to-weighted bound transfer from\n[[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]].\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Existence of mixed optimisers and weak duality, prior to the inductive minimax theorem."

      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/zero_sum/learning/cesaro_payoff_from_robinson.md",
      "body_refs": {

      "body": "# Cesàro Payoff Convergence From Robinson Lemma\n\nThe average realised payoff along a fictitious-play trajectory converges to the\nvalue of the game. The proof is an elementary telescoping identity that uses\nthe Robinson admissible-sequence lemma\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]] only as a black box.\n\n## Setup\n\nLet $A \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m \\times n}$ be a matrix game with value $v := v(A)$\nestablished by [[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]]\n(equivalently, by the minimax theorem). Let $(i_n, j_n)_{n \\ge 1}$ be a\nfictitious-play realisation\n([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.fictitious_play]]).\n\nDefine the **realised cumulative payoff** $R_n$ and the **counterfactual\ncumulative payoffs** $U_m^i$ for each pure row $i$:\n$$\n  R_n := \\sum_{p=1}^n A_{i_p, j_p},\n  \\qquad\n  U_m^i := \\sum_{k=1}^m A_{i, j_k}.\n$$\n$U_m^i$ is the payoff player I would have accrued by always playing pure $i$\nagainst player II's actual sequence $j_1, \\ldots, j_m$.\n\n## Statement\n\n$$\n  \\frac{1}{n} R_n \\;\\longrightarrow\\; v \\quad \\text{as } n \\to \\infty.\n$$\n\n## Proof\n\n**Telescoping identity.** For every $n \\ge 1$,\n$$\n  R_n \\;=\\; U_n^{i_n} \\;+\\; \\sum_{p=1}^{n-1} (U_p^{i_p} - U_p^{i_{p+1}}).\n$$\n*Verification.* Note $U_n^{i_n} = \\sum_{k=1}^n A_{i_n, j_k}$. Then\n$$\n  R_n - U_n^{i_n}\n   = \\sum_{k=1}^n (A_{i_k, j_k} - A_{i_n, j_k})\n   = \\sum_{p=1}^{n-1} (U_p^{i_p} - U_p^{i_{p+1}})\n$$\nby reindexing — each term on the right corresponds to the \"switch\" from row\n$i_p$ to $i_{p+1}$ at step $p+1$, which redefines what the counterfactual\ncumulative would have been.\n\n**Sign of the telescoping increments.** By the fictitious-play best-response\ncondition, $i_{p+1} \\in \\operatorname{argmax}_i (Ay_p)^i = \\operatorname{argmax}_i \\frac{1}{p} U_p^i$,\nhence $U_p^{i_{p+1}} \\ge U_p^{i_p}$. Therefore\n$$\n  U_p^{i_p} - U_p^{i_{p+1}} \\;\\le\\; 0, \\quad p = 1, \\ldots, n-1.\n$$\n\n**Upper bound on $R_n / n$.** The telescoping identity together with the sign\ngives\n$$\n  R_n \\;\\le\\; U_n^{i_n}.\n$$\nSince $i_n \\in \\operatorname{argmax}_i U_n^i / n$ (with $U_n^i / n = (A y_n)^i$ where $y_n$\nis player II's empirical frequency), we have\n$U_n^{i_n} / n = \\max_i (A y_n)^i$. The minimax bracket together with\n$\\mu(n)/n \\to 0$ from\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]] yields\n$\\max_i (A y_n)^i \\to v$. Hence\n$$\n  \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{R_n}{n} \\;\\le\\; v.\n$$\n\n**Lower bound on $R_n / n$.** Apply the dual telescoping identity (player II's\nperspective):\n$$\n  R_n = V_n^{j_n} + \\sum_{p=1}^{n-1} (V_p^{j_p} - V_p^{j_{p+1}}),\n$$\nwhere $V_m^j := \\sum_{k=1}^m A_{i_k, j}$. The best-response condition for II\nmakes the telescoping increments $\\ge 0$, giving $R_n \\ge V_n^{j_n}$. By the\nanalogous limit, $V_n^{j_n} / n = \\min_j (x_n A)^j \\to v$, hence\n$\\liminf R_n / n \\ge v$.\n\nCombining, $R_n / n \\to v$. $\\square$\n\n## Note\n\nThis proof is **independent** of the internal combinatorial structure of\nRobinson's induction\n([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.bracket_invariant]],\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.useful_window]],\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.subgame_reduction]],\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.induction_step]]). It uses\nthe parent lemma only via its conclusion $\\mu(n)/n \\to 0$.\n\nPractically, this makes it the **shortest formalisable item** in the Robinson\nchain — a natural first Lean target.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.7] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Cesàro average-payoff\n  convergence along fictitious play; see the `source` block above for\n  the precise locator."

      "body": "# Continuous Fictitious Play Closes The Duality Gap\n\nContinuous fictitious play is the continuous-time analogue of the empirical\nfrequency recursion. In logarithmic time it is the best-response differential\ninclusion\n$$\n  \\dot x(t)\\in BR_1(y(t))-x(t),\n  \\qquad\n  \\dot y(t)\\in BR_2(x(t))-y(t).\n$$\nEquivalently, for some\n$$\n  \\alpha(t)=x(t)+\\dot x(t)\\in BR_1(y(t)),\n  \\qquad\n  \\beta(t)=y(t)+\\dot y(t)\\in BR_2(x(t)).\n$$\n\nFor continuous fictitious play in a finite matrix game, the duality gap\n$$\n  W(x,y)=L(y)-M(x)\n$$\nconverges to $0$ at speed $O(1/t)$ in the original time scale.\n\n*Proof.* MFoGT's proof differentiates the duality gap along the time-changed\ntrajectory. Using the envelope theorem and bilinearity of $g(x,y)=xAy$,\n$$\n  \\dot W(t)\n  =g(\\alpha(t),\\dot y(t))-g(\\dot x(t),\\beta(t))\n  =M(x(t))-L(y(t))\n  =-W(t).\n$$\nThus $W(t)=W(0)e^{-t}$ after the logarithmic time change, which gives the\n$O(1/t)$ rate in the original continuous fictitious-play process. Since the\noptimal-strategy set is exactly the zero set of $W$, convergence of the gap\nimplies convergence toward $X(A)\\times Y(A)$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.7.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Continuous fictitious play duality gap convergence."

Empirical distributions x_n and y_n of previously played pure actions."

      "body": "# External Regret\n\nIn repeated play of a finite strategic game, the external regret of player $i$\ncompares the realized payoff to the payoff that would have been obtained by\nusing one fixed action throughout the same history.\n\nFor a realized action history $(a^1,\\ldots,a^n)$, the external regret against a\nfixed alternative action $b_i\\in A_i$ is\n$$\n  \\frac1n\\sum_{t=1}^n\n  (g_i(b_i,a_{-i}^t)-g_i(a_i^t,a_{-i}^t)).\n$$\nA procedure has no external regret if the positive part of this quantity\nconverges to $0$ for every fixed alternative action.\n\nExternal regret is weaker than internal regret: it tests only constant\ncounterfactual actions, not recommendation-contingent replacements.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 7, Section 7.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. No-external-regret procedures in repeated play."

      "body": "# Fictitious Play Convergence\n\nLet $(i_n,j_n)_{n\\ge1}$ be a fictitious-play realization in a finite matrix game\n$A$, and let $(x_n,y_n)$ be the empirical frequencies of play.\n\nMFoGT Thm. 2.7.2 has two conclusions.\n\nFirst, the empirical frequencies approach the optimal-strategy sets\n$X(A)\\times Y(A)$. Convergence of fictitious play in finite zero-sum games."

      "body": "# Hannan Set\n\nFor player $i$, the Hannan set is the set of distributions $q\\in\\Delta(A)$ over\naction profiles for which player $i$ has no profitable fixed-action\ncounterfactual:\n$$\n  \\sum_{a\\in A}q(a)g_i(a)\n  \\ge\n  \\sum_{a\\in A}q(a)g_i(b_i,a_{-i})\n  \\quad\\text{for every } b_i\\in A_i.\n$$\n\nEquivalently, $q$ makes player $i$'s realized action payoff at least as good as\nthe payoff from any single action chosen in hindsight.\n\nThe intersection of the Hannan sets over all players is the distributional\ntarget reached when every player has no external regret. It is weaker than the\ncorrelated-equilibrium set because it does not condition deviations on the\nrecommended action.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 7, Section 7.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Hannan set associated to no-external-regret play."

      "body": "# Internal Regret\n\nInternal regret compares realized play with a counterfactual rule that replaces\none action by another whenever the first action was played.\n\nFor player $i$ and actions $a_i,b_i\\in A_i$, the internal regret from replacing\n$a_i$ by $b_i$ along a realized history is\n$$\n  \\frac1n\\sum_{t:a_i^t=a_i}\n  (g_i(b_i,a_{-i}^t)-g_i(a_i,a_{-i}^t)).\n$$\nA procedure has no internal regret if the positive part of this quantity\nconverges to $0$ for every ordered pair $(a_i,b_i)$.\n\nInternal regret is the learning analogue of correlated-equilibrium obedience:\nthe counterfactual deviation is allowed to depend on the action actually\nrecommended or played.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 7, Section 7.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. No-internal-regret procedures and their connection to correlated equilibria."

      "body": "# No External Regret Converges To Hannan Set\n\nIn repeated play of a finite game, if player $i$ follows a procedure with no\nexternal regret, then the empirical distribution of realized action profiles\napproaches player $i$'s Hannan set almost surely.\n\nEquivalently, every limit point of the empirical distributions satisfies the\nfixed-action hindsight inequalities defining the Hannan set for player $i$.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nThe empirical distribution rewrites each fixed-action external regret as a\nlinear functional of the empirical distribution.       "body": "# Robinson Admissible Sequence Lemma\n\n## Setup\n\nLet $A \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m \\times n}$ be a matrix-game payoff. Write\n$\\|A\\| := \\max_{i,j}|A_{i,j}|$.\n\nFor $\\alpha \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\\beta \\in \\mathbb{R}^m$ define\n$$\n  J(\\alpha) := \\{j : \\alpha^j = \\min_k \\alpha^k\\}, \\qquad\n  I(\\beta)  := \\{i : \\beta^i = \\max_k \\beta^k\\}.\n$$\n\nAn **admissible sequence** is $(\\alpha(t), \\beta(t))_{t \\ge 0}$ in\n$\\mathbb{R}^n \\times \\mathbb{R}^m$ satisfying\n\n- (i) $\\min_k \\alpha^k(0) = \\max_k \\beta^k(0)$;\n- (ii) at each $t \\ge 0$, $\\exists i_{t+1} \\in I(\\beta(t))$,\n  $j_{t+1} \\in J(\\alpha(t))$ with\n  $$\n    \\alpha(t+1) = \\alpha(t) + e_{i_{t+1}}^T A, \\qquad\n    \\beta(t+1)  = \\beta(t)  + A e_{j_{t+1}}.\n  $$\n\nThis is a cumulative-payoff encoding of fictitious play\n([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.fictitious_play]]): writing\n$x(t) := \\frac1t \\sum_{s \\le t} e_{i_s}$ and\n$y(t) := \\frac1t \\sum_{s \\le t} e_{j_s}$ for the empirical frequencies,\n$$\n  \\frac{\\alpha(t) - \\alpha(0)}{t} = x(t) A, \\qquad\n  \\frac{\\beta(t) - \\beta(0)}{t}  = A y(t).\n$$\n\nThe central quantity is the **cumulative duality gap**\n$$\n  \\mu(t) := \\max_i \\beta^i(t) - \\min_j \\alpha^j(t).\n$$\n\n## Statement\n\n**Lemma (Robinson 1951).** For every matrix $A$ and every $\\varepsilon > 0$,\nthere exists $s_0 = s_0(A, \\varepsilon)$ such that\n$$\n  \\mu(t) \\le \\varepsilon \\cdot t, \\quad \\forall t \\ge s_0,\n$$\nfor every admissible sequence on $A$.\n\nEquivalently, $\\mu(t) = o(t)$, uniformly over admissible sequences.\n\n## Proof\n\nBy induction on the matrix size $N := m + n$.\n\n**Base** $N = 2$ (i.e., a $1 \\times 1$ matrix): the entry is a constant $a$,\nso $\\alpha(t) = \\alpha(0) + t \\cdot a$ and $\\beta(t) = \\beta(0) + t \\cdot a$.\nAdmissibility (i) gives $\\beta(0) = \\alpha(0)$, hence $\\mu(t) \\equiv 0$.\n\n**Inductive step.** Assume the lemma for every strict submatrix of $A$ and\nfix $\\varepsilon > 0$. Set $\\eta := \\varepsilon / 3$. The proof orchestrates the\nthree sub-lemmas, then applies the pasting lemma with $\\varepsilon$ replaced by\n$2\\eta = 2\\varepsilon/3$ (this is the cleaner constant choice — see Note at end).\n\n1. **Submatrix bound from the IH.** For every strict submatrix $A' \\subsetneq A$,\n   the inductive hypothesis supplies $s(A', \\eta)$ such that $\\mu_{A'}(t) \\le \\eta t$\n   for every admissible sequence on $A'$ and every $t \\ge s(A', \\eta)$. There\n   are finitely many strict submatrices, so\n   $$\n     t^* \\;:=\\; \\max\\!\\left( \\max_{A' \\subsetneq A} s(A', \\eta),\\; \\tfrac{6 \\|A\\|}{\\varepsilon} \\right)\n   $$\n   is finite. (The second argument forces $2\\|A\\|/t^* \\le \\eta$, which is needed\n   to control the pasting residual.)\n\n2. **Window dichotomy on every $[s, s + t^*]$.** Either:\n\n   - **(a)** every row $i \\in I$ and every column $j \\in J$ is *useful* in\n     $[s, s + t^*]$ (i.e., each appears in $I(\\beta(\\cdot))$ or\n     $J(\\alpha(\\cdot))$ at some step inside the window). By\n     [[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.useful_window]] —\n     which internally uses\n     [[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.bracket_invariant]] —\n     $$\n       \\mu(s + t^*) \\;\\le\\; 4 t^* \\|A\\|\n     $$\n     (an *absolute* endpoint bound, independent of $\\mu(s)$); **or**\n\n   - **(b)** some row or column is not useful. By\n     [[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.subgame_reduction]]\n     the window is governed by admissible play on a strict submatrix $A'$, so\n     the submatrix bound from step 1 applies. Combined with admissibility's\n     $2\\|A\\|$ per-step Lipschitz control on $\\mu$, this gives\n     $$\n       \\mu(s + t^*) - \\mu(s) \\;\\le\\; \\eta t^* + 2 \\|A\\|\n     $$\n     (an *increment* bound).\n\n3. **Pasting via Euclidean division.** Write $t = q t^* + r$ with $0 \\le r < t^*$.\n   Apply\n   [[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.induction_step]] with\n   $\\varepsilon_{\\text{step}} := 2\\eta = 2\\varepsilon/3$ (so that the step's\n   \"$\\frac{\\varepsilon_{\\text{step}} t^*}{2}$\" matches the subgame-case increment\n   $\\eta t^*$ from step 2). The pasting lemma yields, for all $t \\ge t^*$,\n   $$\n     \\mu(t) \\;\\le\\; 6 t^* \\|A\\|\n       \\;+\\; \\tfrac{\\varepsilon_{\\text{step}}\\, t}{2}\n       \\;+\\; \\tfrac{2 \\|A\\|\\, t}{t^*}\n     \\;=\\; 6 t^* \\|A\\| \\;+\\; \\tfrac{\\varepsilon t}{3} \\;+\\; \\tfrac{2 \\|A\\|\\, t}{t^*}.\n   $$\n\n4. **Constant absorption.** By the choice $t^* \\ge 6\\|A\\|/\\varepsilon$,\n   the last term $\\frac{2\\|A\\| t}{t^*} \\le \\frac{\\varepsilon t}{3}$. Hence\n   $$\n     \\mu(t) \\;\\le\\; 6 t^* \\|A\\| + \\tfrac{2 \\varepsilon t}{3}.\n   $$\n   Setting\n   $$\n     s_0 \\;:=\\; \\max\\!\\left(t^*,\\; \\tfrac{18\\, t^* \\|A\\|}{\\varepsilon}\\right),\n   $$\n   the residual $6 t^* \\|A\\| \\le \\frac{\\varepsilon t}{3}$ for every $t \\ge s_0$,\n   giving the stated bound $\\mu(t) \\le \\varepsilon t$. $\\square$\n\n## Note on the constant choice\n\nThe pasting lemma's \"natural\" constant ladder produces an end bound of\n$\\frac{3 \\varepsilon_{\\text{step}}}{2} t$ for $t$ large enough. Solving\n$\\frac{3 \\varepsilon_{\\text{step}}}{2} = \\varepsilon$ for the step's $\\varepsilon_{\\text{step}}$\ngives $\\varepsilon_{\\text{step}} = 2\\varepsilon/3$, hence $\\eta = \\varepsilon_{\\text{step}}/2 = \\varepsilon/3$\nfor the IH (since the subgame-reduction increment uses the IH's $\\eta$ directly).\nA looser choice such as $\\eta = \\varepsilon/4$ (with $\\varepsilon_{\\text{step}} = \\varepsilon/2$)\nalso works and gives the cleaner $\\mu(t) \\le \\frac{3 \\varepsilon}{4} t \\le \\varepsilon t$\nbound, at the cost of slightly larger $t^*$ and $s_0$. Either is fine; we\nrecord the tighter $\\varepsilon/3$ choice for definiteness.\n\n## Consequence\n\nCombined with the trivial bracket\n$\\min_j x(t)Ay \\le \\underline v(A) \\le \\overline v(A) \\le \\max_i x(t) A^i$,\nthe lemma yields the existence of a value $v(A) = \\underline v = \\overline v$\nand gives that every accumulation point of $(x(t), y(t))$ is an optimal-strategy\npair. This is the content of\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.fictitious_play_convergence]].\n\nFor the Cesàro average payoff statement\n$\\frac1n \\sum_{p \\le n} A_{i_p, j_p} \\to v$, see the independent telescoping\nargument in\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.cesaro_payoff_from_robinson]].\n\n## References\n\n- [Robinson 1951] J. Robinson, \"An iterative method of solving a game\",\n  *Annals of Mathematics* 54 (1951), 296–301.\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 12] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Hint-decomposition of Robinson's proof into the four internal lemmas cited\n  above."

      "body": "# Bracket Invariant For Admissible Sequences\n\nA technical invariant used by\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]] in the useful-window\nestimate.\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $(\\alpha(t), \\beta(t))_{t \\ge 0}$ be an admissible sequence on a matrix\n$A \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m \\times n}$ (in the sense of\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]]). Set\n$$\n  c := \\min_k \\alpha^k(0) = \\max_k \\beta^k(0)\n$$\n(equal by admissibility condition (i)). Then for every $s \\ge 0$,\n$$\n  \\min_i \\beta^i(s) \\;\\le\\; c \\;\\le\\; \\max_j \\alpha^j(s).\n$$\nIn particular,\n$$\n  \\min_i \\beta^i(s) - \\max_j \\alpha^j(s) \\;\\le\\; 0.\n$$\n\n## Proof\n\nThe two inequalities are independent.\n\n**Upper bracket $c \\le \\max_j \\alpha^j(s)$.** Show $\\max_j \\alpha^j$ is\nnon-decreasing in $s$. At step $s+1$, only the component $\\alpha^{j_{s+1}}$\nchanges, where $j_{s+1} \\in J(\\alpha(s)) = \\operatorname{argmin}_k \\alpha^k(s)$.\n\n- If $A_{i_{s+1}, j_{s+1}} \\ge 0$: $\\alpha^{j_{s+1}}$ increases, the others\n  unchanged. $\\max_j$ stays or grows.\n- If $A_{i_{s+1}, j_{s+1}} < 0$: $\\alpha^{j_{s+1}}$ decreases, but it was an\n  argmin (not argmax unless all components equal). The other components are\n  unchanged, so $\\max_j$ is unchanged.\n\nHence $\\max_j \\alpha^j(s) \\ge \\max_j \\alpha^j(0) \\ge \\min_k \\alpha^k(0) = c$.\n\n**Lower bracket $\\min_i \\beta^i(s) \\le c$.** By induction on $s$.\n\n*Base.* $\\min_i \\beta^i(0) \\le \\max_i \\beta^i(0) = c$.\n\n*Inductive step.* Assume $\\min_i \\beta^i(s) \\le c$. At step $s+1$, only\n$\\beta^{i_{s+1}}$ updates, where $i_{s+1} \\in I(\\beta(s)) = \\operatorname{argmax}_k \\beta^k(s)$.\n\n- *Case A: there exists an argmin $i^* \\ne i_{s+1}$.* Then $\\beta^{i^*}$ is\n  unchanged at step $s+1$, so\n  $$\n    \\min_i \\beta^i(s+1) \\le \\beta^{i^*}(s+1) = \\beta^{i^*}(s) = \\min_i \\beta^i(s) \\le c.\n  $$\n\n- *Case B: every argmin equals $i_{s+1}$.* Combined with $i_{s+1} \\in$ argmax,\n  this forces every $\\beta^i(s)$ to be equal — call this common value $v$. By\n  induction $v = \\min_i \\beta^i(s) \\le c$. After the step the other components\n  remain at $v$; for $m \\ge 2$, picking any $i \\ne i_{s+1}$ gives\n  $\\min_i \\beta^i(s+1) \\le v \\le c$.\n  When $m = 1$ the matrix is $1 \\times n$, the lemma reduces to\n  $\\beta^1(s) \\le \\max_j \\alpha^j(s)$, which holds because then\n  $\\beta^1(s) = c + \\sum_{p \\le s} A_{1, j_p}$ and\n  $\\alpha^{j_s}(s) = c + A_{1, j_s} \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{j_s \\in J}$ along\n  admissible play — direct computation.\n\nThis completes the induction. $\\square$\n\n## Note\n\nThe lower-bracket induction is slightly subtler than the upper-bracket\nmonotonicity because $\\min_i \\beta^i$ is *not* monotone in $s$ — it can both\nrise and fall — but it never exceeds $c$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 12 part (1)(iii)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Bracket inequality\n  $\\min_i \\beta^i(s) - \\max_j \\alpha^j(s) \\le 0$ for admissible sequences."

      "body": "# Euclidean Division Pasting In Robinson Induction\n\nThe arithmetic pasting step that closes the inductive proof of\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]] by combining the two\nwindow-dichotomy cases over $t = q t^* + r$.\n\n## Setup\n\nLet $A \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m \\times n}$ with $\\|A\\| := \\max_{i,j} |A_{i,j}|$.\nSuppose $t^* \\in \\mathbb{N}$ is such that, for every window $[s, s+t^*]$ of\nlength $t^*$ along an admissible sequence on $A$, exactly one of the\nfollowing holds:\n\n- **(a)** every $i \\in I$ and every $j \\in J$ is useful in $[s, s+t^*]$;\n- **(b)** at least one of them is not.\n\nSuppose further that\n- in case (a), [[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.useful_window]]\n  gives $\\mu(s+t^*) \\le 4 t^* \\|A\\|$ (an *absolute* bound on the endpoint);\n- in case (b), [[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.subgame_reduction]]\n  combined with the inductive hypothesis on a strict submatrix gives\n  $\\mu(s+t^*) - \\mu(s) \\le \\frac{\\varepsilon t^*}{2} + 2 \\|A\\|$ (an *increment*\n  bound).\n\n## Statement\n\nUnder the above setup, for every $t \\ge t^*$,\n$$\n  \\mu(t) \\;\\le\\; 6 t^* \\|A\\| + \\frac{\\varepsilon t}{2} + \\frac{2 \\|A\\| t}{t^*}.\n$$\nConsequently, if $t^*$ is chosen so that $2\\|A\\|/t^* \\le \\varepsilon/2$, then\nfor all $t \\ge s_0 := \\max\\!(t^*, 12 t^* \\|A\\| / \\varepsilon)$,\n$$\n  \\mu(t) \\;\\le\\; \\frac{3 \\varepsilon}{2} t.\n$$\nRe-running the argument with $\\varepsilon$ replaced by $2\\varepsilon/3$\ngives the form $\\mu(t) \\le \\varepsilon t$ used in the parent lemma.\n\n## Proof\n\nWrite $t = q t^* + r$ with $0 \\le r < t^*$. The trajectory $[0, t]$ is\ndecomposed into $q$ consecutive windows of length $t^*$ plus a residual\nwindow of length $r$.\n\nSingle-step bound on $\\mu$. Each admissible step changes $\\mu$ by at most\n$2 \\|A\\|$ (each of $\\max_i \\beta^i$ and $\\min_j \\alpha^j$ changes by at most\n$\\|A\\|$). Hence on the residual $r < t^*$,\n$$\n  \\mu(t) - \\mu(q t^*) \\;\\le\\; 2 r \\|A\\| \\;\\le\\; 2 t^* \\|A\\|.\n$$\n\nLet\n$$\n  p := \\max \\{ k \\in \\{0, 1, \\ldots, q-1\\} : \\text{window } [k t^*, (k+1) t^*]\n    \\text{ is in case (a)} \\},\n$$\nwith the convention $p = -1$ if no window is in case (a).\n\n- *If $p \\ge 0$:* the case-(a) bound resets $\\mu$ at the endpoint:\n  $\\mu((p+1) t^*) \\le 4 t^* \\|A\\|$. From there, the remaining $q - p - 1$\n  windows are all in case (b), each contributing increment\n  $\\frac{\\varepsilon t^*}{2} + 2 \\|A\\|$. Summing,\n  $$\n    \\mu(q t^*) \\;\\le\\; 4 t^* \\|A\\|\n      + (q - p - 1)\\!\\left(\\frac{\\varepsilon t^*}{2} + 2 \\|A\\|\\right).\n  $$\n- *If $p = -1$:* every window is in case (b). The cumulative bound is then\n  $\\mu(0) + q (\\frac{\\varepsilon t^*}{2} + 2\\|A\\|)$, with $\\mu(0) \\le 2\\|A\\|$\n  by admissibility condition (i). So\n  $$\n    \\mu(q t^*) \\;\\le\\; 2 \\|A\\| + q\\!\\left(\\frac{\\varepsilon t^*}{2} + 2 \\|A\\|\\right).\n  $$\n\nIn both branches, using $q - p - 1 \\le q \\le t/t^*$ and $2 \\|A\\| \\le 2 t^* \\|A\\|$:\n$$\n  \\mu(q t^*) \\;\\le\\; 4 t^* \\|A\\| + \\frac{\\varepsilon t}{2} + 2 \\|A\\| \\cdot \\frac{t}{t^*}.\n$$\nAdding the residual contribution $\\mu(t) - \\mu(q t^*) \\le 2 t^* \\|A\\|$:\n$$\n  \\mu(t) \\;\\le\\; 6 t^* \\|A\\| + \\frac{\\varepsilon t}{2} + \\frac{2 \\|A\\| t}{t^*}.\n$$\n\nFor the second form, with $t^* \\ge 4\\|A\\|/\\varepsilon$ the last term is\n$\\le \\varepsilon t / 2$, giving $\\mu(t) \\le 6 t^* \\|A\\| + \\varepsilon t$. The\ndominant first term is $\\le \\varepsilon t / 2$ when\n$t \\ge 12 t^* \\|A\\| / \\varepsilon$, and combining yields the\n$\\frac{3\\varepsilon}{2} t$ bound. $\\square$\n\n## Note\n\nThe proof is purely arithmetic given the two case bounds and the single-step\n$2\\|A\\|$ inequality. The hierarchy of constants ($6 t^* \\|A\\|$ absolute,\n$\\varepsilon t / 2$ linear, $2 \\|A\\| t / t^*$ from the last-term residual) is\ndesigned so that each term is either absolutely bounded or absorbable into\n$\\varepsilon t$ for sufficiently large $t^*$ or $t$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 12 parts (3)(c) and (3)(d)] Laraki, Renault,\n  and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Euclidean-division pasting in\n  Robinson's induction."

      "body": "# Subgame Reduction For Non-Useful Indices\n\nA reduction step used by\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]] inside the main\ninduction's \"some row/column is not useful\" case. It is the mechanism by which\nthe inductive hypothesis on strict submatrices is invoked.\n\n## Setup\n\nFor an admissible sequence on $A \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m \\times n}$ and a window\n$[s, s+t^*] \\subseteq \\mathbb{N}$, define usefulness as in\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.useful_window]].\n\nFor a subset $I' \\subseteq I$ let $A|_{I' \\times J}$ denote the submatrix\nformed by the rows in $I'$. Admissibility on $A|_{I' \\times J}$ uses the same\ncondition (i)–(ii) but with $I$ replaced by $I'$ throughout.\n\n## Statement\n\nSuppose row $i \\in I$ is **not** useful in $[s, s+t^*]$, i.e.,\n$i \\notin I(\\beta(t))$ for every $t \\in [s, s+t^*]$. Let\n$I' := I \\setminus \\{i\\}$ and $A' := A|_{I' \\times J}$.\n\nThen the trajectory $(\\alpha(t), \\beta(t)|_{I'})_{t \\in [s, s+t^*]}$, with\nsuitable initial-condition adjustment of size at most $2\\|A\\|$, is an\nadmissible sequence on $A'$. Consequently, if the lemma\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]] holds for $A'$ with\nconstant $s'(A', \\varepsilon/2)$ such that\n$\\mu'(t) \\le (\\varepsilon/2) t$ for $t \\ge s'$, and if\n$t^* \\ge s'(A', \\varepsilon/2)$, then\n$$\n  \\mu(s + t^*) - \\mu(s) \\;\\le\\; \\frac{\\varepsilon t^*}{2} + 2\\|A\\|.\n$$\n\nThe same statement holds with rows and columns swapped (some $j \\in J$ not\nuseful, restricting to $J' := J \\setminus \\{j\\}$ and $A|_{I \\times J'}$).\n\n## Proof\n\nSince $i$ is not useful in $[s, s+t^*]$, at every step $t+1 \\in [s+1, s+t^*]$\nthe chosen index $i_{t+1} \\in I(\\beta(t))$ lies in $I'$. Therefore:\n\n- the component $\\beta^i$ is **not updated** anywhere in the window;\n- every update $\\alpha(t+1) = \\alpha(t) + e_{i_{t+1}}^T A$ uses\n  $i_{t+1} \\in I'$, so the row used belongs to $A'$;\n- $j_{t+1} \\in J(\\alpha(t))$ depends only on $\\alpha$ (unchanged formula).\n\nDefine $\\beta'(t) := \\beta(t)|_{I'} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m-1}$ and\n$\\alpha'(t) := \\alpha(t) \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$ for $t \\in [s, s+t^*]$. Then\n$(\\alpha', \\beta')$ evolves on the window exactly by the admissible rule\nfor $A'$, except possibly for the initial bracket condition.\n\nFor the initial bracket on $A'$ at time $s$: we need\n$\\min_k \\alpha'^k(s) = \\max_k \\beta'^k(s)$. This may not hold exactly for the\ninherited values, but shifting both vectors by a common constant restores it\n(admissibility is translation-invariant in this sense), and the constant\nabsorbed at the end contributes at most $2\\|A\\|$ to the gap $\\mu(s+t^*) -\n\\mu(s)$ — the maximum single-step jump within the window can deviate by this\nmargin once.\n\nNow apply the lemma on $A'$ with $\\varepsilon/2$: there exists\n$s'(A', \\varepsilon/2)$ such that $\\mu'(t-s) \\le (\\varepsilon/2)(t-s)$ for\n$t - s \\ge s'$. Choosing the parent's $t^*$ to dominate $s'(A', \\varepsilon/2)$\ngives at the window endpoint\n$$\n  \\mu'(t^*) \\le \\frac{\\varepsilon t^*}{2}.\n$$\n\nFinally relate $\\mu$ and $\\mu'$ on the window. Because $i \\notin I(\\beta(t))$\nthroughout, $\\max_k \\beta^k(t) = \\max_{k \\in I'} \\beta^k(t) = \\max \\beta'(t)$\nfor every $t \\in [s, s+t^*]$. Since $\\alpha$ is unchanged,\n$\\min_j \\alpha^j(t) = \\min_j \\alpha'^j(t)$ as well. Hence $\\mu(t) = \\mu'(t)$ on\nthe window, and combining with the $2\\|A\\|$ initial-bracket adjustment:\n$$\n  \\mu(s+t^*) - \\mu(s) \\le \\frac{\\varepsilon t^*}{2} + 2\\|A\\|.\n$$\n$\\square$\n\n## Note\n\nThe strict submatrix $A'$ has size $(m-1) + n = m + n - 1 < m + n$, which is\nexactly the inductive parameter in the main lemma. This is why the induction\ncloses.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 12 part (3)(b)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Non-useful-row reduction to a\n  strict submatrix."

      "body": "# Useful Window Bound For Admissible Sequences\n\nA geometric collapse estimate used by\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma]] inside the main\ninduction's \"all rows/columns useful\" case.\n\n## Setup\n\nFor an admissible sequence on $A \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m \\times n}$, an index\n$i \\in I$ is **useful** in the window $[t_1, t_2] \\subseteq \\mathbb{N}$ if\n$$\n  \\exists t \\in [t_1, t_2] : i \\in I(\\beta(t)) = \\operatorname{argmax}_k \\beta^k(t).\n$$\nThat is, $i$ is selected as a best response at some moment in the window.\nSymmetrically for $j \\in J$ via $J(\\alpha(t))$.\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $\\|A\\| := \\max_{i,j} |A_{i,j}|$.\n\n**(iv)** If every $j \\in J$ is useful in $[s, s+t]$ then\n$$\n  \\max_j \\alpha^j(s+t) - \\min_j \\alpha^j(s+t) \\;\\le\\; 2t \\|A\\|.\n$$\nSymmetrically, if every $i \\in I$ is useful in $[s, s+t]$ then\n$\\max_i \\beta^i(s+t) - \\min_i \\beta^i(s+t) \\le 2t\\|A\\|$.\n\n**(v)** If every $i \\in I$ and every $j \\in J$ is useful in $[s, s+t]$ then\n$$\n  \\mu(s+t) \\;\\le\\; 4 t \\|A\\|,\n$$\nwhere $\\mu := \\max_i \\beta^i - \\min_j \\alpha^j$.\n\n## Proof\n\n**(iv).** Fix indices $j_1, j_2 \\in J$. By hypothesis $j_2$ is useful: pick\n$\\tau \\in [s, s+t]$ with $j_2 \\in J(\\alpha(\\tau))$, so\n$\\alpha^{j_2}(\\tau) = \\min_k \\alpha^k(\\tau) \\le \\alpha^{j_1}(\\tau)$.\n\nAlong admissible evolution, each component of $\\alpha$ changes by at most\n$\\|A\\|$ per step (only the argmin component updates, with increment\n$A_{i_{\\tau+1}, j_{\\tau+1}}$ of magnitude $\\le \\|A\\|$). In particular\n$$\n  |\\alpha^{j_k}(s+t) - \\alpha^{j_k}(\\tau)| \\le (s+t-\\tau)\\|A\\| \\le t\\|A\\|,\n  \\quad k = 1, 2.\n$$\nCombining,\n$$\n  \\alpha^{j_2}(s+t) - \\alpha^{j_1}(s+t)\n   \\le [\\alpha^{j_2}(\\tau) - \\alpha^{j_1}(\\tau)] + 2t\\|A\\| \\le 2t\\|A\\|.\n$$\nTaking maximum over $j_2$ and minimum over $j_1$ gives the result.\n\nThe symmetric statement for $\\beta$ is identical with $J(\\alpha)$ replaced by\n$I(\\beta)$ and roles swapped.\n\n**(v).** From (iv) and its dual:\n$$\n  \\max_j \\alpha^j(s+t) - \\min_j \\alpha^j(s+t) \\le 2t\\|A\\|, \\quad\n  \\max_i \\beta^i(s+t) - \\min_i \\beta^i(s+t) \\le 2t\\|A\\|.\n$$\nAdding:\n$$\n  [\\max_i \\beta^i - \\min_i \\beta^i](s+t)\n  + [\\max_j \\alpha^j - \\min_j \\alpha^j](s+t)\n  \\le 4t\\|A\\|.\n$$\nRewriting and inserting the bracket invariant\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.learning.robinson_admissible_lemma.bracket_invariant]]\n($\\min_i \\beta^i(s+t) \\le \\max_j \\alpha^j(s+t)$):\n$$\n  \\mu(s+t) + [\\max_j \\alpha^j(s+t) - \\min_i \\beta^i(s+t)] \\le 4t\\|A\\|.\n$$\nThe bracket invariant makes the second bracketed term non-negative, so\n$\\mu(s+t) \\le 4t\\|A\\|$. $\\square$\n\n## Note\n\nThe bound is *absolute* — it does not depend on $\\mu(s)$. This is the\nmechanism by which the main induction \"resets\" the cumulative gap once a\nwindow of full usefulness has been traversed.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 12 parts (2)(iv) and (2)(v)] Laraki, Renault,\n  and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Useful-window collapse and\n  combined $\\mu$ bound."

      "body": "# Matrix Game\n\nA finite two-player zero-sum matrix game is specified by finite row and column\nsets $I,J$ and a payoff matrix valued in a scalar field $\\mathbb{K}$\n\n$$A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{K}.$$\n\nPlayer I chooses a row, player II chooses a column, player I receives\n$A(i,j)$, and player II receives $-A(i,j)$. The default scalar in\nthe Lean structure is $\\mathbb{Q}$ (no order completeness assumed); the\ncanonical instantiations are $\\mathbb{Q}$ (where the value still lies in\nthe field by LP but the `sSup`-based `maximin/minimax`\ndefinitions are unavailable) and $\\mathbb{R}$ (where order completeness\ngives the full Loomis / minimax theorem).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Def. 2.2.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Finite two-player zero-sum games in matrix form."

      "body": "# Mixed Nash Equilibrium of a Matrix Game\n\nFor a finite matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$, there exist mixed\nstrategies $x^\\ast \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y^\\ast \\in \\Delta(J)$ such that\n\n$$E_A(x, y^\\ast) \\le E_A(x^\\ast, y^\\ast) \\le E_A(x^\\ast, y)$$\n\nfor every $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y \\in \\Delta(J)$ — the standard\nsaddle-point form of mixed Nash equilibrium in a zero-sum two-player game.\n\nThis is the strategy-level packaging of\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]] and is what is usually called \"the\nmatrix game has a (mixed) Nash equilibrium\".\n\nThe Lean development records the equilibrium in two complementary ways and\nproves them equivalent in the embedded strategic game:\n\n* `MatrixGame.IsMixedNashEq xx yy` — the saddle-point predicate directly on\n  the matrix game, easy to reason about and the form used to prove existence\n  (`MatrixGame.exists_mixed_nash_equilibrium`).\n* `MatrixGame.toStrategicGame` — the explicit two-player zero-sum strategic\n  game (payoffs $A$ and $-A$) whose `StrategicGame.IsMixedNashEq` reduces to\n  the saddle-point form. The full bridge theorem\n  `MatrixGame.exists_strategic_game_nash_equilibrium` packages a Nash\n  equilibrium of the embedded strategic game built from the saddle-point pair,\n  using the lemmas `expectedPayoff_toStrategicGame_zero` /\n  `expectedPayoff_toStrategicGame_one` that compute the\n  `StrategicGame.expectedPayoff` as `±A.E (p 0) (p 1)`.\n\nThe supporting `StrategicGame.MixedStrategy` / `MixedProfile` /\n`expectedPayoff` / `IsMixedNashEq` API is polymorphic in the payoff field\n`U` (any `Field U` with `LinearOrder` and `IsStrictOrderedRing`), so it\nspecialises to both $\\mathbb{Q}$ (for constructive `native_decide` examples\nsuch as Rock–Paper–Scissors) and $\\mathbb{R}$ (for the Loomis-based existence\ntheorem).\n\n*Proof.* Apply `MatrixGame.minimax_optimal_strategies` (closed by the\nsimplified-Loomis induction) to obtain $x^\\ast$, $y^\\ast$, and a value $v$\nwith $E_A(x^\\ast, j) \\ge v$ for every pure column $j$ and\n$E_A(i, y^\\ast) \\le v$ for every pure row $i$. By\n[[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]] this transfers to mixed responses:\n$E_A(x^\\ast, y') \\ge v$ for every $y' \\in \\Delta(J)$ and\n$E_A(x', y^\\ast) \\le v$ for every $x' \\in \\Delta(I)$. Taking $x' = x^\\ast$\nand $y' = y^\\ast$ shows $E_A(x^\\ast, y^\\ast) = v$, and the chain\n$E_A(x, y^\\ast) \\le v = E_A(x^\\ast, y^\\ast) \\le E_A(x^\\ast, y)$ holds for\nevery $x$ and $y$, which is exactly the saddle-point form.\n\n## Over ℚ and other ordered fields\n\nThe Loomis existence proof goes through the extreme value theorem on the\ncompact mixed-strategy simplex $\\Delta(I) \\subseteq \\mathbb{R}^{|I|}$. The\nrequired compactness is the standard Heine–Borel statement on $\\mathbb{R}^n$\nand is not available for $\\mathbb{Q}^n$, so *that* route intrinsically\nproduces real-valued strategies. Existence over $\\mathbb{Q}$ and every other\nlinearly ordered field is nonetheless available, sorry-free, through the\nsymmetrisation route `Minimax.minimax`\n([[node:math.minimax.ordered_field_minimax]]): it embeds the game in a\nskew-symmetric matrix and extracts the saddle point as a pure feasibility\nfact (the Theorem of the Alternative), needing no compactness or\norder-completeness. `MatrixGame.exists_mixed_nash_equilibrium` is built on\nthat route and is itself field-generic.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 5, Thm. 5.11 / 5.13] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Existence of mixed Nash equilibrium in a finite matrix game via the saddle-point equivalence."

      "body": "# Maximin is Bounded by Minimax\n\nFor every finite matrix game,\n\n$$\\max_x \\min_j E_A(x,j) \\le \\min_y \\max_i E_A(i,y).$$\n\nThis is the weak-duality inequality: player I's best guaranteed payoff cannot\nexceed player II's best upper bound on player I's payoff.\n\n*Proof.* For every mixed row $x$ and mixed column $y$,\n$$\n  \\min_j E_A(x,j) \\le E_A(x,y) \\le \\max_i E_A(i,y).\n$$\nTaking the supremum over $x$ on the left preserves the first inequality against\nthe fixed upper bound $\\max_i E_A(i,y)$, so\n$$\n  \\max_x \\min_j E_A(x,j) \\le \\max_i E_A(i,y)\n$$\nfor every $y$. Taking the infimum over $y$ gives\n$$\n  \\max_x \\min_j E_A(x,j) \\le \\min_y \\max_i E_A(i,y).\n$$\n\n## Abstract pure-strategy form\n\nOn arbitrary nonempty strategy sets $I, J$ with payoff $g : I \\times J \\to\n\\mathbb{R}$ and pure-strategy extrema (no mixing), the same argument gives\nweak duality\n\n$$\n  \\underline v = \\sup_{i \\in I} \\inf_{j \\in J} g(i,j)\n              \\;\\le\\; \\inf_{j \\in J} \\sup_{i \\in I} g(i,j) = \\overline v.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* For every pair $(i,j)$,\n$$\n  \\inf_{j' \\in J} g(i,j') \\le g(i,j) \\le \\sup_{i' \\in I} g(i',j).\n$$\nTaking the supremum over $i$ on the left and the infimum over $j$ on the right\ngives $\\underline v \\le \\overline v$. $\\square$\n\nThis abstract form is what nodes outside the finite-mixed setting cite. The\nLean formalisation lives in the finite-mixed instantiation above.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Lemmas 2.2.4 and 2.2.8] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. The lower value never exceeds the upper value.\n- [MFoGT, Lem. 2.2.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Abstract pure-strategy weak duality (merged from `zero_sum.core.maxmin_le_minmax`)."

      "body": "# Maximin and Minimax Values\n\nFor a mixed row strategy $x$, player I's guarantee is the worst expected payoff\nagainst a pure column:\n\n$$\\gamma_I(x) = \\min_{j \\in J} E_A(x,j).$$\n\nFor a mixed column strategy $y$, player II's guarantee against player I is the\nlargest payoff player I can obtain from a pure row:\n\n$$\\gamma_{II}(y) = \\max_{i \\in I} E_A(i,y).$$\n\nThe maximin value is \\(\\sup_x \\gamma_I(x)\\), and the minimax value is\n\\(\\inf_y \\gamma_{II}(y)\\).\n\n## Abstract pure-strategy form\n\nThe same definition applies on arbitrary nonempty strategy sets $I, J$ and a\npayoff $g : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$, with the inner extremum ranging over\n**pure** strategies (no mixing). Then the maxmin is\n\n$$\n  \\underline v = \\sup_{i \\in I} \\inf_{j \\in J} g(i,j),\n$$\n\nand the minmax is\n\n$$\n  \\overline v = \\inf_{j \\in J} \\sup_{i \\in I} g(i,j).\n$$\n\nThe maxmin is the best amount player 1 can guarantee, and the minmax is the\nleast amount player 2 can guarantee as an upper bound on player 1's payoff.\nThe Lean library currently formalises the finite mixed-strategy instantiation\nabove; the abstract form is the common conceptual ancestor and the form used\nwhen reasoning over general (e.g. infinite) strategy spaces.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Definitions 2.2.2-2.2.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Guarantees, maxmin, minmax, and game value.\n- [MFoGT, Def. 2.2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Abstract pure-strategy maxmin and minmax (merged from `zero_sum.core.maxmin_minmax`)."

      },
      "body": "# Directional Derivative Of The Value\n\nLet $S$ and $T$ be compact sets and let $f,g:S\\times T\\to\\mathbb R$. Assume that,\nfor every $\\alpha\\ge 0$, the functions $g$ and $f+\\alpha g$ are upper\nsemicontinuous in $s$ and lower semicontinuous in $t$, and that each game\n$(S,T,f+\\alpha g)$ has a value. Then\n$$\n  \\lim_{\\alpha\\to0^+}\n  \\frac{\\operatorname{val}_{S\\times T}(f+\\alpha g)\n        -\\operatorname{val}_{S\\times T}(f)}{\\alpha}\n$$\nexists and equals\n$$\n  \\operatorname{val}_{S(f)\\times T(f)}(g),\n$$\nthe value of the derived game.\n\n*Proof.* Let $s_\\alpha$ be optimal for player 1 in $f+\\alpha g$ and let $t\\in T(f)$.\nComparing $(f+\\alpha g)(s_\\alpha,t)$ with the two values gives a lower bound on\nthe difference quotient by $\\inf_{T(f)}g(s_\\alpha,t)$. Taking limit points of\n$s_\\alpha$ and using semicontinuity places the limit in $S(f)$, giving the lower\nbound by the value of the derived game. The dual argument with optimal strategies\nfor player 2 gives the reverse inequality.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 3.4.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Directional derivative of the value equals the value of the derived game."

      "body": "# General Value Operator\n\nFix strategy sets $S$ and $T$ and a convex cone $F$ of functions\n$S\\times T\\to\\mathbb R$ containing the constant functions. Assume every game\n$(S,T,f)$ with $f\\in F$ has a value. The value operator is\n$$\n  \\operatorname{val}_{S\\times T}:F\\to\\mathbb R,\\qquad\n  f\\mapsto\n  \\sup_{s\\in S}\\inf_{t\\in T}f(s,t)\n  =\n  \\inf_{t\\in T}\\sup_{s\\in S}f(s,t).\n$$\nIt is monotone and translates constants:\n$$\n  f\\le g\\Rightarrow \\operatorname{val}(f)\\le\\operatorname{val}(g),\n  \\qquad\n  \\operatorname{val}(f+c)=\\operatorname{val}(f)+c.\n$$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Value operator on a cone of payoff functions for games with a value."

      "body": "# Value Operator Properties\n\nFor finite real matrix games, the value operator $A \\mapsto \\operatorname{val}(A)$\nis continuous, monotone increasing, and non-expansive for the sup norm:\n$$\n  |\\operatorname{val}(A)-\\operatorname{val}(B)| \\le \\|A-B\\|_\\infty.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* If $A\\le B$ entrywise, then for every mixed row $x$ and mixed column\n$y$ one has $xAy\\le xBy$. Taking maxmin values gives\n$\\operatorname{val}(A)\\le\\operatorname{val}(B)$, so the value operator is\nmonotone. Let $\\delta=\\|A-B\\|_\\infty$. Then\n$$\n  A\\le B+\\delta\\mathbf 1\n  \\quad\\text{and}\\quad\n  B\\le A+\\delta\\mathbf 1.\n$$\nAdding the constant matrix $\\delta\\mathbf 1$ raises every mixed payoff, and\ntherefore the value, by $\\delta$. Monotonicity gives\n$$\n  \\operatorname{val}(A)\\le\\operatorname{val}(B)+\\delta\n  \\quad\\text{and}\\quad\n  \\operatorname{val}(B)\\le\\operatorname{val}(A)+\\delta,\n$$\nwhich is the non-expansive estimate. Non-expansiveness implies continuity.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3, after Thm. 2.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Continuity, monotonicity, and non-expansiveness of val."

      "body": "# Von Neumann Minimax Theorem\n\nEvery finite two-player zero-sum matrix game has a value in mixed strategies:\n\n$$\\max_x \\min_j E_A(x,j) = \\min_y \\max_i E_A(i,y).$$\n\nEquivalently, there are optimal mixed strategies $x^\\ast$ and $y^\\ast$ and a\nvalue $v$ such that player I guarantees at least $v$ against every column and\nplayer II holds player I to at most $v$ against every row.\n\nTwo proof routes attach to this theorem as separate proof-plan nodes:\n\n- [[node:math.minimax.minimax_from_loomis]] (**selected**): finite\n  minimax is the $B = \\mathbf{1}$ specialisation of the Loomis theorem\n  ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_theorem]]). Fully formalised in Lean\n  (`EconCSLib.StrategicGame.MinimaxLoomis`), which inlines the $B = \\mathbf{1}$\n  case of the Loomis induction\n  ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]) rather than first porting\n  the general positive-$B$ Loomis statement. The compactness/continuity\n  building blocks it relies on live in the core simplex layer\n  ([[node:math.simplex.pure]], [[node:math.simplex.continuity]],\n  [[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]]) and the existence + weak-duality\n  step is [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.lam_mu_existence]]; weak duality\n  ([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.maximin_le_minimax]]) supplies one direction of the\n  equality.\n- `Minimax.minimax` (**proved**, ordered-field-generic): a von Neumann\n  symmetrisation proof that works over any linearly ordered field — embed the\n  game in a skew-symmetric matrix and read the saddle point off its value-0\n  optimal strategy, which exists by the Theorem of the Alternative. Sorry-free,\n  needing no compactness or order-completeness\n  ([[node:math.minimax.ordered_field_minimax]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Thm. 2.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Von Neumann minimax theorem for finite zero-sum games."

      "body": "# Nash Payoff Uniqueness in Zero-Sum Games\n\nIn a zero-sum game, any two Nash equilibria give the same payoff to player 0\nand the same payoff to player 1.  Thus the equilibrium payoff is a value of the\ngame, independent of which Nash equilibrium is chosen.\n\nThe proof compares two equilibria through cross profiles.  One player's best\nresponse inequality is converted into the other player's inequality using\nzero-sum payoff negation.\n\n*Proof.* Let $\\sigma=(\\sigma_0,\\sigma_1)$ and\n$\\tau=(\\tau_0,\\tau_1)$ be two Nash equilibria, and write $u$ for player $0$'s\npayoff. Since $\\sigma_0$ is a best response to $\\sigma_1$ and $\\tau_0$ is an\navailable deviation,\n$$\n  u(\\sigma_0,\\sigma_1)\\ge u(\\tau_0,\\sigma_1).\n$$\nSince $\\tau_1$ is a best response to $\\tau_0$ for player $1$, payoff negation\nturns player $1$'s best-response inequality into\n$$\n  u(\\tau_0,\\sigma_1)\\ge u(\\tau_0,\\tau_1).\n$$\nThus $u(\\sigma)\\ge u(\\tau)$. Reversing the roles of $\\sigma$ and $\\tau$ gives\n$u(\\tau)\\ge u(\\sigma)$, so player $0$'s equilibrium payoff is unique. Player\n$1$'s payoff is its negative, hence is unique as well.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 4, Theorems 4.44-4.45] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. All Nash equilibria of a zero-sum game have the same payoff value."

      "body": "# Payoff Negation in Zero-Sum Games\n\nIf $G$ is zero-sum, then at every profile $\\sigma$ the payoff of either player\ndetermines the other:\n\n$$u_1(\\sigma) = -u_0(\\sigma), \\qquad u_0(\\sigma) = -u_1(\\sigma).$$\n\nThis is the algebraic reduction that lets later value and optimality statements\ntrack only the row player's payoff.\n\n*Proof.* The zero-sum hypothesis says\n$$\n  u_0(\\sigma)+u_1(\\sigma)=0\n$$\nat every profile $\\sigma$. Rearranging in the underlying additive group gives\n$u_1(\\sigma)=-u_0(\\sigma)$, and applying the same rearrangement with the players\ninterchanged gives $u_0(\\sigma)=-u_1(\\sigma)$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 4, Section 4.4] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Immediate algebraic consequence of zero-sum payoffs."
    }

      "body": "# The CostM Complexity Monad\n\n`CostM C α` is the **writer monad over an arbitrary additive monoid** `C`: a\nreturn value of type `α` paired with an accumulated cost in `C`,\n$$\n  \\mathrm{CostM}\\,C\\,\\alpha \\;=\\; \\alpha \\times C.\n$$\nSequential composition (`bind`, written `>>=`) adds the cost components,\n$$\n  \\mathrm{bind}(m, f).\\mathrm{cost}\n    \\;=\\; m.\\mathrm{cost} \\,+\\, (f\\,m.\\mathrm{ret}).\\mathrm{cost},\n  \\qquad\n  (\\mathrm{pure}\\,a).\\mathrm{cost} = 0,\n$$\nso a program's total cost is the monoid-sum of the costs charged along its\nexecution.\n\nThe cost type `C` is deliberately abstract: **choosing `C` is what selects the\nresource being measured**, while the monad is identical for all of them.\n\n- `C := ℕ` (additive) — count comparisons, recursive calls, modulus\n  operations: the conventional \"time\" instance.\n- `C := A × B` — track two additive costs at once via `Prod.instAddMonoid`.\n- `C := Visited α` (idempotent, `s + s = s`) — the **set** of subproblems\n  touched; the algebraic shadow of memoization. See\n  [[node:foundation.cost.visited]].\n- `C := Cells` (tropical peak/delta) — **peak** memory, the one resource shape\n  additive cost fundamentally cannot express. See [[node:foundation.cost.cells]].\n\n## Discipline: cost annotations are trusted\n\nThe elaborator does **not** verify that `tick` calls correspond to real work.\nEach algorithm file documents its own cost model — what a unit is, what is\nfree, whether recursive calls are charged — and the author `tick`s\naccordingly. Proofs then separate cleanly along the two structure fields:\n\n- **functional correctness** lives on `m.ret` (alias `⟪m⟫`);\n- **complexity bounds** live on `m.cost`.\n\nThe two are independent: changing the cost model never disturbs a correctness\nproof, and refactoring the algorithm preserves cost annotations by\nconstruction. The Boyer–Moore example ([[node:foundation.cost.examples.boyer_moore]])\nproves a cost bound while deliberately *not* proving correctness, to exhibit\nthe decoupling.\n\n## Lean declarations\n\n- `CostM` — the two-field structure (`ret`, `cost`).\n- `CostM.pure` `[Zero C]`, `CostM.bind` `[Add C]` — the monad primitives;\n  `CostM.instMonad` `[Zero C] [Add C]` and `CostM.instLawfulMonad`\n  `[AddMonoid C]` package them as a lawful monad.\n- `CostM.tick c : CostM C PUnit` charges cost `c`; the `✓[c] body` macro is\n  sugar for `do tick c; body`, and `✓ body` is `✓[1] body` (needs `[OfNat C 1]`).\n- `CostM.Bounded alg size bound` `[LE C]` says `∀ i, (alg i).cost ≤ bound (size i)`;\n  `CostM.IsPolyBounded` specializes to `C = ℕ` with `∃ c k, cost ≤ c · size^k`.\n\nParallel composition (`par`, `parList`) is documented separately in\n[[node:foundation.cost.parallel]].\n\n## References\n\n- [Danielsson 2008] Nils Anders Danielsson, *Lightweight Semiformal Time\n  Complexity Analysis for Purely Functional Data Structures*, POPL 2008. The\n  writer-monad-over-a-monoid pattern for cost analysis.\n\n## Provenance\n\n- The monad core (`structure`, `Pure`/`Bind`/`Functor`/`Seq`, `Monad`/\n  `LawfulMonad`, `tick`, the `✓` notation) is **adapted from `TimeM`** in\n  [leanprover/cslib](https://github.com/leanprover/cslib),\n  `Cslib/Algorithms/Lean/TimeM.lean` (Apache 2.0), by Sorrachai\n  Yingchareonthawornhcai and Eric Wieser. EconCSLib generalizes \"time\" to a\n  general cost monoid `C` and adds `par`/`parList`, `Bounded`/`IsPolyBounded`,\n  and the `CoeHead` projection."
    },

      "body": "# Peak-Memory Cost via the Cells Monoid\n\nAdditive cost ([[node:foundation.cost.costm]]) cannot express **peak** memory,\nbecause the high-water mark of a sequence of allocations and frees is not the\nsum of the per-step changes. `Cells` is the cost monoid that fixes this: an\nelement carries a non-negative `peak` and a signed net `delta` with the\ninvariant `delta ≤ peak` (and `0 ≤ peak`).\n\nComposition is the **tropical / (max,+)** law that tracks the worst high-water\nmark across a sequence — the peak of the second block is reached *after* the\nfirst block's net allocation:\n$$\n  (p_1, d_1) \\star (p_2, d_2)\n    \\;=\\; \\bigl(\\max(p_1,\\; d_1 + p_2),\\; d_1 + d_2\\bigr),\n  \\qquad 0 = (0,0).\n$$\nThis is an additive monoid (the EconCSLib `CostM` framework requires `C` to be\nan additive monoid), but a *non-cancellative* one — the `⋆` above is its `+`.\n\nThe two generators model allocation and release of `n` cells:\n$$\n  \\operatorname{alloc} n = (n, n),\n  \\qquad\n  \\operatorname{free} n = (0, -n).\n$$\nAn `alloc n` raises both the current footprint and the peak by `n`; a\n`free n` lowers the net footprint by `n` while leaving the peak untouched\n(the cells were live at some point).\n\n## Lean declarations\n\n- `Cells` — the structure (`peak`, `delta`, `zero_le_peak`, `delta_le_peak`);\n  its `Zero`/`Add`/`AddMonoid` instances are anonymous.\n- `Cells.alloc`, `Cells.free` — the generators.\n- Projection lemmas `peak_zero`/`delta_zero`, `peak_add`/`delta_add`,\n  `peak_alloc`/`delta_alloc`, `peak_free`/`delta_free` drive the `simp`\n  normal form for peak computations.\n\nThe canonical use is the constant-space Boyer–Moore majority vote,\n[[node:foundation.cost.examples.boyer_moore]], which proves `peak ≤ 2`\nindependent of input length.\n\n## References\n\n- [Danielsson 2008] Nils Anders Danielsson, *Lightweight Semiformal Time\n  Complexity Analysis for Purely Functional Data Structures*, POPL 2008. Cost\n  monoids for resource analysis ([[node:foundation.cost.costm]]).\n\n## Provenance\n\n- `Cells` is an EconCSLib addition (no `TimeM` counterpart upstream), built on\n  the [leanprover/cslib](https://github.com/leanprover/cslib)-derived monad\n  core (Apache 2.0)."
    },

The mechanism is that the single-pass `loop`\nallocates nothing — `loop_cost : (majority.loop \\ldots).cost = 0` — so the only\ncontributions to the peak come from one `alloc 2` / `free 2` pair bracketing\nthe pass. Because peak (not sum) is the resource, the tropical `Cells` monoid\nis essential here; an additive `ℕ` cost cannot state this bound.\n\nThis example deliberately **does not** prove functional correctness (that\n`majority` returns the true majority when one exists). That omission is the\npoint: in `CostM` the complexity bound lives on `.cost` and is provable in\ncomplete isolation from the `.ret` value, demonstrating the\ncorrectness/complexity decoupling described in [[node:foundation.cost.costm]].\n\n## Lean declarations\n\n- `BoyerMoore.majority : List α → CostM Cells (Option α)` with its single-pass\n  `where loop` carrying the candidate and counter.\n- `BoyerMoore.loop_cost` — the loop contributes zero cost.\n- `BoyerMoore.majority_peak_le` — the constant `peak ≤ 2` bound.\n\n## References\n\n- [Danielsson 2008] Nils Anders Danielsson, POPL 2008. Cost monoids for\n  resource analysis ([[node:foundation.cost.cells]])."

          "foundation.cost.examples.par_all"

      "body": "# Parallel Composition in CostM\n\nSequential `>>=` combines cost additively; **parallel** composition combines it\nby the semilattice join `⊔` instead, modelling the *depth* (branch-worst-case)\nview in which independent branches run concurrently and the joint cost is the\nworse of the two:\n$$\n  (\\operatorname{par} m_1\\, m_2).\\mathrm{cost}\n    \\;=\\; m_1.\\mathrm{cost} \\,\\sqcup\\, m_2.\\mathrm{cost}.\n$$\n`par` is **not** a monadic operation: neither operand's value feeds the other,\nso it is only sound when the two sides are genuinely data-independent. It\nrequires `[SemilatticeSup C]`.\n\nThe n-ary `parList ms` extends `par` to a `List` of independent operands:\nreturns are collected in order, and costs are folded with `⊔` from the\nidentity `⊥` (so the empty list costs `⊥`, which is `0` for `C = ℕ`):\n$$\n  (\\operatorname{parList}\\,[m_1,\\dots,m_n]).\\mathrm{cost}\n    \\;=\\; m_1.\\mathrm{cost} \\sqcup \\cdots \\sqcup m_n.\\mathrm{cost}.\n$$\n`parList` additionally needs `[OrderBot C]` for that identity. This is the\nflat fan-out / fan-in, depth-1 schedule with `n` workers.\n\nFor combined work-and-depth tracking one would use `C := ℕ × ℕ` with `+` on\nthe work component and `⊔` on the depth component; that per-component\ncombinator is not provided here.\n\n## Lean declarations\n\n- `CostM.par` `[SemilatticeSup C]` with projection lemmas `ret_par`, `cost_par`.\n- `CostM.parList` `[SemilatticeSup C] [OrderBot C]` with `ret_parList`,\n  `cost_parList`, the base case `parList_nil`, and the cons recurrence\n  `cost_parList_cons`.\n\nWorked examples: balanced-tree depth in [[node:foundation.cost.examples.par_sum]]\nand the n-ary `parList` bound in [[node:foundation.cost.examples.par_all]].\n\n## References\n\n- [Danielsson 2008] Nils Anders Danielsson, *Lightweight Semiformal Time\n  Complexity Analysis for Purely Functional Data Structures*, POPL 2008. The\n  underlying writer-monad cost discipline ([[node:foundation.cost.costm]]).\n\n## Provenance\n\n- `par` and `parList` are EconCSLib additions on top of the `TimeM`-derived\n  monad core from [leanprover/cslib](https://github.com/leanprover/cslib)\n  (Apache 2.0); they have no upstream counterpart at the pinned revision."
