      "body": "# Memoization Footprint via the Visited Monoid\n\n`Visited α` is the cost monoid that records the **set of subproblems touched**\nby a recursive algorithm. It is `Finset α` with union as addition and the\nempty set as zero:\n$$\n  s + t = s \\cup t, \\qquad 0 = \\varnothing.\n$$\nThe defining feature is **idempotence**, `s + s = s`: revisiting a subproblem\nadds nothing. This is the algebraic shadow of memoization — under a memo table\nthe second visit is free, so the cost (the footprint) is exactly the set of\n*distinct* subproblems, not the number of calls. A memoized algorithm's\n`.cost` is therefore the set of table entries it fills.\n\n`Visited α` is a **type synonym** for `Finset α` (`def Visited α := Finset α`),\nintroduced specifically to firewall Mathlib's scoped pointwise `Zero (Finset α)`\ninstance: the cost-monoid `0 = ∅` and `+ = ∪` must not collide with pointwise\narithmetic on finsets. `toFinset`/`ofFinset` move across the synonym boundary.\n\n## Lean declarations\n\n- `Visited` — the `Finset` type synonym; `Visited.toFinset`/`Visited.ofFinset`\n  the round-trip maps and `Visited.singleton a` the one-point footprint.\n- `Zero`/`Add [DecidableEq α]`/`AddMonoid` instances are anonymous.\n- `Visited.ext` plus the `simp` lemmas `toFinset_zero`, `toFinset_singleton`,\n  `toFinset_add` reduce footprint reasoning to ordinary `Finset` set algebra.\n\nWorked examples: the 1-D memoization footprint of Fibonacci\n([[node:foundation.cost.examples.memo_fib]], cost `= range (n+1)`) and the 2-D\nDP-grid footprint of longest common subsequence\n([[node:foundation.cost.examples.lcs]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [Danielsson 2008] Nils Anders Danielsson, *Lightweight Semiformal Time\n  Complexity Analysis for Purely Functional Data Structures*, POPL 2008. Cost\n  monoids for resource analysis ([[node:foundation.cost.costm]]).\n\n## Provenance\n\n- `Visited` is an EconCSLib addition (no `TimeM` counterpart upstream), built on\n  the [leanprover/cslib](https://github.com/leanprover/cslib)-derived monad\n  core (Apache 2.0)."
    },
    {
      "id": "foundation.argmax.list_arg_max_on",
      "title": "Argmax of a List under a Total Preorder",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "formalized",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "foundation",
      "topics": [
        "foundation",
        "foundation.argmax"
      ],
      "uses": [
        "foundation.preference.total_preorder"
      ],
      "used_by": [],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/foundation/argmax.list_arg_max_on.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Argmax of a List under a Total Preorder\n\nFor a function `f : α → β` valued in a `TotalPreorder β` and a non-empty\nlist `head :: tail : List α`, some element of the list maximizes `f`:\n$$\n  \\exists m \\in \\operatorname{head} :: \\operatorname{tail},\\;\n  \\forall x \\in \\operatorname{head} :: \\operatorname{tail},\\; f(x) \\le f(m).\n$$\n\nThe proof is by induction on `tail`, comparing the current maximum against\nthe new head via `TotalPreorder.le_total`.\n\nFrom the existence statement a noncomputable choice\n`List.argMaxOn f head tail` picks a witnessing maximizer. Its API:\n\n- `argMaxOn_mem` -- the chosen element lies in the list.\n- `argMaxOn_ge` -- the chosen element is `≥` every list element in `f`-value.\n- `le_argMaxOn_head` -- specialization: the head's value is `≤` the chosen\n  element's value.\n\nThe variant exists because Mathlib's `List.argmax` is computable but requires\n`[LinearOrder]`, which is too strong for ranking outcomes that may be\nindifferent (the typical situation when a player's payoffs are equal across\ndistinct continuations). The intended consumer is\n`ExtensiveGame.BackwardInduction`, where finite game trees are evaluated by\nrecursively picking an argmax of children.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 3] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Backward induction on finite extensive games."
    },
    {
      "id": "foundation.preference.abstract_relation",
      "title": "Abstract Preference-Relation Axioms",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "formalized",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "foundation",

        "foundation",

      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/foundation/preference.abstract_relation.md",
      "body_refs": {

      "body": "# Abstract Preference-Relation Axioms\n\nFor arguments that quantify over an arbitrary binary relation\n`pref : α → α → Prop` (rather than the bundled `Preorder` instance), the\nfoundation layer exposes a relation-style vocabulary:\n\n- **Strict preference** `strict pref a b := pref a b ∧ ¬ pref b a`\n- **Indifference** `indiff pref a b := pref a b ∧ pref b a`\n- **Completeness** `Completeness pref := ∀ a b, pref a b ∨ pref b a`\n- **Transitivity** `Transitivity pref := ∀ a b c, pref a b → pref b c → pref a c`\n\nThis vocabulary is what preference-based statements and the vNM axiom suite use\nto formulate axioms about a free-standing relation argument, without\ncommitting to the `Preorder` typeclass on `α`. Lottery-specific axioms\n(Independence, Continuity, Archimedean property) are stated on top of\n`Completeness` and `Transitivity` in `Utility.VNMAxioms`.\n\nIn Lean, `strict` and `indiff` are library-wide definitions.\n`Completeness` and `Transitivity` remain inside `namespace VNM` because they\nname axioms in the vNM suite.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 2] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Preference-relation axioms in their\n  relation-style formulation."
    },
    {
      "id": "foundation.preference.indifferent",
      "title": "Indifference Relation",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "formalized",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "foundation",
      "topics": [
        "foundation",
        "foundation.preference"
      ],
      "uses": [],
      "used_by": [
        "foundation.preference.relation",
        "foundation.preference.represents_preference"
      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/foundation/preference.indifferent.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Indifference Relation\n\nOn any `Preorder α`, two elements are *indifferent* when each is weakly\npreferred to the other:\n$$\n  \\operatorname{Indifferent}(a, b) \\quad\\Longleftrightarrow\\quad\n  a \\le b \\;\\text{ and }\\; b \\le a.\n$$\n\nIndifference is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. It is therefore an\nequivalence relation on every preorder. On a `PartialOrder` antisymmetry\ncollapses it to equality; on a general preorder (or total preorder) it can\nrelate genuinely distinct elements, which is the typical situation in utility\ntheory.\n\nIn Lean this is `Indifferent : α → α → Prop` together with\n`Indifferent.refl / symm / trans`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 2, Def. 2.5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Indifference as the symmetric part of weak\n  preference."
    },
    {
      "id": "foundation.preference.relation",

      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/staged/foundation/preference/relation.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Preference Relation (MSZ Ch.2 Narrative)\n\nA weak preference relation compares alternatives by the statement that one\nalternative is at least as good as another. From weak preference one derives:\n\n- *strict preference*, when one alternative is weakly preferred and the\n  reverse weak preference fails;\n- *indifference*, when each alternative is weakly preferred to the other.\n\nFor utility theory the natural abstract structure is a total preorder:\npreference is reflexive, transitive, and complete, but it need not be\nantisymmetric because distinct alternatives can be indifferent.\n\n## Lean substrate\n\nThe Lean-level vocabulary lives in the `foundation.preference` topic; this node\nis the MSZ Ch.2 domain narrative, and it cross-links into the four foundation\ndefinitions that realize it:\n\n- weak preference and indifference: [[foundation.preference.indifferent]]\n- strict preference: [[foundation.preference.strictly_preferred]]\n- total preorder (no antisymmetry required): [[foundation.preference.total_preorder]]\n- relation-style axioms used by vNM: [[foundation.preference.abstract_relation]]\n\nThe `EconCSLib.Foundation.Preference` module is the single source of truth in\nLean; this node is the MSZ Ch.2 narrative wrapper and introduces no Lean\ndefinitions of its own beyond what the `foundation.preference` topic already\nprovides.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 2, Definitions 2.1-2.7] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir,\n  *Game Theory*. Preference, strict preference,\n  indifference, and total preorder vocabulary."
    },
    {
      "id": "foundation.preference.represents_preference",
      "title": "Utility Representation of a Preference",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "formalized",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "foundation",
      "topics": [
        "foundation",
        "foundation.preference"
      ],
      "uses": [
        "foundation.preference.indifferent",
        "foundation.preference.strictly_preferred"
      ],
      "used_by": [
        "foundation.utility.expected_utility_representation"
      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/foundation/preference.represents_preference.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Utility Representation of a Preference\n\nGiven preorders on `α` and `β`, a function `u : α → β` *represents* the\npreference `≤` on `α` when it preserves and reflects weak preference:\n$$\n  \\forall a,\\,b,\\quad a \\le b \\;\\Longleftrightarrow\\; u(a) \\le u(b).\n$$\n\nA representation automatically preserves the derived strict preference and\nindifference relations, witnessed by `RepresentsPreference.lt_iff` and\n`RepresentsPreference.indifferent_iff`. This is the abstract scaffolding used\nby ordinal-utility statements in utility theory (the `foundation.preference` topic)\nand by vNM-style expected-utility theorems.\n\nIn Lean this is `structure RepresentsPreference (u : α → β) : Prop` carrying\nthe single field `le_iff`. The two derived `iff` lemmas are stated and proved\ndirectly from `le_iff` using the Mathlib `Preorder` API.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 2, Def. 2.7] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir,\n  *Game Theory*. Utility representation of a\n  preference relation."
    },
    {
      "id": "foundation.preference.strictly_preferred",
      "title": "Strict Preference Relation",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "formalized",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "foundation",
      "topics": [
        "foundation",
        "foundation.preference"

      "uses": [],

        "foundation.preference.relation",

      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/foundation/preference.strictly_preferred.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Strict Preference Relation\n\nOn any `Preorder α`, strict preference is the strict part of the preorder:\n$$\n  a \\succ b \\quad\\Longleftrightarrow\\quad a < b\n  \\quad\\Longleftrightarrow\\quad a \\le b \\;\\text{ and }\\; \\neg(b \\le a).\n$$\n\nStrict preference is asymmetric, transitive, and irreflexive. These three\nproperties — asymmetry from `lt_asymm`, transitivity from `lt_trans`,\nirreflexivity from `lt_irrefl` — are inherited directly from the Mathlib\n`Preorder` API.\n\nIn Lean this is `abbrev StrictlyPreferred (a b : α) : Prop := a < b`. The\nabbreviation exists for readability in game-theory contexts; downstream code\nmay also use the bare `<` notation interchangeably.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 2, Def. 2.5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Strict preference derived from weak preference.\n- [MSZ, Exercise 2.1(a)] Asymmetry, transitivity, and irreflexivity of strict\n  preference."
    },
    {
      "id": "foundation.preference.total_preorder",
      "title": "Total Preorder",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "formalized",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "foundation",
      "topics": [
        "foundation",
        "foundation.preference"
      ],
      "uses": [],
      "used_by": [
        "foundation.argmax.list_arg_max_on",
        "foundation.preference.relation"
      ],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/foundation/preference.total_preorder.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Total Preorder\n\nA *total preorder* on `α` is a `Preorder` for which `≤` is total:\n$$\n  \\forall a,\\, b \\in \\alpha,\\quad a \\le b \\;\\text{ or }\\; b \\le a.\n$$\n\nUnlike `LinearOrder`, a total preorder is **not** required to be antisymmetric\nor to have decidable order. Distinct elements may be indifferent, which is\nthe typical situation in utility theory (multiple alternatives can yield the\nsame utility) and in matching theory (a doctor can rank two hospitals equally).\n\n`TotalPreorder` is the appropriate weakening of `LinearOrder` whenever a\nresult needs comparability of any two elements but does not need to identify\nindifferent alternatives. Every `LinearOrder` is a `TotalPreorder` via the\nauto-derived `LinearOrder.toTotalPreorder` instance.\n\nIn Lean this is `class TotalPreorder (α : Type*) extends Preorder α`\ntogether with the totality field `le_total` and the reusable lemma\n`TotalPreorder.comparable`. The bridge from `LinearOrder` is supplied by\nthe auto-derived instance `LinearOrder.toTotalPreorder` in the same module\n(declared with `instance`, not enumerated in the declaration list above).\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 2, Definitions 2.1-2.4] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir,\n  *Game Theory*. Reflexivity, transitivity,\n  and completeness of weak preference."
    },
    {
      "id": "foundation.profile.deviate",
      "title": "Standalone Profile and Unilateral Deviation",
      "kind": "definition",
      "status": "formalized",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "foundation",
      "topics": [
        "foundation",
        "foundation.profile"
      ],
      "uses": [],
      "used_by": [],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/foundation/profile.deviate.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Standalone Profile and Unilateral Deviation\n\nFor an arbitrary index type `N` and family of strategy types `S : N → Type*`,\na *strategy profile* is a dependent function\n$$\n  \\sigma : \\prod_{i : \\iota} S(i).\n$$\n\nA *unilateral deviation* by player $i$ to $s' \\in S(i)$ is the profile that\nagrees with $\\sigma$ off $i$ and equals $s'$ at $i$. This is exactly\n`Function.update`, exposed under the game-theoretic alias\n`deviate σ i s'` and the dedicated notation $\\sigma[i \\mapsto s']$.\n\nThe three governing simp lemmas:\n\n- `deviate_self` -- deviating to the current value is the identity:\n  $\\sigma[i \\mapsto \\sigma_i] = \\sigma$.\n- `deviate_same` -- at the deviated index, the new profile returns the new\n  value: $\\sigma[i \\mapsto s']_i = s'$.\n- `deviate_of_ne` -- at any other index, the new profile is unchanged:\n  $\\sigma[i \\mapsto s']_j = \\sigma_j$ when $j \\ne i$.\n\n## Status: long-term compatibility layer\n\nThis node is the **standalone** profile vocabulary. The canonical\nstrategic-game version, `G.Profile` together with `StrategicGame.deviate`\nin `StrategicGame.Basic`, is the preferred interface for game-bound code.\nThe standalone version is preserved indefinitely for two reasons:\n\n1. lemmas about profiles can be stated without committing to a specific\n   `StrategicGame` instance (the proofs reduce to `Function.update` facts);\n2. legacy student-project code and non-strategic-game profile uses\n   (extensive games, social-choice ballots) continue to depend on it.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 4] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Strategy profiles and unilateral deviations."
    }
  ]
}

      "body": "# Von Neumann Minimax Theorem\n\nEvery finite two-player zero-sum matrix game has a value in mixed strategies:\n\n$$\\max_x \\min_j E_A(x,j) = \\min_y \\max_i E_A(i,y).$$\n\nEquivalently, there are optimal mixed strategies $x^\\ast$ and $y^\\ast$ and a\nvalue $v$ such that player I guarantees at least $v$ against every column and\nplayer II holds player I to at most $v$ against every row.\n\nTwo proof routes attach to this theorem as separate proof-plan nodes:\n\n- [[node:math.minimax.minimax_from_loomis]] (**selected**): finite\n  minimax is the $B = \\mathbf{1}$ specialisation of the Loomis theorem\n  ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_theorem]]). Fully formalised in Lean\n  (`EconCSLib.StrategicGame.MinimaxLoomis`), which inlines the $B = \\mathbf{1}$\n  case of the Loomis induction\n  ([[node:math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]) rather than first porting\n  the general positive-$B$ Loomis statement. The compactness/continuity\n  building blocks it relies on live in the core simplex layer\n  ([[node:math.simplex.pure]], [[node:math.simplex.continuity]],\n  [[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]]) and the existence + weak-duality\n  step is [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.lam_mu_existence]]; weak duality\n  ([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.maximin_le_minimax]]) supplies one direction of the\n  equality.\n- `Minimax.minimax` (**proved**, ordered-field-generic): a von Neumann\n  symmetrisation proof that works over any linearly ordered field — embed the\n  game in a skew-symmetric matrix and read the saddle point off its value-0\n  optimal strategy, which exists by the Theorem of the Alternative. Sorry-free,\n  needing no compactness or order-completeness\n  ([[node:math.minimax.ordered_field_minimax]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Thm. 2.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Von Neumann minimax theorem for finite zero-sum games."
    },

      "kind": "theorem",

      "home_topic": "game_theory.zero_sum",

      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [
          {
            "target_id": "game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax",
            "known": true,
            "in_uses": true
          }
        ],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Antisymmetric Matrix Game Has Value Zero\n\nA square matrix $B : I \\times I \\to \\mathbb{R}$ is **antisymmetric** if\n$B = -B^{\\mathsf{T}}$, i.e. $B_{ij} = -B_{ji}$ for all $i,j$ (so in particular\n$B_{ii} = 0$). The matrix game $B$ then has value $0$, and there exists\n$x \\in \\Delta(I)$ such that $(Bx)_i \\le 0$ for every row $i$.\n\n*Proof.* By the minimax theorem\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) the game has a\nvalue $v$. Antisymmetry gives $z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z = 0$ for every mixed $z$, since\n$z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z = -z^{\\mathsf{T}} B^{\\mathsf{T}} z = -(z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z)$.\nApplying this to an optimal $x^\\ast$ for player I,\n$0 = \\sum_j x^\\ast_j (e_j B x^\\ast)$ while each $e_j B x^\\ast \\ge v$, forcing\n$v \\le 0$; the symmetric argument gives $v \\ge 0$, so $v = 0$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 10(1)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Antisymmetric matrix games have value zero."
    },

      "id": "game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.applications.markov_stationary_as_zero_sum_value",
      "title": "Markov Stationary Distribution as Zero-Sum Game Value",
      "kind": "lemma",
      "status": "admitted",
      "evidence": "admitted",
      "home_topic": "game_theory.zero_sum",
      "topics": [
        "game_theory.zero_sum",
        "game_theory.zero_sum.applications"
      ],
      "uses": [
        "game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.applications.stochastic_matrix_invariant_distribution",
        "game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax"
      ],
      "used_by": [],
      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/zero_sum/applications/markov_stationary_as_zero_sum_value.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Markov Stationary Distribution as Zero-Sum Game Value\n\n**Lemma.** Let $A : I \\times I \\to \\mathbb{R}$ be a row-stochastic\nmatrix (entries $\\ge 0$, every row sums to 1), and consider the\n*displacement game* with payoff matrix $B := A - \\operatorname{Id}$.\nThen:\n\n1. The displacement game has value $\\operatorname{val}(B) = 0$.\n2. Every row-optimal mixed strategy $x^* \\in X(B)$ for player 1 is a\n   **stationary distribution** of $A$:\n   $x^* A = x^*$.\n\nThis is the proof structure underlying\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.applications.stochastic_matrix_invariant_distribution]] —\nthe classical von Neumann construction translating\n\"Markov stationary distribution exists\" into \"an optimal mixed\nstrategy in a particular zero-sum game\".\n\n## Why this is a useful framing\n\nThe standard textbook proof of Markov stationary-distribution existence\nuses Brouwer's fixed-point theorem on $\\Delta(I)$. The\nzero-sum-game-theoretic proof bypasses Brouwer entirely:\n\n- Apply the minimax theorem\n  ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) to the displacement game\n  $B = A - \\operatorname{Id}$ — this gives existence of optimal\n  strategies for free.\n- Reduce stationarity to the *saddle-point characterisation* of those\n  optimal strategies (player 1's guarantee inequality, summed across\n  columns, forces equality on every column).\n\nThe whole argument is purely algebraic / combinatorial once minimax is\nin hand, which is itself proved by Loomis induction\n([[math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]) — no topology required.\nThis is a satisfying application of zero-sum theory to elementary\nMarkov-chain theory.\n\n## Bridge to the main theorem\n\nThe detailed argument lives in\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.applications.stochastic_matrix_invariant_distribution]]\n(MFoGT Cor. 2.5.2): the three-step proof there is\n\n1. Show $\\operatorname{val}(B) = 0$ (this lemma's statement 1) by\n   exhibiting matching upper and lower bounds.\n2.       "body": "# Stochastic Matrix Has An Invariant Distribution\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $A : I \\times I \\to \\mathbb{R}$ be a (row-)stochastic matrix: every\nentry is non-negative and every row sums to $1$. Then there exists a\nmixed strategy $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ such that\n\n$$\n  \\forall j,\\quad \\sum_i x_i \\, A_{ij} = x_j\n$$\n\n— i.e. $x A = x$, an **invariant distribution** of $A$.\n\n## Proof\n\nLet $B := A - \\operatorname{Id}$, i.e. $B_{ij} = A_{ij} - [i=j]$, and\nconsider the matrix game with payoff matrix $B$.\n\n### Step 1 — The displacement game has value $0$\n\n**Upper bound $v \\le 0$.** Take Player 2's uniform mixed strategy\n$y_{\\mathrm{unif}}$ with $y_j = 1 / |I|$. For every pure row $i$:\n$$\n  E_i(i, y_{\\mathrm{unif}}) = \\sum_j B_{ij} \\cdot \\tfrac{1}{|I|}\n    = \\tfrac{1}{|I|} \\big(\\!\\sum_j A_{ij}\\big) - \\tfrac{1}{|I|}\n    = \\tfrac{1}{|I|} - \\tfrac{1}{|I|} = 0,\n$$\nusing $\\sum_j A_{ij} = 1$. Hence Player 2's guarantee under\n$y_{\\mathrm{unif}}$ is $\\sup_i E_i(i, y_{\\mathrm{unif}}) = 0$. Since\n$\\mathrm{value} = \\mathrm{minimax} = \\inf_y \\mathrm{guarantee}_{II}(y)$,\nwe get $\\mathrm{value} \\le 0$.\n\n**Lower bound $v \\ge 0$.** For any column strategy $y$, pick\n$i_0 \\in \\arg\\min_j y_j$. Since $A_{i_0 j} \\ge 0$, $y_j \\ge y_{i_0}$,\nand $\\sum_j A_{i_0 j} = 1$:\n$$\n  (A y)_{i_0} \\;=\\; \\sum_j A_{i_0 j}\\, y_j\n                \\;\\ge\\; \\sum_j A_{i_0 j}\\, y_{i_0}\n                \\;=\\; y_{i_0} \\cdot 1 \\;=\\; y_{i_0}.\n$$\nTherefore $E_i(i_0, y) = (Ay)_{i_0} - y_{i_0} \\ge 0$, and\n$\\mathrm{guarantee}_{II}(y) = \\sup_i E_i(i, y) \\ge 0$ for every $y$.\nHence $\\mathrm{minimax} = \\inf_y \\mathrm{guarantee}_{II}(y) \\ge 0$.\n\nCombining, $\\mathrm{value} = 0$.\n\n### Step 2 — A row-optimal strategy is invariant\n\nTake any row-optimal $x^* \\in X(A)$ — existence via\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.matrix_game_nash_equilibrium]] combined with\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.optimal_strategy_sets]]. Then for every pure column $j$,\n$$\n  E_j(x^*, j) \\;\\ge\\; \\mathrm{value} \\;=\\; 0.\n$$\nExpanding $E_j(x^*, j) = (x^* A)_j - x^*_j$, we get\n$(x^* A)_j \\ge x^*_j$ for every $j$, i.e. $x^* A \\ge x^*$\ncomponentwise.\n\n### Step 3 — Total mass forces componentwise equality\n\nSum over $j$. Using $\\sum_j A_{ij} = 1$ and $\\sum_i x^*_i = 1$:\n$$\n  \\sum_j (x^* A)_j = \\sum_i x^*_i \\!\\sum_j A_{ij} = \\sum_i x^*_i = 1\n    = \\sum_j x^*_j.\n$$\nHence $\\sum_j ((x^* A)_j - x^*_j) = 0$, with every term $\\ge 0$, so\nevery term is exactly $0$:\n$$\n  \\forall j,\\quad (x^* A)_j = x^*_j.\n$$\n\nSo $x^*$ is an invariant distribution. $\\square$\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The argument is constructive once an optimal pair is given by\n  the minimax existence theorem ([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]).\n- The choice $B = A - \\operatorname{Id}$ converts \"$x A = x$\" into the\n  saddle-point condition for the matrix game with payoff $B$.\n- The Lean implementation lives in\n  `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.StochasticMatrix` and consists of:\n  - `IsStochasticMatrix` — predicate (rows sum to 1, entries ≥ 0).\n  - `uniformDist` — uniform mixed strategy on a `Nonempty` `Fintype`.\n  - `MatrixGame.exists_invariant_distribution` — main theorem.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Cor. 2.5.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Invariant distribution of a stochastic matrix from minimax."

      "body": "# Strict Domination And Never Best Response\n\nIn a finite strategic game, a mixed strategy $m_i\\in\\Delta(S_i)$ is strictly\ndominated if and only if it is never a best response against any correlated\nstrategy of the opponents.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nIf $m_i$ is strictly dominated by $\\sigma_i$, linearity of expected payoff extends\nthe strict inequality to every correlated strategy of the opponents, so $m_i$\ncannot be a best response.\n\nConversely, form the two-player zero-sum game in which player $i$ compares the\npayoff of a pure action $t_i$ with the payoff of the fixed mixed strategy $m_i$.\nThe hypothesis that $m_i$ is never a best response implies that the auxiliary\nzero-sum game has strictly positive value. An optimal strategy in that game then\nstrictly dominates $m_i$ in the original game.\n\n## Why this lives under `zero_sum.applications`\n\nThis proposition is a strategic-game result, but the MFoGT proof route\nis structural in [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]: the\n\"$m_i$ is never a best response $\\Rightarrow$ strictly dominated\"\ndirection is established by constructing an auxiliary two-player\nzero-sum game and extracting a dominating strategy from its\nminimax-optimal strategy. Filing the node under `zero_sum.applications`\nreflects the proof technique and keeps the top-level `strategic_games`\ntopic from depending back on `zero_sum`. A separation-theorem proof à\nla Pearce 1984 is available as an alternative and would substitute a\nTheorem-of-the-Alternative citation in `math.linear_algebra`; the\nMFoGT route is chosen here for alignment with the rest of the library's\nzero-sum infrastructure.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 4.3.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Strict domination is equivalent to never being a best response against a correlated strategy."

      "body": "## Lean formalisation note\n\nThe Lean file formalises the **mixed case** of the value formula: under\nhypotheses\n`0 < a + d - b - c`, `b ≤ a`, `c ≤ a`, `b ≤ d`, `c ≤ d`\n(which guarantee that the mixed strategies are valid probability vectors),\nthe game value is `(a*d - b*c) / (a + d - b - c)`. The pure-optimal case\ndisjunction described in the blueprint body falls out of dominance\narguments on the matrix entries and is not separately formalised — when\nthe mixed-case hypotheses fail, one of the rows/columns is dominated and\nthe pure pair shows up via `MatrixGame.optimal_pairs_iff_saddle_point`.\n\n# Two-By-Two Value Formula\n\nFor a two-by-two matrix\n$$\n  \\begin{pmatrix}\n  a & b\\\\\n  c & d\n  \\end{pmatrix},\n$$\neither there is a pair of pure optimal strategies, or the optimal strategies\nare completely mixed and the value is\n$$\n  \\frac{ad-bc}{a+d-b-c}.\n$$\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Ex. 2.6.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Mixed Nash Equilibrium of a Matrix Game\n\nFor a finite matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$, there exist mixed\nstrategies $x^\\ast \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y^\\ast \\in \\Delta(J)$ such that\n\n$$E_A(x, y^\\ast) \\le E_A(x^\\ast, y^\\ast) \\le E_A(x^\\ast, y)$$\n\nfor every $x \\in \\Delta(I)$ and $y \\in \\Delta(J)$ — the standard\nsaddle-point form of mixed Nash equilibrium in a zero-sum two-player game.\n\nThis is the strategy-level packaging of\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]] and is what is usually called \"the\nmatrix game has a (mixed) Nash equilibrium\".\n\nThe Lean development records the equilibrium in two complementary ways and\nproves them equivalent in the embedded strategic game:\n\n* `MatrixGame.IsMixedNashEq xx yy` — the saddle-point predicate directly on\n  the matrix game, easy to reason about and the form used to prove existence\n  (`MatrixGame.exists_mixed_nash_equilibrium`).\n* `MatrixGame.toStrategicGame` — the explicit two-player zero-sum strategic\n  game (payoffs $A$ and $-A$) whose `StrategicGame.IsMixedNashEq` reduces to\n  the saddle-point form. The full bridge theorem\n  `MatrixGame.exists_strategic_game_nash_equilibrium` packages a Nash\n  equilibrium of the embedded strategic game built from the saddle-point pair,\n  using the lemmas `expectedPayoff_toStrategicGame_zero` /\n  `expectedPayoff_toStrategicGame_one` that compute the\n  `StrategicGame.expectedPayoff` as `±A.E (p 0) (p 1)`.\n\nThe supporting `StrategicGame.MixedStrategy` / `MixedProfile` /\n`expectedPayoff` / `IsMixedNashEq` API is polymorphic in the payoff field\n`U` (any `Field U` with `LinearOrder` and `IsStrictOrderedRing`), so it\nspecialises to both $\\mathbb{Q}$ (for constructive `native_decide` examples\nsuch as Rock–Paper–Scissors) and $\\mathbb{R}$ (for the Loomis-based existence\ntheorem).\n\n*Proof.* Apply `MatrixGame.minimax_optimal_strategies` (closed by the\nsimplified-Loomis induction) to obtain $x^\\ast$, $y^\\ast$, and a value $v$\nwith $E_A(x^\\ast, j) \\ge v$ for every pure column $j$ and\n$E_A(i, y^\\ast) \\le v$ for every pure row $i$. By\n[[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]] this transfers to mixed responses:\n$E_A(x^\\ast, y') \\ge v$ for every $y' \\in \\Delta(J)$ and\n$E_A(x', y^\\ast) \\le v$ for every $x' \\in \\Delta(I)$. Taking $x' = x^\\ast$\nand $y' = y^\\ast$ shows $E_A(x^\\ast, y^\\ast) = v$, and the chain\n$E_A(x, y^\\ast) \\le v = E_A(x^\\ast, y^\\ast) \\le E_A(x^\\ast, y)$ holds for\nevery $x$ and $y$, which is exactly the saddle-point form.\n\n## Over ℚ and other ordered fields\n\nThe Loomis existence proof goes through the extreme value theorem on the\ncompact mixed-strategy simplex $\\Delta(I) \\subseteq \\mathbb{R}^{|I|}$. The\nrequired compactness is the standard Heine–Borel statement on $\\mathbb{R}^n$\nand is not available for $\\mathbb{Q}^n$, so *that* route intrinsically\nproduces real-valued strategies. Existence over $\\mathbb{Q}$ and every other\nlinearly ordered field is nonetheless available, sorry-free, through the\nsymmetrisation route `Minimax.minimax`\n([[node:math.minimax.ordered_field_minimax]]): it embeds the game in a\nskew-symmetric matrix and extracts the saddle point as a pure feasibility\nfact (the Theorem of the Alternative), needing no compactness or\norder-completeness. `MatrixGame.exists_mixed_nash_equilibrium` is built on\nthat route and is itself field-generic.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 5, Thm. 5.11 / 5.13] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Existence of mixed Nash equilibrium in a finite matrix game via the saddle-point equivalence."

      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Value Operator Properties\n\nFor finite real matrix games, the value operator $A \\mapsto \\operatorname{val}(A)$\nis continuous, monotone increasing, and non-expansive for the sup norm:\n$$\n  |\\operatorname{val}(A)-\\operatorname{val}(B)| \\le \\|A-B\\|_\\infty.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* If $A\\le B$ entrywise, then for every mixed row $x$ and mixed column\n$y$ one has $xAy\\le xBy$. Taking maxmin values gives\n$\\operatorname{val}(A)\\le\\operatorname{val}(B)$, so the value operator is\nmonotone. Let $\\delta=\\|A-B\\|_\\infty$. Then\n$$\n  A\\le B+\\delta\\mathbf 1\n  \\quad\\text{and}\\quad\n  B\\le A+\\delta\\mathbf 1.\n$$\nAdding the constant matrix $\\delta\\mathbf 1$ raises every mixed payoff, and\ntherefore the value, by $\\delta$. Monotonicity gives\n$$\n  \\operatorname{val}(A)\\le\\operatorname{val}(B)+\\delta\n  \\quad\\text{and}\\quad\n  \\operatorname{val}(B)\\le\\operatorname{val}(A)+\\delta,\n$$\nwhich is the non-expansive estimate. Non-expansiveness implies continuity.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3, after Thm. 2.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Continuity, monotonicity, and non-expansiveness of val."

      "body": "# Common Guarantee Gives The Value\n\nIf player I and player II both guarantee the same number $w$, then $w$ is\nthe unique value of the game, and the strategies witnessing the two\nguarantees are optimal.\n\n*Proof.* The two guarantees and weak duality give the chain\n$$\n  w \\le \\underline v \\le \\overline v \\le w.\n$$\nThus $\\underline v=\\overline v=w$, and the witnessing strategies attain the\nvalue. The minimax theorem ([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) closes the\ninner two inequalities, the player-guarantee bound is the outer pair\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.player_guarantee]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Lem. 2.2.8] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. A common guarantee is unique and equal to the value."

      "body": "# Ordered-Field Minimax Statement\n\nThe finite minimax theorem admits an ordered-field form: if the payoff\nmatrix has entries in an ordered field and the proof is carried out\nalgebraically through finitely many weak linear inequalities, then the\nvalue and optimal mixed strategies can be taken over that ordered field.\n\n*Proof.* Use an algebraic proof route for finite minimax, such as the\nlinear-programming route, whose steps are finite systems of weak\nlinear inequalities, pivot operations, and normalisations by positive\nelements. These operations make sense over any ordered field. The terminal\ninequalities are precisely the two minimax optimality systems, so the\nextracted mixed strategies and value lie in the same ordered field as the\nmatrix entries.\n\nThe Lean theorem is `Minimax.minimax`, polymorphic in\n`[Field 𝕜] [LinearOrder 𝕜] [IsStrictOrderedRing 𝕜]`, proved **sorry-free**\n(axioms: `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`). The route is von\nNeumann symmetrisation: shift the game positive, embed it in the\nskew-symmetric matrix on `I ⊕ J ⊕ Unit`, and read the optimal `(x, y, v)`\noff the value-0 optimal strategy of that skew game — which exists by the\nTheorem of the Alternative (`SkewSymmetric.optimal`), a pure feasibility\nstatement needing no LP optimum / order-completeness. The ℝ-specialisation\nalso follows from the Loomis route\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3, paragraph after the proof of Thm. 2.3.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Ordered-field generalization via finite weak linear inequalities."

      "body": "# Ville Theorem By Discretization\n\nLet $X=Y=[0,1]$ and let $f:X\\times Y\\to\\mathbb R$ be continuous. For each\n$n\\ge1$, form the finite grid\n$$\n  X_n=Y_n=\\{0,1,\\ldots,2^n\\}\n$$\nand the finite matrix game\n$$\n  G_n(i,j)=f(i/2^n,j/2^n).\n$$\nLet $v_n$ be the mixed value of $G_n$.\n\n*Proof.* The proof of Ville's theorem has two steps.\n\nFirst, use uniform continuity of $f$ to transfer guarantees from sufficiently fine\ngrid games to the original continuous game. If player 1 plays an optimal mixed\nstrategy on a fine grid, interpreted as a finitely supported Borel probability\nmeasure on $[0,1]$, then player 1 guarantees $\\limsup_n v_n$ up to any prescribed\n$\\varepsilon>0$. Dually, player 2 guarantees $\\liminf_n v_n$ from above. These\ntwo inequalities force existence of a value.\n\nSecond, regard optimal grid strategies as Borel probability measures on the\ncompact interval $[0,1]$. By compactness of probability measures in the weak\ntopology, extract weakly convergent subsequences. Continuity of $f$ lets the\npayoff functional pass to the limit, and the limiting measures are optimal\nstrategies. The finite grid strategies also give the finite-support\n$\\varepsilon$-optimal strategies.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Proof of Ville's theorem by finite discretizations and weak convergence."

      "body": "# Ville Theorem\n\nLet $I=J=[0,1]$ and let $f:I\\times J\\to\\mathbb{R}$ be continuous.  The mixed\nextension over Borel probability measures on $[0,1]$ has a value, and each\nplayer has an optimal strategy.  Moreover, for every $\\varepsilon>0$, each\nplayer has an $\\varepsilon$-optimal strategy with finite support.\n\nThe mixed payoff is\n$$\n  f(\\sigma,\\tau)=\\int_{[0,1]\\times[0,1]} f(x,y)\\,d\\sigma(x)\\,d\\tau(y),\n$$\nwhere $\\sigma$ and $\\tau$ are Borel probability measures on $[0,1]$.\n\n*Proof.* One discretizes the square\n$[0,1]\\times[0,1]$ by finer and finer grids, applies finite minimax to each\nmatrix game, and then extracts weakly convergent subsequences of optimal\nprobability measures. Uniform continuity transfers the finite-grid guarantees to\nthe continuous game. The finite-support $\\varepsilon$-optimal strategies come\nfrom the same grid approximations.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 2.5.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Continuous zero-sum game on [0,1] has a value in mixed strategies."

      "body": "# Finite Game Catalog\n\nIndex of canonical theorems about finite games that are formally proved in\nEconCSLib, distributed across `ExtensiveGame` and `StrategicGame`. Infinite-horizon, continuous-action, and\nstochastic game results live in their own sections of the knowledge base.  The\nchance-node extension of Kuhn's theorem (requiring vNM lottery utility) is\ntracked by [[game_theory.extensive_game.kuhn_spe_existence_with_chance]].\n\n## See also\n\n- [[game_theory.extensive_game.theorems_catalog]] — comprehensive index of extensive-game theorems and their Lean locations.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Ch. 3, 4] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*.\n- [MFoGT, §§2.3, 4.6, 6.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Antisymmetric Matrix Games Have Value\n\nLet $B$ be a real square matrix satisfying $B=-B^T$. Then the matrix game $B$ has\na value. Equivalently, there exists $x\\in\\Delta(I)$ such that\n$$\n  Bx\\le 0.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* The finite minimax theorem gives a mixed value for the square matrix\ngame. Since $B=-B^T$, every mixed strategy $z$ satisfies\n$$\n  zBz=0.\n$$\nFor any row mixed strategy $x$, the average of the column payoffs $xBe_j$ under\n$x$ is $xBx=0$, so some column gives payoff at most $0$ to player $1$ and the\nrow player cannot guarantee more than $0$. Dually, for any column mixed strategy\n$y$, the average of the row payoffs $e_iBy$ under $y$ is $yBy=0$, so some row\ngives payoff at least $0$ and the column player cannot hold the payoff below $0$.\nEquality of maxmin and minmax therefore forces the value to be $0$.\n\nIf $x$ is an optimal column strategy for player $2$, then it holds every row\npayoff to at most $0$, i.e. $(Bx)_i\\le0$ for all $i$. This is the displayed\nequivalent form.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 10(1)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Brown-von Neumann theorem for antisymmetric games."

      "body": "# Strong Complementarity\n\n## Statement\n\nFor a finite zero-sum matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$, there\nexists an optimal pair $(x^*, y^*) \\in X(A) \\times Y(A)$ such that\n\n- for every row $i$: $x^*_i > 0 \\iff A.\\mathrm{Ei}\\,i\\,y^* = A.\\mathrm{value}$\n  (i.e. row $i$ is a best response to $y^*$);\n- for every column $j$: $y^*_j > 0 \\iff A.\\mathrm{Ej}\\,x^*\\,j = A.\\mathrm{value}$\n  (i.e. column $j$ is a best response to $x^*$).\n\n## Proof\n\n*The forward direction* of each biconditional is\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.support_complementarity]] (Prop. 2.4.1(b)) and\nholds for every optimal pair: if $x^*_i > 0$, then row $i$ obtains the\nvalue against $y^*$; dually for columns.\n\n*The reverse direction — existence of an optimal pair where every\nbest-response row has positive probability* — comes from\n[[node:math.linear_programming.strong_complementarity]] applied to the\nmatrix-game LP. The Lean implementation\n(`MatrixGame.exists_strong_complementary_pair`) carries out:\n\n### Step 1 — Shift to make payoffs strictly positive\n\nChoose $K := 1 + |A.\\mathrm{value}| + \\max_{i,j} |A_{ij}|$. Then\n$A'_{ij} := A_{ij} + K > 0$ for every $i, j$, and the shifted value\n$v' := A.\\mathrm{value} + K > 0$. The shift is required because the\nstandard-form LP we apply expects nonneg variables and finite\noptimum; with positive payoffs the value-LP has a clean primal form.\n\n### Step 2 — Encode the row LP in standard form\n\nThe shifted row LP is\n\n$$\n  \\min \\sum_i x'_i \\quad\n  \\text{s.t.} \\quad (A'^{\\mathsf T} x')_j \\ge 1\\ (\\forall j \\in J),\n  \\quad x'_i \\ge 0\\ (\\forall i \\in I).\n$$\n\nOptimal $x'$ rescales to a mixed strategy via $x_i = x'_i \\cdot v'$\n(since $\\sum_i x'_i = 1/v'$ at optimum).\n\n### Step 3 — Build LP-feasible primal and dual from a matrix-game optimal pair\n\nFrom an existing matrix-game optimal pair $(x^0, y^0)$ (via\n[[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.matrix_game_nash_equilibrium]]), define\n$x'^0 := x^0 / v'$ and $u'^0 := y^0 / v'$. Both have LP objective\n$1/v'$, hence are LP-optimal by weak duality.\n\n### Step 4 — Apply LP strong complementarity\n\nInvoke [[node:math.linear_programming.strong_complementarity]] to obtain a\nstrong-CS optimal LP pair $(x'^*, u'^*)$.\n\n### Step 5 — Rescale back and translate the biconditional\n\nSet $x^*_i := x'^*(e\\,i) \\cdot v'$ and $y^*_j := u'^*_j \\cdot v'$\n(where $e : I \\simeq \\mathrm{Fin}\\,(\\#I)$ is the standard equivalence\nused so the LP variables fit `Fin n → \\mathbb{R}`). Verify:\n\n- $(A^{\\mathsf T} x^*)_j = A.\\mathrm{Ej}\\,x^*\\,j$ and\n  $(A^{\\mathsf T} x^* + K)_j = (A'^{\\mathsf T} x^*)_j = (A'^{\\mathsf T} x'^*)_j \\cdot v'\n  \\ge 1 \\cdot v' = v'$,\n  so $A.\\mathrm{Ej}\\,x^*\\,j \\ge A.\\mathrm{value}$ — i.e. $x^*$ is\n  row-optimal. Symmetrically $y^*$ is column-optimal.\n\nThe LP strict complementarity at the column index $i$ (in the strong\npair) is the assertion\n$x'^*(e\\,i) + (1 - \\sum_j u'^*_j \\cdot A'_{i,j}) > 0$. Multiplying\nthrough by $v'$ and using $v' = A.\\mathrm{value} + K$, this becomes\n\n$$\n  x^*_i + (A.\\mathrm{value} - A.\\mathrm{Ei}\\,i\\,y^*) > 0.\n$$\n\nBoth summands are non-negative (by primal/dual feasibility), so at\nleast one is strictly positive: $x^*_i > 0$ **or**\n$A.\\mathrm{Ei}\\,i\\,y^* < A.\\mathrm{value}$. The contrapositive is\nexactly the missing direction: if $A.\\mathrm{Ei}\\,i\\,y^* = A.\\mathrm{value}$\nthen $x^*_i > 0$. Symmetric argument for columns. $\\square$\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The shift in Step 1 is essential for the standard-form LP reduction;\n  without it the value LP \"max $v$\" has $v$ free, which doesn't fit\n  the `min ⟨c, x⟩ s.t. Ax ≥ b, x ≥ 0` form of\n  [[node:math.linear_programming.strong_complementarity]].\n- The Lean implementation restricts `I J : Type` (= `Type 0`) so the\n  `Fintype.sum_equiv` adapter that bridges `I` and `Fin (#I)` lines up\n  with the LP theorem's universe ($\\mathbb{R} : \\mathrm{Type}\\,0$).\n- Combined with [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.support_complementarity]] this\n  produces a *fully two-sided* biconditional in the strong pair: every\n  best-response row has positive probability and every positive-probability\n  row is a best response.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(c)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical\n  Foundations of Game Theory*.\n  Existence of a strongly complementary optimal pair."

      "body": "# Zero-Sum Nash Equilibria As Saddle Points\n\nIn a zero-sum game, a pair of mixed strategies is a Nash equilibrium exactly\nwhen it is a saddle point of the matrix payoff.\n\n*Proof.* Write $u(x,y)=xAy$ for player I's payoff and $-u(x,y)$ for player\nII's payoff. A mixed pair $(x^*,y^*)$ is a Nash equilibrium exactly when\n$$\n  u(x,y^*)\\le u(x^*,y^*)\\quad\\text{for all }x\n$$\nand\n$$\n  -u(x^*,y)\\le -u(x^*,y^*)\\quad\\text{for all }y.\n$$\nThe second inequality is equivalent to $u(x^*,y^*)\\le u(x^*,y)$ for all\n$y$. Together these are precisely the saddle-point inequalities.\n\nIn the Lean formalisation this equivalence is *definitional*: the predicate\n`MatrixGame.IsSaddlePoint` is an `abbrev` for `MatrixGame.IsMixedNashEq`, so\n`isMixedNashEq_iff_isSaddlePoint` is closed by `Iff.rfl`.  The\nstrategic-game-level form ([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.matrix_game_nash_equilibrium]])\nfollows from the same definitional identity combined with the profile\nexpansion lemmas.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(d), proof paragraph] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Saddle points express the identity between optimal strategies and Nash equilibria."

      "body": "# Perron-Frobenius For Positive Matrices\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $M \\in \\mathbb{R}^{n \\times n}$ be a square matrix whose entries are\nstrictly positive: $M_{ij} > 0$ for every $i, j$. Then there exist\n$x \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, $y \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, and\n$\\lambda > 0$ such that\n\n- $x$ and $y$ have **strictly positive components**;\n- $xM = \\lambda\\, x$ (so $x$ is a left eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\\lambda$);\n- $My = \\lambda\\, y$ (so $y$ is a right eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\\lambda$).\n\nThe Loomis value $v$ of the pair $(I, M)$ (identity matrix vs. $M$)\nprovides $\\lambda = 1/v$.\n\n## Proof\n\nApply the general-$B$ Loomis theorem\n([[node:math.minimax.loomis_theorem]]) with $A := I$ (the $n \\times n$\nidentity matrix) and $B := M$. Since $M_{ij} > 0$, the hypothesis\n`IsPositive M` is satisfied. Loomis produces\n$x \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, $y \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, and\n$v \\in \\mathbb{R}$ such that\n\n- $(1)\\quad \\forall j,\\quad v \\cdot (xM)_j \\le x_j$  (from $xI \\ge v \\cdot xM$,\n  using $xI = x$);\n- $(2)\\quad \\forall i,\\quad y_i \\le v \\cdot (My)_i$  (from $Iy \\le v \\cdot My$,\n  using $Iy = y$).\n\n**Step 1: $v > 0$.** Pick $i_0$ with $y_{i_0} > 0$ (which exists because\n$\\sum y_i = 1$). Inequality (2) at $i_0$ gives\n$y_{i_0} \\le v \\cdot (My)_{i_0}$. Since $M > 0$ entrywise and $y \\ge 0$ has\n$y_{i_0} > 0$ (hence $\\sum y_j M_{i_0, j} > 0$), $(My)_{i_0} > 0$.\nTherefore $0 < y_{i_0} \\le v \\cdot (My)_{i_0}$ forces $v > 0$.\n\n**Step 2: $x$ and $y$ are strictly positive.** For every $j$,\n$(xM)_j = \\sum_i x_i M_{ij} > 0$ because $x \\in \\Delta$ has at least one\npositive entry and $M > 0$ entrywise. Combined with (1), $x_j \\ge v \\cdot\n(xM)_j > 0$. So $x_j > 0$ for all $j$. By the same argument applied to (2)\nand $y$, $(My)_i > 0$ and $y_i > 0$ for all $i$.\n\n**Step 3: Tight inner-product sandwich.** Compute\n$$\n  \\langle x, y\\rangle - v\\cdot \\langle xM, y\\rangle\n  = \\sum_j (x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j) \\cdot y_j \\ge 0\n$$\n(each summand is nonneg by (1) and $y_j \\ge 0$). And by\n$\\langle xM, y\\rangle = \\sum_j \\sum_i x_i M_{ij} y_j = \\langle x, My\\rangle$,\n$$\n  v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle - \\langle x, y\\rangle\n  = v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle - \\langle x, y\\rangle.\n$$\nWeighting (2) by $x \\ge 0$ and summing,\n$\\langle x, y\\rangle \\le v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle$. Therefore\n$$\n  \\langle x, y\\rangle \\;\\ge\\; v \\cdot \\langle xM, y\\rangle \\;=\\; v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle \\;\\ge\\; \\langle x, y\\rangle,\n$$\nso both inequalities are tight.\n\n**Step 4: Componentwise equality.** From Step 3,\n$\\sum_j (x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j) \\cdot y_j = 0$. Each summand is nonneg (by\n(1)) and $y_j > 0$ strict (by Step 2). For the nonneg sum to vanish, each\nsummand must vanish, so $x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j = 0$, i.e., $x_j = v \\cdot\n(xM)_j$ for every $j$. As a row-vector identity, $xM = (1/v) \\cdot x$.\n\nDually, $\\sum_i (v \\cdot (My)_i - y_i) \\cdot x_i = 0$ with each summand\nnonneg and $x_i > 0$ strict, so $y_i = v \\cdot (My)_i$, i.e.,\n$My = (1/v) \\cdot y$.\n\nSetting $\\lambda := 1/v > 0$, we have $xM = \\lambda \\cdot x$ (left\neigenvector) and $My = \\lambda \\cdot y$ (right eigenvector), both with\n$x, y$ strictly positive. $\\square$\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The argument is purely algebraic and works over $\\mathbb{R}$ (where\n  general-$B$ Loomis is formalised in `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.Loomis`).\n- Strict positivity of $x$ and $y$ is automatic given strict positivity of\n  $M$, **without** needing a separate \"irreducibility\" argument.\n- The same Loomis instance simultaneously produces the **left** eigenvector\n  $x$ and the **right** eigenvector $y$ at the same eigenvalue $\\lambda\n  = 1/v$. This eigenvalue is the **Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue** of $M$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 1(2)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Application of Loomis theorem\n  to positive matrices."

      "body": "# Weak Domination And Completely Mixed Tests\n\nIn a finite strategic game, a mixed strategy $m_i\\in\\Delta(S_i)$ is weakly\ndominated if and only if it is never a best response against a completely\ncorrelated strategy of the opponents.\n\nHere \"completely correlated\" means a correlated strategy in the relative interior\nof $\\Delta(S_{-i})$, assigning positive probability to every opponent profile.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nWeak domination gives a strict expected-payoff improvement against every\nfull-support correlated opponent strategy, so $m_i$ is not a best response to any\nof them. For the converse, MFoGT reduces to an auxiliary finite zero-sum game. If\nthe value is positive then strict domination follows. If the value is zero, optimal\nsupport and best-response complementarity identify an opponent pure profile\nagainst which an optimal strategy gives a strict improvement while never lowering\nthe payoff elsewhere.\n\n## Why this lives under `zero_sum.applications`\n\nThis proposition is a strategic-game result, but the MFoGT 4.3.6 proof\nroute is structural in [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.support_complementarity]]:\nthe converse uses both the value of the auxiliary zero-sum game and\nsupport/best-response complementarity to extract a separating opponent\nprofile. Filing the node under `zero_sum.applications` reflects the\nproof technique and keeps the top-level `strategic_games` topic from\ndepending back on `zero_sum`. A separation-theorem proof à la Pearce\n1984, which would let the result live under\n`strategic_games.dominance` while citing only\n`math.linear_algebra.theorem_of_alternative`, is an alternative route.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 4.3.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Weak domination is equivalent to never being a best response against a completely correlated strategy."

      "body": "# Finite-Opponent Separation Minimax\n\nAssume:\n\n1. $S$ is a measurable space and $X$ is a nonempty convex set of probability\n   measures over $S$;\n2. $T$ is a finite nonempty set;\n3. $g:S\\times T\\to\\mathbb R$ is measurable and bounded.\n\nThen the game $(X,\\Delta(T),g)$ has a value, and player 2 has an optimal strategy.\n\n*Proof.* Let $v=\\sup_X\\inf_T g(x,t)$. Consider the convex payoff-vector set\n$$\n  D=\\{(g(x,t))_{t\\in T}:x\\in X\\}\\subseteq\\mathbb R^T\n$$\nand the upper orthant $C=\\{a:a_t\\ge v+\\epsilon\\text{ for all }t\\}$. These two\nconvex sets are disjoint. A separating hyperplane gives nonnegative weights on\n$T$, normalized to a mixed strategy $y\\in\\Delta(T)$, such that\n$g(x,y)\\le v+\\epsilon$ for all $x\\in X$. Letting $\\epsilon\\downarrow0$ gives the\nvalue, and compactness of $\\Delta(T)$ gives an optimal strategy for player 2.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 3.3.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# General Mixed Minimax Theorem\n\nLet $G=(S,T,g)$ be a zero-sum game such that:\n\n1. $S$ and $T$ are compact Hausdorff topological spaces;\n2. for each $t\\in T$, $g(\\cdot,t)$ is upper semicontinuous, and for each $s\\in S$,\n   $g(s,\\cdot)$ is lower semicontinuous;\n3. $g$ is bounded and measurable for the product Borel sigma-algebra.\n\nThen the mixed extension\n$$\n  (\\Delta(S),\\Delta(T),g)\n$$\nhas a value. Each player has a mixed optimal strategy, and for every\n$\\epsilon>0$ each player has an $\\epsilon$-optimal strategy with finite support.\n\n*Proof.* Apply the compact mixed-versus-finite-support minimax proposition twice: once to\n$(\\Delta(S),\\Delta_f(T),g)$ and once dually to $(\\Delta_f(S),\\Delta(T),g)$. Let\n$v^+$ and $v^-$ be the resulting values. Optimal strategies $\\sigma$ and $\\tau$\nfor the two one-sided games satisfy inequalities against all pure opponent\nstrategies. Fubini's theorem gives\n$$\n  v^+\\le \\int g\\,d(\\sigma\\otimes\\tau)\\le v^-.\n$$\nSince always $v^-\\le v^+$, equality follows.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 3.3.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Mixed minimax theorem for compact Hausdorff strategy spaces."

      "body": "# Intersection Lemma\n\nLet $C_1,\\ldots,C_n$ be nonempty convex compact subsets of a Euclidean space.\nAssume that $\\bigcup_{i=1}^n C_i$ is convex and that every intersection of\n$n-1$ of the sets is nonempty:\n$$\n  \\bigcap_{i\\ne j} C_i\\ne\\emptyset\n  \\quad\\text{for every }j=1,\\ldots,n.\n$$\nThen\n$$\n  \\bigcap_{i=1}^n C_i\\ne\\emptyset.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* The proof is by induction on $n$. The case $n=2$ uses strict separation of two\ndisjoint compact convex sets: if $C_1$ and $C_2$ were disjoint, their convex union\nwould have to cross the separating hyperplane, contradiction. For the induction\nstep, separate $C_n$ from $\\bigcap_{i<n}C_i$ and intersect the other sets with the\nseparating hyperplane. The induction hypothesis applied in the hyperplane gives a\npoint that contradicts strict separation.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Lem. 3.2.1] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Convex compact intersection lemma used in Sion's theorem."

      "body": "# Monotone Decreasing Values Limit\n\nLet $G_n=(S,T,f_n)$ be a family of zero-sum games such that:\n\n1. $(f_n)$ is a weakly decreasing sequence of uniformly bounded functions\n   $S\\times T\\to\\mathbb R$;\n2. each $f_n$ is upper semicontinuous in the first variable;\n3. each $G_n$ has a value $v_n$;\n4. $S$ is compact.\n\nLet $f=\\inf_n f_n$. Then the game $G=(S,T,f)$ has value\n$$\n  v=\\inf_n v_n,\n$$\nand player 1 has an optimal strategy in $G$.\n\n*Proof.* The values $v_n$ form a decreasing bounded sequence, so\n$v=\\inf_n v_n$ exists. For each $n$, let $S_n(\\varepsilon)$ be the closed set of\nstrategies in $S$ that guarantee at least $v_n-\\varepsilon$ in game $G_n$.\nUpper semicontinuity in the first variable and compactness of $S$ make these\nsets compact, and monotonicity of the payoffs makes them nested after replacing\n$\\varepsilon$ by a summable sequence. Compactness gives a common limit strategy\n$s^*$. Since $f=\\inf_n f_n$, this strategy guarantees at least $v$ in the limit\ngame. Conversely, every strategy's guarantee in $f$ is bounded above by its\nguarantee in each $f_n$, hence by $v_n$; taking the infimum over $n$ gives an\nupper bound $v$. Thus $G$ has value $v$ and $s^*$ is optimal for player $1$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Limit of values for a decreasing family of upper-semicontinuous zero-sum games."

      "body": "# Monotone Family Assumption Counterexamples\n\nMFoGT Exercise 3.5.3(2) gives two one-player examples showing why the hypotheses\nin the monotone-family value theorem are not cosmetic.\n\nIn the first example,\n$$\n  S=[0,+\\infty),\\qquad f_n(s)=\\mathbf 1_{s\\ge n}.\n$$\nFor each $n$, the value is $v_n=1$, but the pointwise infimum has value $0$.\nThe failure is that $S$ is not compact.\n\nIn the second example, $S=[0,1]$ is compact and $f_n$ is continuous and\npiecewise linear with\n$$\n  f_n(0)=f_n(2/n)=f_n(1)=0,\\qquad f_n(1/n)=1.\n$$\nAgain $v_n=1$ for each $n$, while the limiting value is $0$. The failure is that\nthe sequence $(f_n)$ is not monotone decreasing.\n\nThese examples explain the role of compactness of $S$ and monotone decrease of\nthe payoff sequence in `zero_sum.continuous.monotone_decreasing_values_limit`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 3(2)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Examples showing why compactness and monotonicity assumptions matter in the monotone-family value theorem.\n- [MFoGT, Section 9.3, Exercise 3 hints] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.       "body": "# Quasi-Concavity And Semicontinuity\n\nLet $E$ be a convex subset of a vector space. A function $f:E\\to\\mathbb R$ is\nquasi-concave if every upper section\n$$\n  \\{x\\in E:f(x)\\ge\\lambda\\}\n$$\nis convex. It is quasi-convex if $-f$ is quasi-concave.\n\nIf $E$ is a topological space, $f$ is upper semicontinuous if every upper section is\nclosed. It is lower semicontinuous if $-f$ is upper semicontinuous.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Def. 3.2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Quasi-concavity, quasi-convexity, upper semicontinuity, and lower semicontinuity."

      "body": "# Sion Boundary Counterexample\n\nLet $S=T=[0,1]$ and define $f:S\\times T\\to\\{0,-1\\}$ by\n$$\n  f(s,t)=\n  \\begin{cases}\n    -1, & t=0\\text{ and }s<1/2,\\\\\n    -1, & t=1\\text{ and }s\\ge 1/2,\\\\\n    0, & \\text{otherwise}.\n  \\end{cases}\n$$\nThis game has no value in pure strategies, while Sion's hypotheses fail only at\nthe boundary point $t=1$.\n\nThe pure quantities are\n$$\n  \\sup_s\\inf_t f(s,t)=-1,\\qquad \\inf_t\\sup_s f(s,t)=0.\n$$\nNevertheless, the mixed extension does have a value, equal to $-1/2$. Player 1\ncan guarantee this by playing uniformly on $[0,1]$, or by mixing equally between\n$0$ and $1$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 3.5, Exercise 2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Counterexample satisfying Sion hypotheses except at one boundary point.\n- [MFoGT, Section 9.3, Exercise 2 hints] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Computes the pure gap and mixed value."

      "body": "# Sion Minimax Theorem\n\nLet $G=(S,T,g)$ be a zero-sum game where $S$ and $T$ are subsets of Hausdorff\ntopological real vector spaces. Assume:\n\n1. $S$ and $T$ are convex;\n2. at least one of $S,T$ is compact;\n3. for each $t\\in T$, $g(\\cdot,t)$ is quasi-concave and upper semicontinuous in\n   $s$;\n4. for each $s\\in S$, $g(s,\\cdot)$ is quasi-convex and lower semicontinuous in\n   $t$.\n\nThen $G$ has a value:\n$$\n  \\sup_{s\\in S}\\inf_{t\\in T}g(s,t)\n  =\n  \\inf_{t\\in T}\\sup_{s\\in S}g(s,t).\n$$\nMoreover, if $S$ is compact then player 1 has an optimal strategy, and if $T$ is\ncompact then player 2 has an optimal strategy.\n\n*Proof.* Assume, for example, that $S$ is compact and suppose the two sides are separated\nby a real number $v$. Open-cover compactness first reduces to finite subsets of\nstrategies, then to compact convex hulls. Minimality of the finite reduction and the\nintersection lemma produce a point $t_0$ against which all reduced player-1\nstrategies yield payoff greater than $v$, and symmetrically a point $s_0$ against\nwhich all reduced player-2 strategies yield payoff less than $v$. The value\n$g(s_0,t_0)$ gives a contradiction.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Thm. 3.2.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Pure-strategy minimax theorem under convexity, compactness, and semicontinuity hypotheses."

      "body": "# Strong Complementarity\n\nFor a finite zero-sum matrix game $A : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$ there exists an\noptimal pair $(x^\\ast, y^\\ast) \\in X(A) \\times Y(A)$ that is **strongly\ncomplementary**:\n\n$$\n  x^\\ast_i > 0 \\iff e_i A y^\\ast = \\operatorname{val}(A),\n  \\qquad\n  y^\\ast_j > 0 \\iff x^\\ast A e_j = \\operatorname{val}(A).\n$$\n\nThe forward implications ($\\Rightarrow$) hold for *every* optimal pair and are\nexactly [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.core.support_complementarity]].\nThe strengthening here is the existence of a pair for which the reverse\nimplications ($\\Leftarrow$) also hold simultaneously.\n\n*Proof.* Shift the payoffs by a constant $K$ so the value becomes positive, and\nread off the row/column linear programs of the shifted game. LP strong\ncomplementary slackness supplies an optimal LP pair satisfying strict\ncomplementarity; rescaling back by the shifted value yields an optimal\nmatrix-game pair satisfying the biconditional above.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(c)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Strong complementarity of optimal strategies via LP strong complementary slackness."

      "body": "# Support Complementarity\n\nLet $x \\in X(A)$ and $y \\in Y(A)$. If $i \\in \\operatorname{supp}(x)$, then\nthe pure row $i$ obtains the value against $y$. If\n$j \\in \\operatorname{supp}(y)$, then the mixed strategy $x$ obtains the\nvalue against the pure column $j$.\n\n*Proof.* Let $v=\\operatorname{val}(A)$. Since $y$ is optimal for player II,\neach pure row payoff satisfies $e_iAy\\le v$. Since $x$ is optimal for player\nI, the average of these row payoffs under $x$ is\n$$\n  xAy=\\sum_i x_i(e_iAy)=v.\n$$\nAn average of numbers all bounded above by $v$ can equal $v$ only if every\nterm with positive weight is equal to $v$. Hence $e_iAy=v$ for\n$i\\in\\operatorname{supp}(x)$. The column statement is dual: optimality of\n$x$ gives $xAe_j\\ge v$ for every $j$, while optimality of $y$ gives\n$$\n  xAy=\\sum_j y_j(xAe_j)=v.\n$$\nThus every positively weighted column in $y$ satisfies $xAe_j=v$.\n\nThe Lean formalisation provides separate theorems for the two directions:\n`MatrixGame.support_complementarity_row` (rows in $\\operatorname{supp}(x)$\nhit the value) and `MatrixGame.support_complementarity_column` (columns in\n$\\operatorname{supp}(y)$ hit the value).\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(b)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Complementarity on supports of optimal strategies."

      "body": "# Optimal Pairs Are Exactly Saddle Points\n\nFor a finite matrix game $A$, the product $X(A)\\times Y(A)$ of\noptimal-strategy sets is exactly the set of saddle points of $A$.\n\n*Proof.* Let $v=\\operatorname{val}(A)$. If $x\\in X(A)$ and $y\\in Y(A)$, then\n$xAy'\\ge v$ for every mixed column $y'$ and $x'Ay\\le v$ for every mixed row\n$x'$. Applying these inequalities to $y$ and $x$ gives $xAy=v$, so\n$$\n  x'Ay\\le xAy\\le xAy'\n$$\nfor all $x'$ and $y'$. Thus $(x,y)$ is a saddle point. Conversely, if\n$(x,y)$ is a saddle point, then taking $x'$ and $y'$ as pure strategies and\napplying the simplex-side order characterisations\n([[node:math.simplex.bounded_by_value]]) gives\n$$\n  E_A(x,y)\\le \\operatorname{guarantee}_I(x), \\qquad\n  \\operatorname{guarantee}_{II}(y)\\le E_A(x,y).\n$$\nWeak duality [[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.maximin_le_minimax]] sandwiches both quantities\nbetween $v$ on the appropriate side, forcing equality. Hence $x\\in X(A)$ and\n$y\\in Y(A)$.\n\nThe Lean formalisation factors through two characterisation iff-theorems\n(`mem_optimalRowStrategies_iff_E_ge` and `mem_optimalColumnStrategies_iff_E_le`),\nwhich then combine into `MatrixGame.optimal_pairs_iff_saddle_point`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(d)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. X(A) x Y(A) is the set of saddle points."

      "body": "# Mixed Strategy Simplex\n\nFor a finite set $S$, the mixed strategy simplex $\\Delta(S)$ is the set of\nprobability vectors on $S$:\n$$\n  \\Delta(S)=\\{x \\in \\mathbb{R}^S : x_s \\ge 0 \\text{ for all } s,\\ \n  \\sum_{s \\in S} x_s = 1\\}.\n$$\nThe Lean library uses Mathlib's `stdSimplex ℝ S` for this set, with\n`stdSimplex.pure i` for the Dirac point mass at $i$ and `wsum x f` (a\ndefinitional abbreviation for the dot product `x ⬝ᵥ f`) for the weighted\nsum of a function $f \\colon S \\to \\mathbb{R}$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Section 2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Delta(S) is the simplex of probabilities on a finite set S."

        "math.minimax.minimax_from_loomis"

      "file_path": "../EconCSLib/docs/knowledge/nodes/zero_sum/maximin_le_minimax.md",
      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Maximin is Bounded by Minimax\n\nFor every finite matrix game,\n\n$$\\max_x \\min_j E_A(x,j) \\le \\min_y \\max_i E_A(i,y).$$\n\nThis is the weak-duality inequality: player I's best guaranteed payoff cannot\nexceed player II's best upper bound on player I's payoff.\n\n*Proof.* For every mixed row $x$ and mixed column $y$,\n$$\n  \\min_j E_A(x,j) \\le E_A(x,y) \\le \\max_i E_A(i,y).\n$$\nTaking the supremum over $x$ on the left preserves the first inequality against\nthe fixed upper bound $\\max_i E_A(i,y)$, so\n$$\n  \\max_x \\min_j E_A(x,j) \\le \\max_i E_A(i,y)\n$$\nfor every $y$. Taking the infimum over $y$ gives\n$$\n  \\max_x \\min_j E_A(x,j) \\le \\min_y \\max_i E_A(i,y).\n$$\n\n## Abstract pure-strategy form\n\nOn arbitrary nonempty strategy sets $I, J$ with payoff $g : I \\times J \\to\n\\mathbb{R}$ and pure-strategy extrema (no mixing), the same argument gives\nweak duality\n\n$$\n  \\underline v = \\sup_{i \\in I} \\inf_{j \\in J} g(i,j)\n              \\;\\le\\; \\inf_{j \\in J} \\sup_{i \\in I} g(i,j) = \\overline v.\n$$\n\n*Proof.* For every pair $(i,j)$,\n$$\n  \\inf_{j' \\in J} g(i,j') \\le g(i,j) \\le \\sup_{i' \\in I} g(i',j).\n$$\nTaking the supremum over $i$ on the left and the infimum over $j$ on the right\ngives $\\underline v \\le \\overline v$. $\\square$\n\nThis abstract form is what nodes outside the finite-mixed setting cite. The\nLean formalisation lives in the finite-mixed instantiation above.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Lemmas 2.2.4 and 2.2.8] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. The lower value never exceeds the upper value.\n- [MFoGT, Lem. 2.2.4] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Abstract pure-strategy weak duality (merged from `zero_sum.core.maxmin_le_minmax`)."
    },

      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [],

      "body": "# Maximin and Minimax Values\n\nFor a mixed row strategy $x$, player I's guarantee is the worst expected payoff\nagainst a pure column:\n\n$$\\gamma_I(x) = \\min_{j \\in J} E_A(x,j).$$\n\nFor a mixed column strategy $y$, player II's guarantee against player I is the\nlargest payoff player I can obtain from a pure row:\n\n$$\\gamma_{II}(y) = \\max_{i \\in I} E_A(i,y).$$\n\nThe maximin value is \\(\\sup_x \\gamma_I(x)\\), and the minimax value is\n\\(\\inf_y \\gamma_{II}(y)\\).\n\n## Abstract pure-strategy form\n\nThe same definition applies on arbitrary nonempty strategy sets $I, J$ and a\npayoff $g : I \\times J \\to \\mathbb{R}$, with the inner extremum ranging over\n**pure** strategies (no mixing). Then the maxmin is\n\n$$\n  \\underline v = \\sup_{i \\in I} \\inf_{j \\in J} g(i,j),\n$$\n\nand the minmax is\n\n$$\n  \\overline v = \\inf_{j \\in J} \\sup_{i \\in I} g(i,j).\n$$\n\nThe maxmin is the best amount player 1 can guarantee, and the minmax is the\nleast amount player 2 can guarantee as an upper bound on player 1's payoff.\nThe Lean library currently formalises the finite mixed-strategy instantiation\nabove; the abstract form is the common conceptual ancestor and the form used\nwhen reasoning over general (e.g. infinite) strategy spaces.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Chapter 2, Definitions 2.2.2-2.2.6] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Guarantees, maxmin, minmax, and game value.\n- [MFoGT, Def. 2.2.3] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Abstract pure-strategy maxmin and minmax (merged from `zero_sum.core.maxmin_minmax`)."
    },

      "body": "# Pointwise Bounds Are Simplex Bounds\n\nFor a finite index `I`, strictly ordered field `𝕜`, value `v ∈ 𝕜`, and\nfunction `f : I → 𝕜`,\n$$\n  (\\forall i,\\; v \\le f(i)) \\;\\Longleftrightarrow\\;\n  (\\forall x \\in \\operatorname{stdSimplex} \\mathbb{K}\\, I,\\; v \\le \\operatorname{wsum} x\\, f).\n$$\n\nThe symmetric `le_iff_simplex_le` gives the analogous statement for upper\nbounds. Both directions are short:\n\n- pointwise $\\Rightarrow$ simplex uses `wsum_const` plus `wsum_le_wsum`;\n- simplex $\\Rightarrow$ pointwise specializes to the point-mass simplex\n  element `stdSimplex.pure i` and applies `wsum_pure_apply`.\n\nThese bridges are the workhorses of Loomis-style minimax arguments: they\nreduce a quantification over the entire mixed-strategy simplex to a\nquantification over pure strategies, where finiteness of `I` makes the\nremaining argument elementary.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ, Chapter 5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, *Game Theory*. Reduction of mixed-strategy quantifiers to\n  pure-strategy quantifiers in zero-sum analyses."

      "home_topic": "game_theory.zero_sum",

      "body_refs": {
        "refs": [
          {
            "target_id": "game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax",
            "known": true,
            "in_uses": true
          }
        ],
        "missing_from_uses": []
      },
      "body": "# Antisymmetric Matrix Game Has Value Zero\n\nA square matrix $B : I \\times I \\to \\mathbb{R}$ is **antisymmetric** if\n$B = -B^{\\mathsf{T}}$, i.e. $B_{ij} = -B_{ji}$ for all $i,j$ (so in particular\n$B_{ii} = 0$). The matrix game $B$ then has value $0$, and there exists\n$x \\in \\Delta(I)$ such that $(Bx)_i \\le 0$ for every row $i$.\n\n*Proof.* By the minimax theorem\n([[node:game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) the game has a\nvalue $v$. Antisymmetry gives $z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z = 0$ for every mixed $z$, since\n$z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z = -z^{\\mathsf{T}} B^{\\mathsf{T}} z = -(z^{\\mathsf{T}} B z)$.\nApplying this to an optimal $x^\\ast$ for player I,\n$0 = \\sum_j x^\\ast_j (e_j B x^\\ast)$ while each $e_j B x^\\ast \\ge v$, forcing\n$v \\le 0$; the symmetric argument gives $v \\ge 0$, so $v = 0$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 10(1)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Antisymmetric matrix games have value zero."
    },

      "body": "# Markov Stationary Distribution as Zero-Sum Game Value\n\n**Lemma.** Let $A : I \\times I \\to \\mathbb{R}$ be a row-stochastic\nmatrix (entries $\\ge 0$, every row sums to 1), and consider the\n*displacement game* with payoff matrix $B := A - \\operatorname{Id}$.\nThen:\n\n1. The displacement game has value $\\operatorname{val}(B) = 0$.\n2. Every row-optimal mixed strategy $x^* \\in X(B)$ for player 1 is a\n   **stationary distribution** of $A$:\n   $x^* A = x^*$.\n\nThis is the proof structure underlying\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.applications.stochastic_matrix_invariant_distribution]] —\nthe classical von Neumann construction translating\n\"Markov stationary distribution exists\" into \"an optimal mixed\nstrategy in a particular zero-sum game\".\n\n## Why this is a useful framing\n\nThe standard textbook proof of Markov stationary-distribution existence\nuses Brouwer's fixed-point theorem on $\\Delta(I)$. The\nzero-sum-game-theoretic proof bypasses Brouwer entirely:\n\n- Apply the minimax theorem\n  ([[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.von_neumann_minimax]]) to the displacement game\n  $B = A - \\operatorname{Id}$ — this gives existence of optimal\n  strategies for free.\n- Reduce stationarity to the *saddle-point characterisation* of those\n  optimal strategies (player 1's guarantee inequality, summed across\n  columns, forces equality on every column).\n\nThe whole argument is purely algebraic / combinatorial once minimax is\nin hand, which is itself proved by Loomis induction\n([[math.minimax.loomis_induction_proof]]) — no topology required.\nThis is a satisfying application of zero-sum theory to elementary\nMarkov-chain theory.\n\n## Bridge to the main theorem\n\nThe detailed argument lives in\n[[game_theory.strategic_game.zero_sum.applications.stochastic_matrix_invariant_distribution]]\n(MFoGT Cor. 2.5.2): the three-step proof there is\n\n1. Show $\\operatorname{val}(B) = 0$ (this lemma's statement 1) by\n   exhibiting matching upper and lower bounds.\n2. Take any $x^* \\in X(B)$; saddle-point inequality gives\n   $x^* A \\ge x^*$ componentwise.\n3. Sum across $j$ and use row-stochasticity: total mass forces\n   $x^* A = x^*$ pointwise.\n\nThis node is the *conceptual restatement* of that argument — the\nunderlying meta-pattern is \"minimax theorem + saddle-point\ncharacterisation + a counting / mass-balance step ⇒ existence of a\nmatrix-algebraic object\".\n\n## References\n\n- von Neumann's original 1928 paper already contains this technique.\n- [MFoGT Cor. 2.5.2] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*.\n- Owen, G. (1995). *Game Theory*. Ch. 3."

      "body": "# Perron-Frobenius For Positive Matrices\n\n## Statement\n\nLet $M \\in \\mathbb{R}^{n \\times n}$ be a square matrix whose entries are\nstrictly positive: $M_{ij} > 0$ for every $i, j$. Then there exist\n$x \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, $y \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, and\n$\\lambda > 0$ such that\n\n- $x$ and $y$ have **strictly positive components**;\n- $xM = \\lambda\\, x$ (so $x$ is a left eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\\lambda$);\n- $My = \\lambda\\, y$ (so $y$ is a right eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\\lambda$).\n\nThe Loomis value $v$ of the pair $(I, M)$ (identity matrix vs. $M$)\nprovides $\\lambda = 1/v$.\n\n## Proof\n\nApply the general-$B$ Loomis theorem\n([[node:math.minimax.loomis_theorem]]) with $A := I$ (the $n \\times n$\nidentity matrix) and $B := M$. Since $M_{ij} > 0$, the hypothesis\n`IsPositive M` is satisfied. Loomis produces\n$x \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, $y \\in \\Delta(\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n)$, and\n$v \\in \\mathbb{R}$ such that\n\n- $(1)\\quad \\forall j,\\quad v \\cdot (xM)_j \\le x_j$  (from $xI \\ge v \\cdot xM$,\n  using $xI = x$);\n- $(2)\\quad \\forall i,\\quad y_i \\le v \\cdot (My)_i$  (from $Iy \\le v \\cdot My$,\n  using $Iy = y$).\n\n**Step 1: $v > 0$.** Pick $i_0$ with $y_{i_0} > 0$ (which exists because\n$\\sum y_i = 1$). Inequality (2) at $i_0$ gives\n$y_{i_0} \\le v \\cdot (My)_{i_0}$. Since $M > 0$ entrywise and $y \\ge 0$ has\n$y_{i_0} > 0$ (hence $\\sum y_j M_{i_0, j} > 0$), $(My)_{i_0} > 0$.\nTherefore $0 < y_{i_0} \\le v \\cdot (My)_{i_0}$ forces $v > 0$.\n\n**Step 2: $x$ and $y$ are strictly positive.** For every $j$,\n$(xM)_j = \\sum_i x_i M_{ij} > 0$ because $x \\in \\Delta$ has at least one\npositive entry and $M > 0$ entrywise. Combined with (1), $x_j \\ge v \\cdot\n(xM)_j > 0$. So $x_j > 0$ for all $j$. By the same argument applied to (2)\nand $y$, $(My)_i > 0$ and $y_i > 0$ for all $i$.\n\n**Step 3: Tight inner-product sandwich.** Compute\n$$\n  \\langle x, y\\rangle - v\\cdot \\langle xM, y\\rangle\n  = \\sum_j (x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j) \\cdot y_j \\ge 0\n$$\n(each summand is nonneg by (1) and $y_j \\ge 0$). And by\n$\\langle xM, y\\rangle = \\sum_j \\sum_i x_i M_{ij} y_j = \\langle x, My\\rangle$,\n$$\n  v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle - \\langle x, y\\rangle\n  = v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle - \\langle x, y\\rangle.\n$$\nWeighting (2) by $x \\ge 0$ and summing,\n$\\langle x, y\\rangle \\le v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle$. Therefore\n$$\n  \\langle x, y\\rangle \\;\\ge\\; v \\cdot \\langle xM, y\\rangle \\;=\\; v \\cdot \\langle x, My\\rangle \\;\\ge\\; \\langle x, y\\rangle,\n$$\nso both inequalities are tight.\n\n**Step 4: Componentwise equality.** From Step 3,\n$\\sum_j (x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j) \\cdot y_j = 0$. Each summand is nonneg (by\n(1)) and $y_j > 0$ strict (by Step 2). For the nonneg sum to vanish, each\nsummand must vanish, so $x_j - v \\cdot (xM)_j = 0$, i.e., $x_j = v \\cdot\n(xM)_j$ for every $j$. As a row-vector identity, $xM = (1/v) \\cdot x$.\n\nDually, $\\sum_i (v \\cdot (My)_i - y_i) \\cdot x_i = 0$ with each summand\nnonneg and $x_i > 0$ strict, so $y_i = v \\cdot (My)_i$, i.e.,\n$My = (1/v) \\cdot y$.\n\nSetting $\\lambda := 1/v > 0$, we have $xM = \\lambda \\cdot x$ (left\neigenvector) and $My = \\lambda \\cdot y$ (right eigenvector), both with\n$x, y$ strictly positive. $\\square$\n\n## Remarks\n\n- The argument is purely algebraic and works over $\\mathbb{R}$ (where\n  general-$B$ Loomis is formalised in `EconCSLib.StrategicGame.Loomis`).\n- Strict positivity of $x$ and $y$ is automatic given strict positivity of\n  $M$, **without** needing a separate \"irreducibility\" argument.\n- The same Loomis instance simultaneously produces the **left** eigenvector\n  $x$ and the **right** eigenvector $y$ at the same eigenvalue $\\lambda\n  = 1/v$. This eigenvalue is the **Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue** of $M$.\n\n## References\n\n- [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 1(2)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin,\n  *Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory*. Application of Loomis theorem\n  to positive matrices."
